events.title: The tech industry has a public image problem, Arianna Huffington says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has joined a group of “brilliantly intelligent” corporate leaders who “just lack wisdom,” Arianna Huffington said Monday. Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Huffington called the Nvidia scandal a teachable moment. “We see incredibly intelligent people all around who are incredibly deluded, incredibly destructive, and self-destructive,” said Huffington, the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavioral change tech company. “We need to invest in making humans better.” Speaking alongside Huffington on the panel, Willett Advisors CEO Steven Rattner said the idea of bringing Huang back as CEO is “ridiculous.” Some in the tech industry are calling for Huang to come back, though the Nvidia board reportedly isn’t considering it . Rattner said the comparison between Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to his post after an ouster in 2023, “doesn’t even come close to computing. You can’t bring Jensen back.” Both Huffington and Rattner agreed the tech industry needs to do a better job making a case for itself to a skeptical and anxious public. “The crisis that the tech industry faces is the fact that people hate the tech industry and they hate AI,” Rattner said, referencing the recent US midterm elections that were widely seen as a rebuke of tech. He said tech leaders face the same responsibility as politicians or public officials “to communicate and explain to people. And the tech industry just blew it.” Huffington said that people’s anxieties and fears stem from how life — not just the economy — is changing. “There was no effort to really tell a story that would touch people’s hearts and minds, that would explain how AI would benefit their lives.” Rattner, who led the Obama administration’s 2009 rescue of the auto industry, said the US government shouldn’t take stakes in AI companies. “We did not to have stakes in the auto companies. We had to have stakes in the auto companies because they needed our money and there was no other way to do it except putting equity in,” he said. “I think it’s a slippery slope and a murky bit of business when you start doing that.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Asia shares stumble on tech weakness ahead of Nvidia earnings
events.summary: Asian shares fell after the US stepped up efforts to curb China’s access to advanced AI chips. Asian shares fell as tech stocks weakened after the US tightened rules on China’s access to advanced AI chips. Nvidia’s earnings are now a key test for AI demand, export risks, and the effect of Jensen Huang’s departure. The market mood turned more negative on AI, with Goldman Sachs saying sentiment is "about as negative as we’ve seen in quite some time“. Copper also dropped, showing wider concern about the AI outlook. The US dollar stayed near its highest since April 2025 as traders bet on more Fed rate hikes. The yen remained near 160, while the Australian dollar was steady after RBA minutes backed a possible rate rise. SINGAPORE – Asian shares followed Wall Street lower on Nov 17, weighed down by weakness in technology companies after the US stepped up efforts to curb China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, escalating the race for technological dominance. South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI slid 2% shortly after the open, while Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.3%. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.63%. Overnight, Washington said it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia. The new rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to data centres like those in Thailand and Malaysia that Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models. The move came just days after Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned following reports of an affair with a woman who worked at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centres. It has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China. “We’ve seen the AI debate change pretty dramatically over the past month or so,” analysts at Goldman Sachs said. “Judging by conversations with clients last week, sentiment around the theme is about as negative as we’ve seen in quite some time, and we are seeing that pessimism reflected more clearly in positioning and valuations. “Equities can grind higher after the recent positioning reset, but like being more selective from here.” A key moment for markets on Nov 17 will be Nvidia’s earnings after the bell, with investors watching for signs of whether its debt-fuelled AI spending will continue into 2027 and how Huang’s departure could affect the company’s influence across the AI ecosystem. Torsten Sippel, UBS’s head of voice cash trading for the Americas, said: “With a roughly 7.8% implied move and a strong beat-and-raise already embedded, the bar looks increasingly tied to forward growth, AI ecosystem financing and export-control risk rather than the quarter alone.” US stock futures were steady in Asia, while EUROSTOXX 50 futures slid 0.66% and DAX futures lost 0.57%. Concerns about the AI outlook continued to roil the metals market, with copper prices falling to their lowest levels in more than four months overnight. Shares of Australian-listed miner Capstone Copper Corp tumbled nearly 6% to an eight-month low. The US dollar was perched near its highest point since April 2025 on Nov 17, helped by growing bets on more aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes as inflationary pressures in the world’s largest economy persist. Against a basket of currencies, the dollar was a touch higher at 103.61. Markets now see a slim chance of a 50-basis-point Fed hike in December, with recent hawkish remarks from policymakers reinforcing expectations of tighter monetary policy. “There will be another superfluity of Fed speakers this week, with almost zero probability for a turn back toward ‘dovishness’,” said Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group. “After all, nothing in the economic data since last week would warrant such a turn following the hawkish calls by the senior Fed staffers offered last week.” The strength in the dollar left the yen struggling near the key 160 level, leaving traders on alert for any intervention from the Japanese authorities to shore up the currency. The Australian dollar edged 0.02% higher to US$0.6739 (S$0.87) , little changed after minutes from the Reserve Bank of Australia’s November board meeting released on Nov 17 showed the majority of members judged that a hike in November was needed as inflation risks were still skewed to the upside and financial conditions might not be as restrictive as required. US crude futures were down 0.41% to US$85.37 a barrel, as signs of recovering oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz reinforced expectations of a supply surplus, though fresh tanker incidents underscored the risks to Middle East exports. REUTERS

events.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex CEO
events.summary: Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs , including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 4 days ago The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process". Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models. The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping , whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development. The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China. The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said. How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? Published 3 days ago How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 3 days ago The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad . The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore. Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent. But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors. Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns. But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

events.title: Medical students should ‘learn the hard way,’ AI startup CEO says
events.summary: The CEO of a major medical AI startup said on Monday that medical students should do paper exams and master the material, even if they also use AI. “The risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,” OpenEvidence CEO Daniel Nadler said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. He would advise students to “train classically, learn classically, learn the hard way, do paper exams, do paper tests, make sure you actually know it,” he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie. Nadler’s company aims to cover a niche within the medical business, synthesizing complex medical information with AI trained on millions of medical papers. The startup has hit a $15 billion valuation on the promise that AI can condense the complexities of the medical field into information palatable to physicians. The threat of cognitive offloading, or deskilling, is real. Early studies have found that deferring work to AI can weaken neural networks, leading to lower cognitive performance. Nadler says the concern is especially pressing for younger generations, those who have grown up in academic environments with access to AI. He noted that all of his company’s engineers use “dozens and dozens of AI buddies.” Benjamine Liu, the CEO of Formation Bio, which uses AI to accelerate drug development, also noted onstage on Monday that in the pharmaceutical industry “AI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams.” Noting that the GLP-1 drugmakers “did more revenue than OpenAI and Anthropic combined last year,” he told Sergie that “some people underestimate how big pharma is.” “We’re early innings in these things that help you live longer and healthier — and in an area that our industry sometimes misses,” Liu said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden
events.summary: The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces. Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi territorial gains in the country’s southwest. Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the operations, conducted as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 15 air strikes, 526 artillery attacks, 53 drone strikes and 67 rocket attacks. list 1 of 4 Houthis advance in Yemen as government forces move to defend Aden list 2 of 4 The Red Sea cannot be secured without restoring the Yemeni state list 3 of 4 Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis list 4 of 4 Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb In a statement on X, al-Nuzaili said the attacks had destroyed or damaged 71 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, as well as command-and-control centres, observation posts and fortifications. He said government forces, backed by the Popular Resistance, were continuing to confront Houthi movements in the provinces of Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf, while operations were also under way on southern fronts. The military said it would continue its offensive until it achieved its objectives, while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces, which have withdrawn from strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and are repositioning to defend Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry reported that the Houthis had cut off a key government supply route along the Red Sea coast, forcing troops to abandon several positions as concerns grew over a possible Houthi offensive towards Aden. The military escalation coincided with a political development, as Yemen’s parliament unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising their activities, financing and supply of weapons. According to the state-run Saba news agency, the bill provides for prosecuting those involved in violations attributed to the group, freezing and confiscating affiliated assets, and imposing tougher penalties for offences, including attacks on civilians, planting landmines and targeting international shipping. The legislation will now be submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, for enactment. The latest developments come six weeks after government forces launched “Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, seeking to regain territory controlled by the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa.

events.title: OpenAI CFO says latest funding round was unplanned, prompted by news report
events.summary: Anthropic’s IPO is “good for the ecosystem” and “good for us,” Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI said Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that the company was unconcerned with being second. Retail investors are ready for access to frontier models, not just hyperscalers which come with “pros and cons,” she said. After OpenAI closed a $122 billion fundraise in March this year, Friar said that the company was closing out a smaller fundraise at a $1.25 trillion valuation. But she suggested that the latest round was unplanned and “opportunistic,” and was prompted after a “very well- respected, well-known publication… announced we were fundraising, which we weren’t.” “That caused a whole bunch of inbounds from investors, and so we said, okay, if we can be super fast and in kind of a six week period, go in and out of the market, be done by the midterms, let’s do it because why not?” Friar said. Friar also said that OpenAI’s advertising model has been very successful, garnering more than $1 billion in revenue in under 200 days — a record for the company. Addressing the public resentment in the US over data centers, Friar said that for companies to regain trust, “you have to show up in those communities” and “be accountable.” She noted that in Georgia, where the company is hoping to build a 3.2 gigawatt data center, OpenAI has sponsored school lunches, a local park, and an AI summit for small businesses. But she acknowledged that OpenAI is still seeing the backlash to the AI buildout that was evident in the US midterm elections. “People are getting way too bombarded by kind of the rage element to not feel that there’s something they should be reacting to,” Friar said. “But when you go talk to people in real life, and show up for them, you have a very different conversation, and I believe a very different outcome.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: The question burning up Silicon Valley: Should Jensen Huang be brought back?
events.summary: Lisi Niesner/Reuters; BI Silicon Valley is divided over Jensen Huang, following his resignation over his infidelity. Some tech leaders, such as former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, want Huang back in charge at Nvidia. Huang is more controversial in the AI community, and with some women in tech. Where do you stand on Jensen ? That question is roiling Silicon Valley as it reckons with the tech titan's fall from grace. Venture capitalists, tech founders, and Nvidia employees are rallying to his defense — and some are pushing to bring him back. But others see the rush to forgive him as a familiar Silicon Valley reflex: excusing a powerful man's conduct while minimizing the damage to the people and institutions around him. The Nvidia cofounder and CEO resigned last week following reports that he had multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and a subordinate. To some, that's overshadowed by his achievements. "Jensen is one of the great builders of our time. We cannot starve the future of his innovation and industrial breakthroughs," reads a comment from Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick on Stand With Jensen , an online petition with more than 186,000 signatures. "To err is human," Kalanick — who said he is crowdsourcing "wild ideas" to get Huang reinstated — added. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider on Monday. Kalanick joins a growing chorus of people in tech defending Huang, including Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Nvidia executives, all of whom have signed the petition. For others, Huang's downfall was well-deserved given the ethical and national security implications of his conduct. Huang has long rankled some corners of tech because of his constant lobbying to sell powerful AI chips to China. One notable venture investor privately disagreed with Huang's friendly approach to China, given the chronic chip shortage in the US. The investor was frustrated that Huang had done little to address the industry's growing compute crisis, with some startups struggling to secure the resources needed to continue scaling. Nvidia had a lot of compute primarily reserved for research and development, the person said. Huang's business tactics are being scrutinized more than ever given his relationship with one of Nvidia's biggest customers, who some in the US government believe was part of an espionage scheme. That's without even mentioning his reported affair with an employee, executive Kimberly Powell, while he painted himself as a family man. One woman VC said Huang's infidelity and potential national security implications have barely surfaced in her Silicon Valley women's group chats. Some women investors, she said, have expressed that they feel sorry for Huang's wife. But, she said, "The general sentiment is, 'He's such a great leader, who cares what he does in his private life?'" Another woman VC said she and other women in venture were hardly surprised by the news, having grown accustomed to such conduct in the Valley. "Any time there is ego, power, and money, this is what happens," she said. "The tech right and founder class is rallying behind Jensen against all reason," Zvi Mowshowitz, who publishes an influential AI Substack, told Business Insider. At stake isn't just whether Huang gets back on top of Nvidia or not — an unlikely prospect — but the legacy of a key figure behind the AI boom. The godfather of the AI boom For years, Nvidia was best known for the graphics cards it sold to PC gamers. Huang was prescient in predicting that the high-powered chips would power the AI revolution. In a fateful moment, he personally delivered an Nvidia supercomputer, the DGX-1, to OpenAI's office in 2016. It was signed by then-OpenAI researcher Dario Amodei, who now runs Anthropic — which is set for a trillion-dollar blockbuster IPO this week. Huang's role in helping birth the thriving AI startup ecosystem is partly why so many venture capitalists are still Huang fans, industry insiders said. Nvidia's rise has been lucrative for them, too. Nvidia often invested in AI startups at high valuations, boosting the value of their portfolio companies by the billions. The funding also benefited Nvidia because it could be used to buy even more Nvidia chips. If the next Nvidia CEO takes a less aggressive investment approach, it could be the beginning of an AI industry correction, some investors cautioned. Tatiana Koffman, a GP at Moonwalker Capital, said Nvidia's board should finish its investigation, and that Huang should be reinstated if it finds no credible proof of a security breach. "We're painting Jensen with a moral brush for something leaders have done time and time again. He's one of the greatest engineers of the last two generations, and few people have done more for American innovation," she said. A divided AI community In the AI policy and safety world, Huang's push to sell Nvidia chips to China raised concerns about giving a US competitor powerful AI hardware. As worries about AI going rogue reached a fever pitch, Huang's staunch defense of the technology also raised eyebrows. "I would say Jensen's views have been at odds with a lot of the AI community," said former OpenAI employee Will Depue. Huang's brash statements annoyed some of the most senior people in the industry. After Huang said that Anthropic was trying to control AI through safety regulations, Amodei called Huang's claim "the most outrageous lie I've ever heard." Lior Susan, founder and CEO of VC firm Eclipse — which has invested in startups that Nvidia has also backed, like autonomous driving company Wayve — said the industry will endure beyond any single man. “Jensen was huge for the industry of AI and robotics, but the rise of robotics did not happen because of one person, and the rapid technological transformations we are witnessing will not slow down,” Susan told Business Insider. “There is a world after Jensen, and there is still so much progress to be made.” Have a tip? events.title: Irish court jails man for life over Dublin knife attack that sparked riots
events.summary: Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023. A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to life behind bars for the attempted murder of three children in Dublin on November 23, 2023, in an attack that triggered rioting and looting in the Irish capital. Riad Bouchaker, an Algerian national and Irish citizen, was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court in Dublin on Monday after being found guilty in July on eight charges arising from the knife attack outside a school nearly three years ago. list 1 of 3 Hundreds of anti-immigrant protesters burn vehicle, attack police in Dublin list 2 of 3 Irish police arrest 23 people in second night of anti-immigration unrest list 3 of 3 Ireland tightens immigration rules to check population growth His victims included a five-year-old girl, a six-year-old girl, a five-year-old boy and a woman in her mid-30s. The youngest girl was stabbed in the heart, resulting in severe disability after her brain was deprived of oxygen for 40 minutes following the attack. The girl, who is now eight, cannot speak and communicates only by blinking. She uses a wheelchair and is fed through a tube in her stomach because she is unable to swallow safely. Bouchaker was also found guilty of assaulting childcare worker Leanne Flynn, who suffered serious injuries as she tried to protect the children. Speaking outside the court, Garda Superintendent Colm Murphy, the senior investigating officer, acknowledged the actions of those who intervened, the Press Association reported. “I just want to take this opportunity to acknowledge the actions of those that immediately reacted to the situation as it unfolded, in particular to Leanne Flynn, who undoubtedly her actions on the day saved lives,” he said. Within hours of the attack, false information about the suspect’s identity spread online, fuelling anger among anti-immigration activists and far-right groups. The worst rioting seen in the Irish capital for decades erupted in the city centre as crowds clashed with police, set vehicles on fire and looted shops. The violence shocked the country and triggered days of debate over immigration, online misinformation and public order. Nearly 100 people were arrested, and more than 80 were charged with offences. Bouchaker had pleaded not guilty to three counts of attempted murder and three counts of assault causing harm. He also denied one count each of intentionally or recklessly causing serious harm and brandishing a dangerous weapon, a kitchen knife. Judge Tony Hunt told the jury that two years before the attack, Bouchaker had suffered from a benign brain tumour that required surgery. Hunt also said that due to interventions by bystanders immediately after the attack, Bouchaker suffered a head injury that required hospital treatment. He was found fit to stand trial, and “there is no suggestion that he was suffering mental disorder at the time of the incident”, the judge said. Evidence was heard from more than 80 witnesses, including eyewitnesses, emergency responders, police and forensic experts.

events.title: Trump cyber director: FAA, other outages not a cyberattack
events.summary: White House cyber director Sean Cairncross said Monday that a cyberattack was not behind the Trump administration’s nationwide ground stop of air traffic or other outages reported on Monday, attributing the problems to upgrades of old technology. “No, this is not any sort of coordinated, nefarious cyberattack from a malicious actor,” Cairncross told Semafor. “What we are seeing, and frankly I’d expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems.” He said the US government is tracking all recent software outages in the last few days. Cairncross told Semafor in an earlier interview that the Trump administration has no plans to release, or require compliance with, its voluntary framework for review of new advanced AI models — adding that frontier labs have cooperated. “The labs have been extremely good about being in communication with us and giving their new models for evaluation to be assessed,” Cairncross said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Putting a strict regulatory regime in place “isn’t going to work at the speed that we need,” he added. Cairncross said that the administration did not release the full text of the framework, which was set in motion by a June executive order, to enable a “frank conversation” with AI companies. He did say he believed the White House will soon make “it much more clear how this is working in practice.” The White House has taken a lighter-touch regulatory approach to the AI industry compared with Europe or the Biden administration; it has also taken steps to block states from stepping in. On the question of cybersecurity, Cairncross was bullish on AI’s defense capabilities, which were “unimaginable even a short time ago,” he said. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, appearing on stage with Cairncross, pointed out that Russia’s hacking capabilities have improved along with AI in the last year. Michal said the country’s ultra-wired government has been increasingly under attack, blaming private actors, as well as Russia, North Korea and Iran. When asked whether cyber attacks could be considered acts of war, Michal said he believes some could rise to the NATO definition of “attack” covered by the alliance’s Article 5. “It’s mainly a question about the consequences,” he said. — Laura McGann

events.title: Bloom Energy sees 'nothing but a huge opportunity' amid AI headwinds
events.summary: The CEO of fuel cell maker Bloom Energy said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he’s not worried about rising natural gas prices or political pushback to data centers, as the economy-wide scramble for electrons marks an “architectural shift” for the grid that will favor onsite power production. Bloom, whose gas-fueled mini power plants are used by data centers, hospitals, retailers, and other big power consumers, has faced some headwinds recently: Its share price is down 20% in the past month thanks in part to economy-wide jitters about the pace of the AI buildout, and its flagship data center project in New Mexico has been held up by permitting issues . Still, CEO KR Sridhar said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday, “I see nothing but a huge opportunity.” Power use continues to surge across the economy, and if the price of natural gas — Bloom’s crucial input — rises because of increased demand or trade disruptions like the war in Iran, “our value proposition gets even better,” Sridhar told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport, as the technology can operate more efficiently than conventional gas turbines. Bloom is on a steep growth trajectory: Its net profit hit $250 million in the third quarter, up from a $23 million loss in the same period last year. The company is expanding its manufacturing base, and targeting projects in the Middle East and elsewhere, Sridhar said. Though he is eyeing projects abroad, the company will continue to invest in the US. “We should not cede this opportunity to any other country, but from our perspective, we will be happy to sell our power to neighboring countries,” he said. “Nothing is NIMBY-proof,” he said, of backlash to data centers in the US. Still, “AI happens to be a catalyst pushing everything to the right very steeply.” — Tim McDonnell

events.title: I'm the CEO of Klook. I spend my free time scrolling through customer complaint emails — and Hyrox training.
events.summary: Klook This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Lin, the 40-year-old cofounder and CEO of travel platform Klook, who is based in Hong Kong. The following has been edited for length and clarity. In 2014, I left a stable banking job to cofound Klook, a platform where people can book travel experiences. I was 27, had no experience in tech or product, and bootstrapped the business with the savings my cofounders and I had built up. Now, the company is almost 2,000 employees-strong across 25 offices. As a 40-year-old CEO, I spend most of my time on work and fitness. Here's how I bring my A-game on busy work days. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. An 8 a.m. dopamine boost Fitness is really important to me. It's a dopamine boost in the morning; it works better than coffee. Each week, I go to the gym five to six times, mostly in the morning before work, around 7 or 8 a.m. That helps me wake up. I have a light meal, and then I hit the gym for some strength training. I participated in Hyrox in Bangkok a few weeks ago. Klook is Hyrox's travel partner across Asia, and I like to show support. After my morning workout, I have a light meal that helps me start the day feeling very energetic. I reach the office around 9 a.m., then AI automations help me kick off I have several AI projects in the works that help me keep on top of my game. I have an AI automation set up that sends me a weekly Monday morning summary email, giving me a quick refresh on what's happening each week. Other AI automations work like think tanks for me, acting like a consultant, industry expert, communication strategist, analyst, and so on, brainstorming with me. One thing I enjoy about AI is that it feels like you're working with many experts every day. When it comes to drafting emails, I feed AI the skeletons of the content and structure and let it write a draft for me because English isn't my first language, but the critical thinking and judgment have to come from me. I need to remind myself to be mindful because they all sound right, and I need to be the one deciding what information is really suitable for me. Before AI, when you worked on a project or task or sent emails, you would get a few hours or days of break before you got a response, or the next piece of information. Right now, that part is pretty much instant, so we end up basically working nonstop. I feel like I'm being mentally challenged more and more every day. I scroll through customer complaint emails — and enjoy reading them I'm copied on all Klook customer inquiry or complaint email chains, and I enjoy reading them every day as they come in. In the last 12 years, that's one habit I haven't changed. The emails often look like: "I booked a day for this activity, but can I change to another day? The system doesn't support it," or "I wrote my name wrong. Can I get entry into this venue without the right name? Can you change it?" It's something AI can help summarize, but I like to get them randomly every day, even on weekends, because you cannot predict when a customer will submit a complaint. It's like TikTok — swipe, swipe, you never know what's coming next. It's quite addictive. I don't respond directly to them — that would be a bit awkward — but scrolling through complaints gives me enough frequent data points and real case studies to get a sense of our customers' problems. When we actually conduct analyses or prioritize which problems to solve, I have enough tangible examples. I'm in the office until at least 7 p.m. Most days, I'm in the office until 7 to 8 p.m., although other days can get quite late. That's also why I try to protect my morning workouts to kick-start the day, as my evening workouts aren't guaranteed. As a CEO, my time is very fragmented : I spend half an hour on one task, 15 minutes on another, and an hour on something else. I get sucked into a lot of projects and meetings but often don't have time to sit and think about how they're linked to see if anything's missing. Every week, I block off two to three hours from my calendar for personal reflection. I'll use that to finish a project or task, or consolidate information. My second workout, followed by bed at 1 a.m. After work, about twice a week at night, I hit cardio. I do a light zone-two run . That means a four- to eight-kilometer run at a not-too-crazy pace, depending on how busy my day has been. This helps me build endurance and sleep better, although I'm already a pretty deep sleeper. The last hour or so of my day is my quiet time. This involves some email clean-up, prepping for the next day, and reading things outside technology and travel to give myself a different perspective. I'm normally asleep by 1 a.m. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Democrats dig in for grueling leadership fight
events.summary: The News Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., mimed a coin flip on Monday night when asked if he’ll support Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer over his insurgent opponent, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. It was a joke — but one that also showed how Democrats are wrestling with the decision. “Leave it to the Democrats. We flip nine seats and the person who actually helps put it together and do all that, all of a sudden there’s a revolt,” Hickenlooper said. He quickly made clear he didn’t mean that as a Schumer endorsement: “I haven’t picked a position. I do think it’s useful to go and look at: How could the caucus be better?” If the first few days of the leadership race are any indication, it’s going to be a very long two weeks for Senate Democrats. Several declined to comment on Monday night after days of celebrating their big election wins, with one senator saying Schumer’s challenge is all reporters are asking about. But that’s because it’s such an unusual moment for the party: The vast majority of sitting Senate Democrats have never experienced a contested leadership race for the top job. And Van Hollen’s rebel campaign isn’t following crushing losses — but instead a historic victory. “No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer. Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anyone else in the caucus and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge,” said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. “The voters are also demanding change.” Kaine, who will chair the Budget Committee next year, also declined to publicly come out for or against Schumer. Van Hollen’s pitch for change Van Hollen is not exactly an obvious change agent: He previously chaired the party’s campaign arms in both the House and Senate and has been in elected office since 1991. But he is seeking to draw bright contrasts with Schumer, pushing for a prohibition in the next spending bill on offensive weapons for the Iran war and highlighting Schumer’s opposition to the Obama era Iran nuclear deal. And while Schumer has several times the public support of Van Hollen, most of the incoming 56 Democratic Caucus members next year have declined to publicly endorse either one. Van Hollen said he knows “for a fact” some public reporting about senators’ support for Schumer is not true: “Some are voting for me and others are undecided on that list.” “People are still listening. They’re very interested in having a debate,” Van Hollen said on Monday evening. One of his supporters, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said he thinks the Maryland Democrat has a real chance to defeat Schumer. Most Democrats still see Schumer as the heavy favorite given the election results, however. Still, a number of other longtime Democratic senators who know Schumer well are keeping their powder dry. Asked about the race, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said only that he’s “laser-focused” on his agenda next year leading the Finance Committee and pushing Medicare for All, a billionaire’s income tax and repealing tariffs. “Everybody deserves to be heard and then our caucus will make a decision,” said Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., who will chair the Appropriations Committee. “I have not declared anything,” The next leader will decide when Murray or Wyden’s legislation will come to the Senate floor over the next two years — giving them incentive to stay neutral. And many Democrats are still digesting how to handle a secret ballot election that comes after the party’s most commanding win since Barack Obama became president. “Every candidate should make their pitch. And I’ll hear out any candidate for leader,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who obliterated his opponent in his reelection bid. “I’m grateful to everyone for their efforts, including Leader Schumer.” Schumer has served as Democratic leader for a decade, during which time the party’s activist base has soured on him; he’s also the architect of multiple Democratic majorities and made the most of a 50-seat Democratic majority during the first two years of Joe Biden’s presidency. But no leader hangs on forever: both former Democratic Leader Harry Reid and former Republican Leader Mitch McConnell lost a handful of votes in their last leadership races, before stepping down from the job. Schumer’s given no indication he would do that, but he’s up for reelection in 2028 and has a big decision ahead of him. And Van Hollen knows it. “That’s a decision for him,” he said of Schumer’s 2028 plans. Room for Disagreement Some Democrats said it’s healthy to have this debate after more than three decades without a real contested battle for the leadership race. “We’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats,” Kaine said. “We like democracy.” “It just comes with the territory,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. Burgess’s view Van Hollen’s leadership challenge to Schumer has made things very awkward for Senate Democrats. The contest will supercharge the debate about the party’s agenda in 2027 as well as how they handle the lame duck. And regardless of the outcome, it’ll have long term consequences for the usually tight-knit caucus. Notable Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer but not by an overwhelming margin , according to polling from Data for Progress.

events.title: Breaking: David Jones creditors owed almost half a billion dollars
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million, adminstrators confirm David Jones creditors have been updated. ( ABC News: Fletch Yeung ) David Jones is deeply in debt, with its liabilities revealed so far reaching almost half a billion dollars. The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. 6,242 employees: Estimated claims of $11 million including annual leave, long service leave and potential redundancy payments Secured creditors Hilco: Estimated claim of $155 million and ACP estimated claims of $80 million 940 unsecured creditors: Estimated claims of $180 million 802,319 gift cards: Estimated claims of $33 million The debts are being revealed right now at the first creditors' meeting for the embattled department store, which was placed into voluntary administration earlier this month. It has already been announced that about half of its stores nationally will close. Administrators are now trying to find a buyer for David Jones to keep the legacy brand alive. The business was placed in voluntary administration on November 5. The 188-year-old department store's collapse came after negotiations broke down with Scentre Group, the owner of key shopping centre chain Westfield, which confirmed David Jones was behind on its rent since September. Store suppliers have told ABC News they have been struggling to get invoices paid for months. Some have debts owed of more than $100,000. McGrath Nicol's role as voluntary administrator is now to tally the company's debts and possibly find a buyer to recoup cash for entities owed money, such as suppliers and landlords. The retailer's key secured lender, Hilco, will be first in line to claw back money. It has appointed a receiver, FTI Consulting, to David Jones and now controls its day-to-day operations. Last week, the receiver confirmed it was closing 19 of the retailer's 38 stores by the end of 2027 . The retailer, which has 38 stores nationally, was placed in voluntary administration less than a week ago. FTI has not confirmed how many jobs will go as a result of the store closures, with the main retail union estimating it could be 2,000. David Jones has more than 6,000 staff in total. McGrath Nicol has previously talked up interest in the business, with its partner describing interest from buyers as "extraordinary". Expressions of interest closed on Friday, with it expected to take at least a month for a buyer to be formally announced. events.title: AI leaders helping drive ‘unnaturally negative’ narrative, Palo Alto Networks CEO says
events.summary: The leaders of the world’s most advanced AI companies are helping drive an “unnaturally negative” narrative around the technology, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. In an interview with MIT Technology Review’s Mat Honan, Arora argued that the focus on AI’s risks is overshadowing its potential benefits of the fast-moving technology. “I find it strange that sometimes the leaders of frontier [large language models] want to come up here and talk about the dark side of AI. Every technology has a dark side,” Arora said at the event, adding that the negative narrative has “been driven by some of the people who should be espousing the benefits.” Arora described AI as a “transformational technology” with “the potential of uplifting a huge amount of humanity” and “democratiz[ing] intelligence.” “A villager sitting in India or anywhere in the world will have the ability to not just read 10 websites, but have them summarized and have the best intelligence available to them,” he said. Arora also challenged concerns that growing domestic resistance to data center construction could slow innovation, arguing that constraints on computing capacity would instead accelerate efforts to make the technology more efficient. “Scarcity breeds innovation,” Arora said. “If you say there’s only so many data centers that can be built, think about the amount of companies that are going to come back and say, wait, I’ve got this compression technology which makes tokens more efficient.” But Arora also acknowledged that AI’s growing capabilities are inevitably intensifying cybersecurity risks by making it easier to uncover vulnerabilities in software. “All the bad software we’ve written for the last 50 years as humans, is now going to be found out,” he said, warning that as more vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited, the higher the risk of systems being forced offline as companies scramble to patch longstanding weaknesses. “I don’t think there’s a panacea. I don’t think there’s a quick solve. I just think we’re gonna power through all of these and grind ourselves through them,” he said. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
events.summary: Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said there had been ‘no change in Russia’s position’ as Russia and Ukraine strike major infrastructure. Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week. list 1 of 4 Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia? list 2 of 4 Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker list 3 of 4 How Russia is preparing Iran for the next escalation list 4 of 4 Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia? “Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address. He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday. Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions. Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements. US envoy reports progress, warns of difficult choices Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe. “Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X. He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals. The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi , where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war. Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion. Europe prepares to join, Moscow withholds agreement Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators. Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added. European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow. Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.” Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”. “We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said. Russia rules out a temporary respite Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces. He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time. Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war. “I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.” The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

events.title: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
events.summary: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh convened a San Francisco conference examining AI's effects on productivity, employment and the economy. He raised questions about whether AI could produce job displacement and lower service prices. Technology executives and economists offered differing perspectives on the speed of AI adoption. The findings could eventually inform Fed policy, although Warsh offered no immediate conclusions about interest rates. Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact. "We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear. The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses , but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed. With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy. Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI. Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend. It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island. Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said. Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear. The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his longstanding critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs. Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking. The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event. Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said. "To the extent our economy is a free-market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about." Warsh returned repeatedly to one scenario for the economy that draws on past experience. The so-called China shock unfolded after that country joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and moved heavily into low-cost manufacturing. Americans saw prices on clothing and furniture drop rapidly, for instance, but at the cost of severe job losses. One widely cited estimate found the U.S. lost a million manufacturing jobs and 2.4 million jobs overall in the years that followed. Warsh suggested to one of the panelists that the widespread adoption of AI might produce its own version of the China shock, this time focused on service workers. "I don't want to hold this too tightly," Warsh said. "But if in some ways over the last generation or generation and a half, the China shock, for lack of a better word, lowered prices of goods in the United States, the way that I heard you talking about the philosophy of this new technology is it might do something for services.

events.title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
events.summary: One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership. Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership. The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios. Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes , a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic. Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision. Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings. Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals. The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress. One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference. Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes. "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal. Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October. A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals. The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in. But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation. "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said. What they're saying: Freedom Caucus members oppose Main Street's proposal. "It's not going to happen," outgoing HFC Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Axios. "They introduce it every year." "That's inappropriate," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga) told Axios of Flood's original proposal. Clyde also told Axios he doesn't think the proposal will get anywhere, saying that he thinks enough feel the same as he does to kill it. Reality check: With Republicans headed into one of the smallest minorities in recent history, the changes would have little effect in the upcoming Congress. But members want to settle the conference's accountability rules now, so when they regain the majority, the same divisions won't threaten to derail their agenda. "This is us simply setting the table so that when we do return to the majority, we can do so built on a foundation that addresses some of the hiccups we experienced during the 119th Congress," Flood told Axios. "We're in the minority now, this is the time to set the rules. This is the time to get this thing right," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. "The goal is to take away the ability of an extremely small group to extort leadership," the member added. "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.

events.title: Singapore’s key exports surge 79.8% in October, driven by strong non-electronics shipments
events.summary: The growth in non-electronic NODX was driven by structures of ships and boats, pharmaceuticals and specialised machinery. Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports rose 79.8% in October, far above the 37.7% forecast, led by strong non-electronics shipments, said Enterprise Singapore. Non-electronics exports jumped 81.9%, driven by ships and boats structures, pharmaceuticals up 253.1%, and specialised machinery up 57.3%. Electronics rose 73.9% on AI demand, while exports to the US, China and Taiwan grew strongly; India, Indonesia and Thailand saw declines. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports (NODX) jumped in October, extending from September’s increase, mainly driven by strong non-electronics shipments , while electronics continued to rise amid sustained AI-driven demand. Non-oil domestic exports (NODX) expanded 79.8% from a year ago, following September’s rise of 68.3%, led by non-electronics, data from Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) on Nov 17 showed. The latest figure beat the 37.7% forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll. Non-electronics shipments surged 81.9% year on year in October, building on the previous month’s 54.1% increase. The growth in non-electronic NODX was driven by structures of ships and boats, pharmaceuticals, which expanded 253.1%, as well as specialised machinery, which rose 57.3%. The year-on-year growth for “lumpy exports” of structures of ships and boats was not cited, as the exceptionally high percentage increase reflects a low base effect in the same period in 2025. Surging 73.9% in October following a 107.6% rise the previous month, electronic product shipments continued to climb on the back of robust AI demand. Growth was driven by a 189.6% jump in disk media products, while shipments for personal computers grew 81% and 53.1% for integrated circuits, or chips. NODX to the United States, China and Taiwan expanded in October, while NODX to India, Indonesia and Thailand contracted. NODX to Taiwan expanded 79.3%, extending September’s 96.9% rise, driven by a 149% jump in electronic NODX. NODX to India fell 35.8% in October, following a 5.7% decline in September, dragged down by a 51.9% decline in non-electronic shipments. Key exports to the US, Singapore’s single-largest export market, expanded 214.6%, while those to China increased 144.9%.

events.title: UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
events.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism. During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked. “I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.” The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”. Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected. The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure. The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said. Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016. “Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.” Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”. Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers. Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

events.title: AI agents still act like ‘Day 1 employees,’ Glean CEO says
events.summary: AI agents are nowhere near having the “context” to outperform skilled humans, Glean CEO Arvind Jain said Monday. “When you deploy AI agents, and you actually point them to the right data and knowledge that they need to do their work, they still come and act more like Day 1 employees,” Jain told the editor-in-chief of The Verge, Nilay Patel, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “That’s the gap that needs to close before we can come and talk about fancy things like job elimination.” Jain, who co-founded the AI platform Glean in 2019, said “nobody’s anywhere close” to building AI systems capable of replacing experienced workers. Glean, he said, is meant to bring “tacit knowledge” and experience with a company to its internal AI systems, to combat that “Day 1 employee” problem. Despite AI’s limitations, Jain also said companies are under “enormous pressure” to adopt it. That may be one reason, he said, for recent high-level technological disruptions, like the outages this week reported by banks and airlines. “Sometimes businesses didn’t get time to actually set the right foundation” before rolling out AI tools, Jain said. Jain also predicted a future in which around 90% of work can be done by open-source and non-frontier AI models, though the remaining “10% of the tasks will actually still consume the majority of your AI spend.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
events.summary: Ethiopia’s unresolved Oromia-Somali border dispute fuels renewed violence, displacing thousands. Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as efforts to resolve a longstanding territorial dispute have yet to produce a lasting settlement. The violence, which escalated in the border town of Moyale in October, has spread to surrounding areas, including the neighbouring districts of Arero and Wachile, leaving communities insecure and uncertain when normal life will resume. The disruption has affected livelihoods across several parts of the zone, particularly the livestock trade – a major source of income for rural communities. Residents have reported interruptions to business activities and transport services. A resident of Moyale town, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that people remained fearful as tensions persisted between forces affiliated with the two regional administrations. The resident said gunfire, especially at night, had heightened personal safety concerns, while violence had restricted movement around the town and made routine activities increasingly difficult. Businesses, people raising livestock and transport operators had also been affected, leaving residents uncertain about when the situation would return to normal. A territorial dispute reignites violence According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), the latest escalation began on October 18, when Somali regional police clashed with ethnic Oromo militia members following the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of its flag in a disputed locality of Moyale. The conflict monitor’s East Africa senior analyst, Jalale Getachew Birru, reported that a 13-year-old Oromo girl was killed during the confrontation. However, accounts of how she died differ: some people said she was caught in crossfire, while others claimed she was killed after trying to remove the flag. Members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened and stopped the initial fighting, according to ACLED. The following day, Oromo residents staged a demonstration against the office opening and the girl’s death, blocking the main road and forcing businesses to close. Elders and security officials from both sides later agreed to remove the Somali regional flag and suspend the office’s opening. However, the agreement did not prevent further confrontations. ACLED reported that Somali residents also demonstrated against the arrangement on October 20, closing the main road and disrupting transport services. Fighting escalated again on October 22, when Somali regional police clashed with Oromia regional police and Oromo militia members in several locations in Moyale. ACLED also reported clashes involving Oromo and Somali militias in parts of Arero and Wachile districts. The violence is rooted in longstanding disagreements over administrative boundaries, political representation and access to land and natural resources. These disputes have repeatedly fuelled tensions between Borana Oromo and Somali communities along the regional border. Federal government under pressure to intervene A security official familiar with the situation in Moyale told Al Jazeera that clashes were continuing and that attempts to broker an agreement between representatives of the Oromia and Somali regional administrations had failed. He said resolving the crisis required direct and immediate involvement by the federal government. The federal government’s role has consequently become a central question in efforts to contain the violence. Although members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened during the initial October 18 confrontation, ACLED documented further clashes involving regional police and militia members from October 22 onwards. The crisis has also drawn attention beyond Ethiopia’s borders. On November 9, Kenya’s Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said he had spoken with his Ethiopian counterpart and urged the government in Addis Ababa to help restore stability so that people who had fled into Kenya could return home. Reporting by Kenya’s The Star newspaper said Mudavadi put the number of Ethiopians who had crossed into Kenya at approximately 40,000 at the time. He said the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it would work towards restoring normality. Unresolved boundaries and political tensions Cameron Hudson, a political and security analyst and former director for African affairs at the US National Security Council, said the crisis reflected wider challenges facing Ethiopia’s federal system and its management of regional disputes. Hudson said federal forces were already preoccupied with security challenges elsewhere in the country.

events.title: Customers report service outages at major US banks
events.summary: Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services. Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related". Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening. The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage , a network failure that grounded all US flights , and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage". Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website. Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News. A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details. Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage Published 2 days ago Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech Published 3 days ago Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds". The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US. The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank. Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported. Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions. US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent. Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments. Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted. As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages. Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights". That issue resolved within a few hours. The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity. The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines. The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US. On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues. The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.
