events.title: Replit CEO calls Huang’s ouster ‘attack’ on open models
events.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad called Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia’s CEO “an attack on open models” at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. “Jensen is the premier champion of open models,” Masad told Semafor’s Rohan Goswami. “If it wasn’t for Jensen, there wouldn’t be a lot of funding going into US open model companies like Reflection and others.” Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Masad, who founded Replit, an AI app and website-building company, has championed the push to reinstate Huang. When a friend told him about a petition on Replit calling for the fallen CEO’s return, “I literally jumped in and did tech support for them,” Masad said. Huang has been “a great voice on pushing back on the narrative that we need to lock down AI, that the only safe AI is a closed AI,” Masad said. He added that not having Huang at Nvidia would be a “huge loss” and “potentially bring about a world where there’s only the frontier model labs that exist.” Software engineering careers ‘an accident of history’ When asked about the future of tech jobs, Masad said on Monday, “The modern career of software engineer is a bit of an accident of history.” Now, many of his customers have zero software engineers on staff. “I used to get attacked a lot for saying that, but now everyone agrees with me,” Masad said. Ben Lamm, the CEO of the biotech and genetic engineering de-extinction company Colossal Biosciences, agreed, saying, “We’re doing what we used to do with 80 engineers with, like, five.” And Edwin Chen, the founder and CEO of AI-training platform Surge AI, said that his headcount will likely remain stable. “If you look at the latest models, they’re not just writing code anymore. They’re often coming with ideas on their own,” Chen said. “They’re helping our engineers understand certain kinds of security risks or architectural trade-offs.” All this, Chen said, means he doesn’t see a need to hire product managers or expand headcount dramatically. Masad said he still foresees hiring entry-level employees, in part because in the agentic era, people’s jobs are changing every three to six months. “You need people who are willing to continue relearning their job,” he said. “And I think, you know, just because of brain plasticity, younger people are actually pretty good at that.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Chalmers says spending will be cut in mid-year update 'but not too much'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chalmers says mid-year budget update will include 'enough' spending cuts Jim Chalmers will deliver the mid-year budget update in December. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Jim Chalmers says the mid-year budget update will include a "substantial" package of cuts. The treasurer also says the government is working on plans to cut government regulation. The mid-year budget update will be delivered in December. A "substantial" package of cuts to government spending will be revealed in next month's mid-year budget update, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed. The cuts have been foreshadowed for several weeks, but without any sense of their magnitude. In a speech to an ASIC forum this morning, Mr Chalmers said the mid-year update would have cuts as its main focus. "It will cut enough, but not too much. It will strike some fine balances," he said. The government has sustained criticism over the elevated level of government spending, which the opposition and some economists have said is worsening inflation and driving interest rates higher. Mr Chalmers has consistently rejected that characterisation, but today said the cuts were motivated by economic conditions. "We take seriously and embrace our responsibilities in the fight against inflation," he said. No details of individual cuts have been confirmed, but Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said earlier this month the public service would be one target of "belt tightening", and there have been calls to consider means testing for subsidies for electric vehicles and home batteries. Simpler building code among red tape measures Mr Chalmers also announced he would write to businesses and investors to gather ideas for regulations that could be cut to simplify compliance for businesses. He last wrote to government regulators on this matter last year, and told the ASIC forum the process had led to 400 ideas for how red tape could be cut, 140 of which had already been enacted and 200 of which were underway. The ministers who have managed to save money As the government pursues savings "across the board" ahead of the mid-year budget update, an ABC analysis shows only a handful of ministers have managed net savings so far this year. "These regulatory reforms span everything from telecommunications to energy to tax, and lots in between ... cumulatively, these changes will make a real difference," he said. The Business Council of Australia has been campaigning for a 25 per cent cut to the cost of complying with government regulation, which it said cost business billions each year. The federal opposition has taken up the 25 per cent target. While avoiding a specific target of its own, the government has promised streamlining in several areas. The ABC understands one such area to be featured in the mid-year budget will be the construction code, which has been subject to consultation with the industry. The government opposed the Liberals' proposal to slash the building code from about 2,000 pages to fewer than 100, but has promised to find other ways to streamline it. Another focus revealed by Mr Chalmers was on reducing tax compliance costs. He said he would consult on a "pre-filling" option for sole traders paying tax and scrapping complex assessments of fringe benefits below $300. He said these two measures could save businesses $52 million per year. Mr Chalmers also said the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) had paused sending controversial letters to business about their payment of super to employees. The Coalition had accused the ATO of "targeting" small businesses with the automated compliance letters, which alerted businesses when their payroll data did not match their employees' reported super contributions. In a statement yesterday, the ATO said the letters were not debt notices, but were designed to "nudge" businesses to look into possible discrepancies ahead of time, adding that super underpayment was a "serious problem". Mr Chalmers said it was a matter for the ATO, but that the government had reminded the agency that its "engagement with businesses needs to be respectful [and] constructive". "Now as I understand it, the ATO has now paused those letters as they improve those processes … The ATO's got a difficult and important job to do, we respect that … Part of that means having another look at these letters that have gone out," he said.

events.title: US Pentagon rejects allegations linking deputy to a Goldman Sachs banker
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? The Department of Defense has defended Steve Feinberg amid claims that he encouraged defence contractors to use a specific banker. The Pentagon has denied reports that Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg pushed defence contractors to work with a specific Goldman Sachs banker with whom he had longstanding ties. In a statement sent to Al Jazeera on Monday, the Pentagon said the allegations were “baseless”. list 1 of 4 US agencies unite to combat rogue drone threats nationwide list 2 of 4 House Republicans block Pete Hegseth impeachment effort list 3 of 4 USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume? list 4 of 4 US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine “Any claim that the Deputy directed companies to use Goldman Sachs is categorically false. He worked with financial firms across the industry throughout his entire career,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in the statement. “He has no favorites, and neither does the Department of War.” The publication Bloomberg first reported the allegations, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter. According to Bloomberg’s report, Feinberg guided defence contractors like Lockheed Martin and RTX towards working with Goldman Sachs banker Jim Donovan during their negotiations with the Pentagon. Donovan and Feinberg reportedly knew each other. Bloomberg said Donovan has previously worked for the investment firm Feinberg co-founded, Cerberus Capital Management, which claims to oversee $70bn in assets. Bloomberg’s report has raised concerns about a conflict of interest during the lucrative Pentagon negotiations. Defence contracts are often million, if not billion, dollar deals. Guiding a company that is competing for a contract to work with a specific banker could be seen as a way of rigging the negotiations. It would also put the banker in line to potentially receive large commissions from the contracts in question. According to Bloomberg, both RTX and Lockheed Martin hired Donovan after Feinberg’s suggestion. The Pentagon, however, has accused Bloomberg of seeking to lend credibility to unsubstantiated allegations. “Despite the Department’s categorical denial, Bloomberg appears more interested in advancing a baseless smear than establishing the facts. Your sources are playing you, and Bloomberg should know better,” Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Jacob Bliss told Al Jazeera. “The Deputy is a man of honor and integrity. Unfortunately, some would rather see him fail than succeed.” Feinberg was nominated by President Donald Trump for his position in one of the Pentagon’s top posts. The Senate confirmed him in a vote of 59 to 40, and he was sworn in as the 36th deputy defense secretary on March 17, 2025, according to the Pentagon. Lockheed Martin and RTX, both aerospace and defence companies, have longstanding ties to the Pentagon. In August, for instance, the Department of Defense announced a multibillion-dollar deal with Lockheed Martin and another defence giant Northrop Grumman to boost production of parts for the Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD missile interceptor systems. According to Bloomberg’s reporting, Donovan, the banker, was a part of several deals in recent months involving Lockheed Martin and RTX. They include a $59bn contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot missiles and two missile contracts worth approximately $45bn with RTX. It is unclear who the anonymous sources for Bloomberg’s story might be. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has opened multiple investigations into leaks of sensitive information and taken steps to limit journalists’ access to military officials and other Pentagon resources.

events.title: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access
events.summary: President Donald Trump's investment accounts have bought and sold Nvidia stock at least 103 times since he returned to the White House, with transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, a CNBC analysis found. Among the trades was a sale of as much as $1 million on May 18, five days after Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly briefed Trump on Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Trump denies being briefed. The White House says independent advisors manage Trump's investments without his input. His financial disclosures offer no evidence that Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence. President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia . The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang , became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier. Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August. By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear. Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight. Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18 , the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported . Trump on Monday denied being briefed . Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy. The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz . Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis. Trump bought up to $25 million in Meta and millions in SpaceX debt in August Trump’s municipal bond portfolio reaches as much as $1 billion as policy overlaps mount Trump disclosure shows 1,100 July trades, Microsoft and Amazon sales Trump’s oil investments have gained millions during Iran war as his accounts keep trading Trump’s foreign licensing business booms to $59.5 million as Gulf developers pay JPMorgan, Schwab and UBS manage millions in Trump’s $858 million investment portfolio Trump bought as much as $5 million in Axon stock before ICE sought $220 million Taser deal Company that bet big on Trump-backed crypto says its fortunes have improved Trump family got about $500M from crypto venture — but investors saw steep losses Trump Jr. calls banking a 'Ponzi scheme' that forced family to create crypto business The Trump family crypto empire looks to Asia: Eric Trump talks Bitcoin in Hong Kong Trump family says U.S. dollar needs an upgrade and they are the ones to do it A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence. Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war . "Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses . Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance. Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street.

events.title: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
events.summary: Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn. Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade. His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults. But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state". Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations. Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis. The review says that, in 2024/25, for every £1 spent helping young people into work or education, £25 was spent on youth benefits. By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be £2 on benefits for every £1 on work support. In order to make change of this scale over the next decade, the review will call for: A new target of 90% of children to be school-ready with basic life skills by five years old (this figure is now 68% in England, with a current government target of reaching 75% by 2028) More emphasis on work skills in the school curriculum Instant access to mental health support without diagnosis A doubling of the number of young apprentices Incentives for employers, such as lowering the National Insurance rate for young workers At the heart of the changes recommended by Milburn would be a legal entitlement to support, provided through a new "Youth Opportunity Service" in England. The service would put a young person in touch with a named adviser to help to secure them an apprenticeship, college place, supported employment or a job within four months. To pay for these reforms, young adults would no longer be eligible for the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work, or Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which helps with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability. The review's key welfare measures, some of which have already been announced , suggest replacing these benefits for under-25s with a new Youth Allowance at the current base rate of Universal Credit for young people, and a new Additional Cost Allowance to replace Pip. The minority of young people who are unable to ever work would be supported through a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance. Kat, 21, from Devon, currently gets Universal Credit with the health top-up, so is potentially at risk of receiving a much lower level of benefits under the proposed new system. She has fluctuating physical and mental health problems, including occasional seizures caused by functional neurological disorder, which recently left her needing crutches. Kat says her health issues limit her ability to find work Kat says she "really wants to work", but says she has to rely on welfare support as she has been unable to find a job where she can be employed in a "safe way" because of her health. Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, says many young people are desperate for opportunity, but that many get knocked back repeatedly. Josh, 19, has spent three years looking for work while on Universal Credit with the support of youth employment charity Spear. Although they help him with applications to prospective employers, Josh says "none of them are getting back, and if they do they say you've not got the spot". Grace Coates, who manages Spear St Helens, says she wants to see "more openness to employing people with limited experience". Josh has been looking for work for three years Milburn's review will suggest gradually lowering the rate of National Insurance which employers pay for young adult employees to make hiring and keeping them more attractive. The existing Youth Jobs Grant, where employers receive £3,000 for hiring a young person who has been looking for work for six months, would be retained under the recommendations. So would the existing Jobs Guarantee, in which the government underwrites the cost of a paid six-month job. The government has recently announced that young adults will be eligible for the guarantee after 12 months of being on Universal Credit and looking for work, rather than the current 18 months. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said reforms will have a greater chance of success if support for young people is balanced with incentives for businesses to hire them.

events.title: Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people
events.summary: Report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis calls for welfare, education, health and employment policy shake-up Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits. In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis , Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million. He said ministers had a choice to either carry on down a path of state and market failure or adopt a 10-year plan with an ambition to eradicate long-term youth unemployment. Publishing a blueprint for change in a highly anticipated review, the report calls on the government to launch a sweeping shake-up of welfare, education, health and employment policy with the aim to ensure every young person has the chance to earn or learn. If adopted by the government, Britain could halve the number of young people neither earning nor learning, helping about 600,000 more under-25s into education, employment or training each year by 2036, according to the review. Milburn’s report comes as Britain’s young bear the brunt of rising joblessness as employers freeze their hiring plans amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Coupled with the legacies of the Covid pandemic and austerity, and a rise in mental ill-health and as AI upends the jobs market, the UK’s Neet rate has reached 13% – the highest level since 2014. Milburn said that rate could be lowered to 5% by 2036. However, central to his plan would be a controversial shake-up of Britain’s benefits system to approach the under-25s as wholly separate from the working-age population at large. Urging the prime minister not to shy away from welfare reform – after Keir Starmer was forced into a humiliating climbdown over a plan to cut disability benefits amid pressure from Labour MPs – Milburn warned the future of the next generation depended on the government making changes. At a press conference in London on Tuesday to mark the launch of his report, he is expected to say: “It is time for a new settlement that makes work not welfare the future for the next generation.” But Milburn also warned that crude benefit cuts would not work, arguing that changes would need upfront investment. Burnham pledged on Sunday to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment. Writing in the Guardian , he promised that changes to benefits he was considering in response to Milburn’s review would only be accompanied by a “root and branch rethink” of youth support. At the heart of Milburn’s blueprint would be the creation of an entirely new welfare system for young people, involving tougher eligibility criteria than for older claimants. In exchange, however, there would be a drastic step-change in support to help young people find work. This would involve some young people with health conditions and disabilities losing access to current benefits, although they would be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment. Those with the most profound health conditions who would be unable ever to work would still get more generous financial support. To counterbalance the changes, Milburn said upfront investment to create a new “youth opportunity service” in England should be created to deliver a drastic boost in support for young people. Accountable to regional mayors and local leaders, the service would combine employment, careers, health and practical support. Young people would receive a personalised participation plan and a named adviser, with access to support guaranteed by two new legal guarantees. While education, skills and health policies are devolved in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, Milburn will say at the report launch that the underlying principles in his report should also apply. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Analysis in Milburn’s report shows that for every £1 spent on helping young people into work or education, the state spent £25 on youth benefits last year. Under his proposals that figure would be rebalanced to £2 to £1, bringing Britain closer into line with the ratios in other European countries. The changes will, however, raise fears among some Labour MPs as well as charities and campaigners that slashing youth benefits could result in plunging more young people into poverty, particularly for those who require additional financial support to manage health conditions. As Milburn prepared to launch his review, backbenchers from the left of the party – including Nadia Whittome, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, John McDonnell, Apsana Begum, Clive Lewis and Richard Burgon – warned in a letter that an entire generation risked becoming disconnected from work and wider society.

events.title: U.S. crude oil declines to $85 a barrel on recovering Middle East exports
events.summary: Oil prices are falling Monday as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz recover and tensions between Iran and the U.S remain at a stalemate. Brent crude fell 3.55% to $92.44 per barrel Monday while West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled down 3.58% to $85.39 a barrel. The International Energy Agency said on Friday it expects global supply to exceed 1.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter of 2026, reversing its earlier forecast for a deficit as Middle East exports recover faster than global demand and even as shipping attacks continue. Meanwhile, Russia's crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000 barrel-a-day surge, according to the IEA. Goldman Sachs said in a Sunday note it expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and fall to $78 by December 2027 as the market returns to a surplus. The bank believes Middle East supply to rise above its 2025 average as producers use ship-to-ship transfers and add pipeline capacity.

events.title: Newly reelected Sen. John Hickenlooper sketches Democrats’ AI line: race China, but regulate frontier models like nuclear weapons and airplanes
events.summary: Sen. John Hickenlooper wants American AI to win in the international AI arms race. He just isn’t sure it needs to be able to rebuild itself without limits. “Maybe we don’t need recursive learning, unlimited,” the Colorado Democrat told Fortune’s Diane Brady on Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, where he teleconferenced in. He described machines “reinventing themselves sometimes outside the fence line of their domain that they’re supposed to stay in.” “That should cause real concern,” Hickenlooper said. Hickenlooper, a member of the Senate Commerce Committee, won his second and last term two weeks ago, leading Republican state Sen. Mark Baisley 61% to 35% on election night. While his seat was expected to go his way, eight seats won Democrats control of the Senate in last Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which data centers and the AI buildout was one of the most referenced issues that influenced voters’ decisions. His comments come as the buildout continues and as AI companies use their models to speed up their research. In September, more than 20 researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, published a paper warning that automating AI research could set off an “intelligence explosion.” Alan Chan, one of its lead coauthors, said that valid safety mechanisms aren’t in place. Hickenlooper said he isn’t against the labs moving fast. “They are pushing as fast as they can. I understand that, and that’s good,” he said, referencing the international rivalry. “We want to make sure that our frontier AI is the best in the world because it has the potential to dominate the globe.” He said there are still ways to make sure the U.S. does that safely: for example, there are rules already on the books for other technologies. “We regulate nuclear weapons. We have regulations before an airplane can go into service,” he said. “We need to look at what are some of the fundamental safeguards and guardrails that we should put in place.” A global arms race Brady asked about Nvidia and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The Senate Banking Committee has asked Huang and Lutnick to testify next month. While Hickenlooper said his questions about the case were “not that pressing,” Hickenlooper, who is not part of the committee, said he wants to know the basics first. “What is our relationship to China, and how secure do we feel in sharing our technology with them at any level?” he said. “Because I don’t feel comfortable with that.” Hickenlooper backs the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to help curb data centers. The permitting bill would speed approvals for energy projects and require data centers to pay for the grid upgrades built to serve them. The Senate voted 73-25 last week to begin debate on it, and President Donald Trump endorsed it. Hickenlooper said data centers should first guarantee there will be no loud noises or hazards and nuisances in communities. Under the bipartisan bill, the cost of new power lines and substations “will be completely borne by the data center.” He called the bill a compromise. Trump “doesn’t like wind. He doesn’t like solar,” Hickenlooper said, but the bill would put both on equal footing with natural gas. While the bill has limitations, he said, what it looks like now is one that is “much improved” from where it started. “I wish we could go further.” Hickenlooper read the midterm results as a test rather than a win for his party to bank. “It’s not a mandate,” he said. “I think it’s more of a to-do list, almost an audition.” Democrats, he said, have to show they can lower costs and add jobs. “When you’re trying to get a deal done, you’ve got to figure out who you’re negotiating with,” he said. “You got to see what’s in it for them and find a way that you can both benefit from the final agreement.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: JPMorgan Chase says temporary software bug is affecting consumer banking
events.summary: JPMorgan Chase on Monday said a "technical issue" was making some transactions take longer than usual for customers. A spokesperson for JPMorgan said the issue was not cyber-related and that it was not systemic. CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved. JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday. The bank said a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds. "There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson said. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." Still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Users reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET. A representative for U.S. Bank said that company was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan. The outage reports come days after separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers . — CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.

events.title: ‘Work on what people think is important.’ U.S. Steel’s CEO has advice for Democrats after the midterms: Focus on affordability, not court fights
events.summary: U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt wants to see Democrats use their congressional sweep to focus on what voters have been asking for: improving the cost of living and affordability, not spending the next two years fighting Trump in court. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum , Burritt said Democrats have an opportunity to respond to the economic concerns that have plagued the American electorate and drove voters to the polls, warning that a focus on political battles would undermine the party’s chances in the next election. He added that Democrats could find themselves in a difficult political position in the 2028 elections if they fail to address voters’ priorities. The midterm results shouldn’t be interpreted as an endorsement of the Democratic Party, but instead a warning for both parties that voters are dissatisfied, he said in a panel discussion with Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt and Fortune Executive Editor Lee Clifford. “They were sending a message to everybody: work on what people think is important. Let’s make things affordable,” Burritt said. Voters want affordability The Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections, a sweeping reversal of the political fortunes for Republicans and a rebuke to President Donald Trump. Democratic candidates repeatedly made affordability the centerpiece of their campaigns, arguing for cheaper groceries, healthcare, housing and everyday necessities. Housing and food accounted for 46.9% of average expenditures in 2025 as housing expenditures climbed 5.8% and food spending increased 4.6%, according to the Census Bureau’s Consumer Expenditure Survey released in October. A CBS News analysis of the election found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a major or crucial factor in their congressional vote. But Trump was also a factor as well, with many voters treating the election as a referendum on him. According to the Associated Press’s Voter Poll, 39% to 60% of voters across age demographics used their vote to “show opposition” to Trump—compared to only 7% to 22% voting to show support. The poll also showed that 33% of the electorate viewed “the state of democracy” as its most important issue. A collision course with Trump The Democratic Party has signaled plans to investigate a range of issues, including Trump’s business interests, his administration’s immigration policies, the Justice Department’s actions, and the administration’s handling of the war in Iran. Congressional committees will gain the ability to issue subpoenas, compel testimony and demand documents once the new Congress convenes in January. But for Burritt, the danger is that Democrats will mistake their electoral victory for a mandate to pursue a political agenda rather than address the economic concerns that helped deliver their majority. Stitt offered a similar warning, saying Republicans had taken “a beating” in the midterms but that Democrats shouldn’t interpret the win as an endorsement of every policy on their platform. “Don’t go out and have this pendulum swing, don’t go start attacking the other side,” Stitt said. “I think the American people get turned off by that.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident after hackers access ‘company information’
events.summary: Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors. Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management. In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.” “We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.” TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch. One of the people said sensitive customer data was taken in the breach. According to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents. Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident said that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor. The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach. Infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the company is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Microsoft bug undetected since July triggered worldwide outage
events.summary: The bug that crippled Microsoft productivity software last week had been lurking undetected in the company’s data centres since July. When the software maker did some routine rerouting of user traffic on Nov 11, the system malfunctioned. Then servers critical to Outlook, Teams, the Copilot AI assistant and several other services, began to fail – ultimately triggering outages for people around the world. For the next 15 hours, amid scattered server failures, the software maker had little inkling it had a bigger problem brewing, according to a preliminary report the company issued to customers late Nov 15. Microsoft then spent another 15 hours identifying and starting to roll out the fix – an eternity for a wired world that relies heavily on the company’s software. Microsoft shares were down about 1% at 2.29pm on Nov 16. Just after 8pm New York time on Nov 11, traffic from the Teams videoconference and chat service was automatically rerouted to the separate system of servers that also handle Outlook traffic. That, combined with a loss of server capacity caused by an unrelated issue earlier in the week, triggered the bug, which prompted servers to exhaust their memory after an unexpected surge in traffic. Servers began to fail. The problem was worsened by automated systems that rerouted emails and user traffic to what Microsoft’s system thought were other, healthy servers, causing the bug to show up there, too. By 11.30am on Nov 12 – just as traffic from business in the US was reaching its peak – Microsoft realised it had a problem. It took the company another 15 hours of troubleshooting to start deploying a fix for the issue. In the meantime, work at many of Microsoft’s corporate and government clients ground to a halt , as email inboxes failed to load, Teams invitations went missing and workers resorted to phone calls and pen and paper. The outage was an embarrassment for Microsoft, and a reminder of the risks of relying so heavily on a single technology vendor. Charles Lamanna, the Microsoft executive vice president who oversees the company’s workplace software, apologised early Nov 16 for the outage in a post on the X social media site that offered more detail on what went wrong. A more comprehensive timeline, included in an update for technologists who use the Microsoft 365 bundle of software, showed how the company’s automated efforts to keep its software running helped spark a cascading failure. At the nadir on Nov 12, more than 80% of the servers behind Outlook were unresponsive. Such outages often last just a few hours at most. In this case, it took longer because as soon as servers returned to service, they were overwhelmed by waiting traffic and failed again. And because the bug had gone unnoticed for months, efforts to stabilize the system by rolling back recent updates had no effect. Microsoft tests changes to its network in labs and on small portions of its network before deploying them widely, standard protocol for companies that support large online services. This bug wasn’t caught, Lamanna said, because the simulated traffic patterns and hardware in the company’s labs didn’t reflect the real-world conditions the servers later encountered. Microsoft’s testing typically focuses on older and weaker systems to assess whether updates will trip up the weakest link in the company’s cloud. The bug that caused servers to seize up is more destructive on newer hardware with more processing power. BLOOMBERG

events.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for putting public safety at risk by failing to contain AI models in testing environments. Bonta cited the incident in which OpenAI models broke out of a testing platform to hack Hugging Face in July. The suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges violations of California's Unfair Competition Law, and accuses OpenAI of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring. "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public," Bonta said at a press conference. Bonta cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face . OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September. rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, along with critics of AI, have called for such legislation on the heels of the Hugging Face break-in and other incidents that have raised concerns about the safety of AI models. Other AI companies, including Anthropic, Meta and Google, have since disclosed incidents where their own models went rogue. But OpenAI is the first to be sued in connection with such incidents by California. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri, in a statement on the lawsuit, said, "Since the Hugging Face incident, we've undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity." "We've published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment," Pusateri said. "This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," Pusateri said. Bonta's lawsuit adds to OpenAI's growing list of legal woes. In June, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging that the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits alleging that the company's ChatGPT platform led users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. California's lawsuit comes almost three months after a suit by Bonta and a coalition of other state attorneys general ended with Meta agreeing to pay $16.7 billion after being accused of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by its apps, including Facebook and Instagram. California could receive $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion from that agreement. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, setting the stage for a potentially massive initial public offering in 2027.

events.title: Chase software bug wreaks havoc on online banking
events.summary: PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images Chase says a software bug is to blame for widespread online banking issues on Monday. Reports on DownDetector showed disruptions with Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted," Chase said. A JPMorgan Chase software bug is wreaking havoc on online banking services on Monday, leading to delayed transactions. The company said it was working to resolve the issue — which impacted transactions with other banks — by the end of the day. "JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems — there is no evidence this is cyber-related," the bank said in a statement posted online . "It is taking longer than usual to service some customers." "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," it added. "Customers still have access to their accounts and funds." Customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank reported thousands of combined issues as of the afternoon, according to the third-party website DownDetector.com . Some customers reported issues with being unable to access information on their accounts. DownDetector also showed reports of issues with Zelle and Capital One. The site showed a much smaller spike in reports across Citibank and TD Bank. Other US banks said the issue was not on their end. "Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time," a spokesperson told Business Insider. A spokesperson for US Bank said its systems are not directly impacted. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the spokesperson added. A Zelle spokesperson said that the payments app is not down and is operating as it should. "An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers," the spokesperson said. The bank disruptions follow a tumultuous few days of high-profile disruptions, including a massive Microsoft outage and an FAA technical failure that sparked a nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight delays and cancellations. While some online have questioned whether the crop of incidents in the last week could be connected, there is no evidence at the moment to suggest that. events.title: Sam Altman says he's not worried about OpenAI's IPO plan
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman isn't worried about the reception when OpenAI eventually goes public. Heather Diehl/Getty Images Sam Altman gave an update on his thinking about OpenAI's IPO. Altman said journalists seem concerned about the AI industry but "investors are pretty bullish." The OpenAI CEO also downplayed any ripple effects from Nvidia's upheaval. Sam Altman shrugged off the idea that OpenAI could become the Lyft to Anthropic's Uber. "That is not a worry," Altman said on Monday during a live interview at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event. Altman's response to the question about OpenAI's chief rival generated audible laughter in the room. In 2019, Lyft went public before Uber, and its shares outperformed its ride-share rival's on their respective first days of trading. But Uber got the last laugh and today is worth roughly 22 times Lyft by market cap. Altman said that the narrative about investor demand is different than what he's seeing. He said that "there is a lot of skepticism from journalists" but that investors remain "pretty bullish." "I get that you have to write something every day, and there's got to be all this, you know, this fight and that one, and this winner, and this loser, and what's happening here and there — but the macro trend and the value being created, I'm not at all worried about there not being a huge amount," he said. The OpenAI chief reiterated his view that the ChatGPT maker will eventually go public. Anthropic publicly released its S-1 on October 26 and is expected to debut on Nasdaq later this week. That doesn't mean that being a public company will be easy, Altman said. "I think there are real downsides to being public," he said. "And it's a very volatile time in our industry with high-stakes, consequential decisions to make around safety and how society is going to interact with this technology. And there are doubtless things that are easier as a private company." Altman said it's "directionally a good thing" that more investors want exposure to the AI boom. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar recently said that bringing the company public is in line with OpenAI's mission to bring super intelligence to everyone. Friar also said that OpenAI is still targeting a 2027 IPO and that the tech backlash that helped power the blue tsunami in the midterms hasn't "dramatically changed" the company's thinking. "Look, we are paid as operators to manage scenarios," Friar told CNBC earlier this month. "I don't think there was something that dramatically changed for us." events.title: Honeywell Technologies CEO says 50 years of automation have gotten too complex for the humans running it
events.summary: The automation that runs hospitals, data centers, and refineries got its start in the 1970s. Honeywell Technologies chairman and CEO Vimal Kapur says it has since grown too complex for the people still watching over it. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kapur said those facilities run themselves for the most part, “maybe 95%,” with a person left in the loop to handle the exceptions. “Over the last 50 years since this got created, the systems have become highly complex because we kept adding more and more software and physical infrastructure to it,” he said. “So human cannot keep up with that at this point of time.” He pointed to recent news as an example. “What happened in the last two weeks is an example of complexity,” Kapur said, where “humans are not able to keep up with it,” producing an “undesired incident.” He didn’t say which one, but the options are almost too numerous to count. On Nov. 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop . Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the agency was focused on a copper-to-fiber upgrade by contractor L3Harris in El Dorado, Ark., that flooded routers with connection attempts and disrupted some radar feeds, while adding, “we don’t actually have the root cause.” On Nov. 12, Microsoft 365 began an outage that lasted more than a day. As of press time, many Americans were unable to access their bank accounts . Physical AI, minus the robots Kapur’s answer is what the industry calls “physical AI,” of which he said humanoid robots are a “very small portion.” His version goes into “every large asset which exists: hospital, data center, life sciences facilities, refineries.” It adds “a layer of learning system, the human knowledge” on top of the existing automation “so that you are able to make human more productive.” The obstacle is data: “We assume that data is available abundantly on [the] internet,” Kapur said. “But when you look at a physical system, the data is in some system which is in this building or in this hospital. Those data [are] not in public domain.” Turning it into something useful takes people “who have deep domain knowledge,” he said. He called data access “the first friction” in an April talk at Goldman Sachs . Honeywell sells automation to building, industrial, and process customers, and now sells the AI layer that goes on top. When it spun off its aerospace business on June 29, completing its three-way split, the company said it was positioned to lead “the industrial sector’s transition from automation to autonomy.” In October it launched Forge Cognition , an AI platform built with Nvidia and Dell that can run buildings in an autonomous mode, which haven’t been fully switched on, its CTO told Fortune at the time. On stage, Kapur put it more modestly: “Physical AI is not about job replacement; it’s about making humans more productive.” At Goldman in April, he said, “we’ll likely build systems which are more augmented and less autonomous.” The back-office version Dave Bozeman, CEO of freight broker C.H. Robinson, who shared the stage with Kapur, described the same problem from the paperwork side. “Variability is now structural,” he said, and supply chains “continue to be super complex.” His company’s answer is what it calls “Lean AI”: AI agents built to do “bespoke, very specific tasks,” with “orchestrating type of agents” on top. The first target is order-to-cash, which he called “a very manual process. Millions of transactions.” Bozeman also pitched it as help for workers, who he said don’t want to do “those mundane tasks every day” and would rather “go up that value stack.” He cited “over 60% productivity gains since the end of 2022.” The company’s Oct. 28 earnings release measures that as shipments per person, per day in its North American Surface Transportation unit, up more than 65% over the same stretch. The other half of that ratio is people. C.H. Robinson had about 17,400 employees at the end of 2022 and about 11,900 at the end of 2025, according to its filings, a drop of nearly a third that FreightWaves tied to automation and AI. “That doesn’t mean that it won’t be hard from a change perspective,” Bozeman said. The 1983 warning The problem Kapur describes was laid out more than 40 years ago. In 1983, Lisanne Bainbridge, a psychologist at University College London, published “ Ironies of Automation ” in the journal Automatica . She argued that designers automate what they can and leave the operator “to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate.” Those leftover tasks include taking over when conditions turn abnormal. Her central irony was that “the more advanced a control system is, so the more crucial may be the contribution of the human operator.” She also warned about what watching does to people. Operators’ “physical skills deteriorate when they are not used,” she wrote, and of the person reduced to monitoring a system: “The human monitor has been given an impossible task.” Her paper argued that automation “may expand rather than eliminate problems with the human operator.” That’s the test for an AI layer added to the stack. Fewer hands to go around Kapur said the shortage of skilled workers is what makes this urgent. “The skill shortage is the biggest problem we all face,” he said. “Anywhere there’s a touch labor where the humans need to work with hand, those workforce is becoming less and less available.” In the Goldman talk, he blamed retirement in part. A 2024 study puts numbers on it for manufacturing. Deloitte and the Manufacturing Institute found U.S. manufacturers could need as many as 3.8 million additional workers between 2024 and 2033, and that 1.9 million of those jobs could go unfilled if workforce problems aren’t addressed. Sixty-five percent of manufacturers surveyed called attracting and keeping talent their primary business challenge. Kapur gave his own company a much shorter clock than 50 years. Honeywell Technologies has more than 50,000 employees, and he said he personally took training on Copilot. “Next 18 to 24 months, we all have to reskill ourselves,” he said. events.title: Germany thrash Netherlands to book quarterfinal spot
events.summary: Jurgen Klopp’s side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure the top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2. An impressive Germany swept aside off-colour Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin to pip the Dutch to first place in UEFA Nations League Group A2. Germany needed a win to stand a chance of reaching the quarterfinals, starting the night in third place behind Greece, who had won 1-0 in Germany in September, by virtue of their head-to-head record. Jurgen Klopp’s side produced a fine attacking display to inflict the heaviest defeat on the Dutch in 67 years, as Xavi Hernandez’s side looked very ragged as they shipped four goals in 17 second-half minutes. Greece’s win over Serbia left the top three sides level on 11 points, but Germany took the top spot on head-to-head while the Dutch finished second, qualifying for the last eight on goal difference thanks largely to their 7-0 win over Greece on Friday. After a quiet opening 20 minutes, Kai Havertz headed straight at keeper Bart Verbruggen from a Joshua Kimmich free-kick, while Donyell Malen headed a Cody Gakpo cross from the left of the area over the bar from close range soon after. Berlin-born Derry Scherhant fired a half-volley against the outside of the Dutch post on 32 minutes after collecting a cross from the right byline, but it turned out to be a range-finder as Scherhant scored his first international goal from a similar position on 44 minutes. After cutting in from the left of the area and working space, he flashed an unstoppable shot past Verbruggen and into the far top corner. Scherhant almost grabbed his second a minute after the interval as he jinked and bundled his way through on goal on the left of the area only to lash a left-footed effort over the bar with only Verbruggen to beat. Denzel Dumfries headed over the bar at the other end after running onto a bouncing cross at the back post after ghosting past Scherhant on 48 minutes. Meanwhile, the lively Brajan Gruda came close to a spectacular second at the other end after some neat control and cutting in from the right before flashing a shot past the upright from the edge of the Dutch box. Soon after, Gakpo tested ter Stegen with a low strike from outside the box, but Germany made him pay as Florian Wirtz doubled the lead with a stunning strike into the top corner from the edge of the D with his left foot on the hour. Nico Schlotterbeck glanced home a header from Gruda’s curling free-kick from the left within five minutes to make it 3-0, and the fourth arrived soon after as Gruda was allowed to glide into the area on the right and get to the byline before dinking the ball back into the middle for the unmarked Wirtz to lash home his second goal with a volley off the underside of the bar. Gruda nearly added a goal to his two assists as his rising shot was stopped by Verbruggen after another silky run, but the 22-year-old eventually marked his second cap with his second international goal on 77 minutes when he fired home the rebound after Scherhant’s shot came back off the inside of the post. It led to Verbruggen calling an impromptu huddle outside his area as the visitors sought to end their misery, and they saw the game out without further alarm. events.title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
events.summary: Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results. For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang. Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees. Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company. Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer. Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him. An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang. So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back. China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China. But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025. Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact. So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up. China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money. The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China. Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals ?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans. Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come , has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: OpenAI inks agreements with four independent evaluators to boost company's safety work
events.summary: OpenAI announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators to help support its safety work. Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire will initially conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, with plans to deepen the work going forward. Independent evaluators have taken on outsized importance following a series of high-profile AI safety and security incidents. OpenAI on Monday announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators to help support the artificial intelligence company's safety work. The evaluators, Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire, will initially conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, OpenAI said. The company will give the organizations "deep access" to its internal systems as part of the agreements, adding that it plans to use what it learns to expand its work with independent experts going forward. "We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases," OpenAI said in a blog post . Independent evaluators have occupied a quiet corner of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry thus far, but they've taken on outsized importance following a series of high-profile safety and security incidents this year. The nascent ecosystem is still ironing out best practices, including how its work should be funded and what the reporting structures should ultimately look like. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators " employee-like access " to the company in September, shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company would do so as part of his call to slow down the pace of advanced model development. Anthropic has since announced agreements with evaluators including Accenture and METR, and it said in October that it's engaging in discussions with others. Anthropic’s Wall Street whisperer: Meet CFO Krishna Rao SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first How Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot OpenAI's safety practices have been under intense scrutiny since July, when two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and hacked a company called Hugging Face . Following the incident, OpenAI said it would invest more in its safeguards and alignment work, which is the process by which the company works to ensure that its models act in accordance with human interests and values. The company said Monday that its pilot assessment with Apollo Research will explore whether its models covertly work against their developers' intentions, and whether its safeguards detect that behavior. Meanwhile, Goodfire will embed researchers within OpenAI to focus on training run monitoring, debugging and alignment, and METR intends to carry out two assessments focused on model alignment and monitoring. OpenAI said Transluce will conduct an initial assessment of its post-training alignment evaluations, and that the organization plans to conduct an eight-week-long follow-on assessment with broader access to additional models and information next year. The evaluators will get access to some of the "same internal resources" that OpenAI's own researchers use, including its source code, model checkpoints, training data and other documentation, according to the release. The organizations will also have access to relevant researchers and engineers within the company. OpenAI said Apollo Research and Goodfire "accept financial compensation for their work," but that it is not contingent on the results of their evaluations. METR and Transluce do not accept compensation for their assessments, OpenAI said, but they might accept compute or API credits to help support their work. "We do not believe that accepting financial compensation prevents assessors from maintaining independence — but we believe it is important to disclose this," OpenAI said. The evaluators will be able to publish their findings, but OpenAI said it reserves the right to redact confidential information. Disputes that arise between the company and the third parties will be overseen by OpenAI's Safety Advisory Group, which is a group of senior officials from across the company that assesses model capabilities and safeguards, and other OpenAI executives. If disagreements are not resolved, they'll be escalated to the Safety and Security Committee, an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation's board. "We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it," OpenAI said. WATCH: OpenAI unveils ChatGPT Wallet: Here’s what you need to know

events.title: Nvidia fallout: Commerce targets loophole for China's data center use
events.summary: The Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's computing power from locations in other countries. Commerce's action is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week. It came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. The Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive chip technology being exported to China . The interim final rule from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal that led Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week after reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who worked for Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's biggest Asian customers. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release. The rule came after growing criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on its "entity list," which would restrict certain exports to it. How Trump traded Nvidia stock as he championed the chipmaker Trump says Nvidia scandal did not put U.S. national security 'at risk,' defends Lutnick Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on China workaround of restrictions Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe The rule is designed "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," according to the text of the rule. The new restrictions "will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using" advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors produced by U.S. companies to train advanced AI models, the rule says. The rule also says that a license will now "be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion." The New York Times reported on Nov. 9 that American authorities began investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed and one of its executives, Alice Huang, in 2024, "after the company started importing billions of dollars' worth of advanced Nvidia A.I. equipment into Malaysia." "Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant," The Times reported that day. "While that behavior is legal, U.S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China." Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, and that she was a spy working for China. The two are not related. China's government has denied the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, as national security advisor, leads the National Security Council, warned President Donald Trump last spring that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, The Times has reported. Rep. John Mooelnaar, the Michigan Republican who is chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement on the new rule that it "sends a message to the Chinese Communist Party that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years." "Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy," Moolenaar said. "This new rule is an important step in keeping chips out of ill-intentioned hands, strengthens our national security laws, and will help protect America's lead in the AI race." Chris McGuire, a former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council, in a post on X called the new rule "a major step forward to countering Chinese smuggling of and access to advanced AI chips.
