events.title: China's rare earth curbs put new emphasis on Latin American investment
events.summary: Latin America is seeking to become a viable destination for investment in critical minerals , as western governments seek alternative supplies to reduce dependency on Chinese imports. China is the dominant player in the global critical minerals supply chain. It holds a market share of 70 per cent or greater for 19 of 20 minerals listed as strategically important by the International Energy Agency, and accounts for about 90 per cent of global rare-earth processing. China imposed sweeping export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements in April 2025, before increasing that list in October. The IEA estimates those controls would cost $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China if fully introduced. Beijing last week announced it was extending a pause on the curbs until January. "I think we're learning the hard way that we need to be more competitive in these environments," said Andrew Wilson, executive director at the Centre for International Private Enterprise. Mr Wilson spoke to The National on the sidelines of a critical minerals summit in Washington. Latin America and the Caribbean hold 38.3 per cent of global lithium reserves and 32.5 per cent of copper reserves, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Experts argue this places Latin America as a key centre in supply diversification, with lithium demand expected to triple by 2040. The region also holds major shares of silver and graphite, well as other metals and speciality minerals used for advanced technologies, aerospace and defence. Foreign direct investment in the region is volatile, despite averaging 11 per cent in recent decades, according to the OECD. "The question is, how do we regain those markets, regain the security guarantees, the economic guarantees, without sacrificing standards, compliance, rule of law and otherwise?" Mr Wilson asked. "It's important for us to be pushing countries where we want to invest to up their game through our own leadership, our own corporate requirements, than it is to lose those opportunities to investors who cornered the market. But the region faces challenges including high financing costs, infrastructure gaps, skill constraints and trust with local stakeholders, according to the IEA's 2026 global critical minerals outlook. It only refines about 20 per cent of its mined output of key energy minerals, except for lithium. The IEA estimates if lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths were refined locally and two-thirds of copper production were processed in the region, the economic value generated would increase by nearly 50 per cent from current levels and reach bout $220 billion by 2035, the IEA said. Gulf states are also been deepening their investment ties into the Americas. Abu Dhabi's ADQ and US-based investment firm Orion Resource Partners in January announced a joint venture to invest in companies in Latin America, Africa and Asia. US President Donald Trump 's administration also entered into bilateral preliminary agreements with Argentina and Peru in February. The UAE and Brazil signed a $2.5 billion preliminary agreement last year to explore and develop strategic minerals essential for the global energy transition. Brazil released a list of 27 critical and strategic minerals last week in an effort to boost investment and increase domestic processing. Copper, lithium, uranium and rare earths were among metals listed as a top priority for government support. The UAE and Argentina also began talks on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, to increase investment access across mining and minerals, AI and other sectors. Saudi Arabia also signed non-binding agreements with Brazil and Chile during the Future Minerals Forum in Riyadh this year, as the kingdom looks to expand its international partnerships and investment co-operation in the mining and minerals sector.

events.title: US stocks close sharply lower on AI jitters ahead of Nvidia results, Anthropic IPO
events.summary: The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with the S&P 500 dropping nearly 2% and the Dow falling more than 1.4%. NEW YORK - A broad selloff dragged US stocks lower on Nov 16 as fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO soured enthusiasm for AI stocks, raising the stakes for the chipmaker’s earnings report on Nov 17 and Anthropic’s initial public offering later in the week. The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with the S&P 500 dropping nearly 2% and the Dow falling more than 1.4%. The Nasdaq suffered the steepest percentage loss, tumbling 2.5%, as the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index weighed on the tech-heavy index. The SOX lost 5.3%. “It’s the back-and-forth in this market of the AI-related stocks catching a bid versus this rotation trade,” said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. “Over the last couple of weeks, it’s like a day-to-day thing where, you know, some days the AI names absolutely rip and then the very next day, you know, they’re in a freefall.” “There are signs underneath the surface that investors aren’t panic-selling and running away from the asset class altogether, but are probing other corners of the equity market,” Mayfield added. Nvidia slid 4.1%, extending its losses after Huang’s resignation following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy , adding to concerns over the emerging technology’s rapid expansion and potential risks. Huang’s departure prompted the Trump administration to issue a new rule restricting China’s access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia ahead of US President Donald Trump’s expected meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. It marks an abrupt reversal of fortune for the sector. In mid-June the SOX index was up 106.6% year-to-date. But that luster has faded in recent months, reducing its 2026 gain to around 43%, still about four times the gains of the broader S&P 500 so far this year. That retreat helped pull the Nasdaq more than 10% below its all-time closing high reached on Oct 6, confirming the index is in a correction. Analysts expect Nvidia to post a 90.4% year-on-year earnings jump on revenue of US$109.10 billion (S$140 billion). The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.41%, to 51,608.17, the S&P 500 lost 145.08 points, or 1.92%, to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 626.51 points, or 2.49%, to 24,509.76. Warsh remarks, rate-hike probability US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said on Nov 16 that technologies will have a significant impact on the economy , but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee’s latest meeting, due for release on Nov 18, could offer clues on the policy outlook ahead of next month’s interest-rate decision. Markets are pricing in a near-certain 95.7% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, according to CME FedWatch. Among individual stocks, chipmakers Intel and Micron both dropped more than 7%. Neocloud provider CoreWeave dipped 6.1% and rival Nebius dropped 7.6%. Hyperscalers Alphabet, Amazon and Meta slid between 2.4% and 4.1%. Server maker Dell dropped 7.0%, while Super Micro Computer fell 6.9%. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.45-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 68 new highs and 590 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 1,131 stocks rose and 3,697 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.27-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 21 new 52-week highs and seven new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 489 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 17.91 billion shares, compared with the 18.66 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Michigan’s next governor hasn’t talked to Trump yet—but wants to work with him on a 50% auto tariff set for her first day
events.summary: Michigan Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson hasn’t spoken to President Donald Trump since winning the state’s governor’s race as part of the blue tsunami that swept across the nation earlier this month. “Not yet, but I intend to,” Benson said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit in an interview with Fortune editorial director Kristin Stoller. “We’ve all got to work together to better our economy, to better Michigan.”  Top of mind, though, is a tariff that could land on her first day in office. After negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down in August, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian-made cars, trucks, and parts to 50% beginning Jan. 1, 2027. That’s the same day Benson takes over from term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Benson said she hopes for opportunities to collaborate, “first and foremost, in reducing the impact of these tariffs.” She recalled touring auto parts distributor Detroit Axle in October, where she said the owner told her: “I’m sending millions of dollars into paying these tariffs, and it’s money that I had saved to expand my business, to create more jobs.” Last year, Detroit Axle said it might have to shut down a warehouse and lay off more than 100 workers, although it later backtracked. But owner Mike Musheinesh told the Associated Press, “It’s a market of who is able to survive; it’s not a matter of who can thrive.” Benson said a governor can uniquely go to Canada and broker a Michigan-specific agreement to protect jobs and lower costs, something she promised to pursue on the campaign trail. She also said she intends to negotiate “aggressively” with the federal government for carve-outs that lessen the tariffs’ impact. While campaigning, she argued levies on Canadian imports had set the average Michigan household back $5,600—more than any other state. Tariffs are just one piece of Benson’s broader plan to fix affordability.  “Our campaign was about affordability through the lens of costs down, wages up, knowing that there’s two sides of that coin,” Benson told Fortune . Michigan’s per capita incomes “have also been stagnant for far too long,” she said, adding that most jobs in the state’s economy pay $60,000 or less. In 2025, Michigan ranked in the lower half of median wages in the U.S., according to the Michigan Center for Data and Analytics. Benson said part of the governor’s job is bringing in new, higher-paying jobs and training workers to fill those roles so paychecks will “go up and not stay stagnant.” On the cost side, she pitched herself as “the CEO of state government,” saying she plans to streamline how the state delivers health care, housing development, and childcare to save money. “You’re actually running an institution, and you have metrics and a strategic plan and delivering results,” she said regarding referring to herself as the CEO of Michigan. As Michigan’s secretary of state, she overhauled the state’s DMV offices, which she said eliminated wait times and made the agency “a poster child for efficiency.” Michigan voters also sent progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate over Republican Mike Rogers. Benson said the commonality between the two wins was “costs down and wages up,” along with ending corruption.  “It’s a team effort,” she said of lowering costs. “It’s partnerships, but there’s a lot you can do as the CEO of the state to drive down costs and bring more well-paying jobs in.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Bill Ackman says it’s ‘unlikely’ he’ll get involved to bring Huang back
events.summary: Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said Monday it was “unlikely” that he would get directly involved in an effort to reinstate former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Ackman, an outspoken activist investor who runs Pershing Square Capital Management, has come to Huang’s defense following the revelations that Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Ackman acknowledged that the situation presents “a pretty interesting activist setup.” There’s still legal uncertainty about what exactly happened, Ackman told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman, but if Huang’s missteps were a “personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy, there’s a very powerful case for putting him back in place.” While “truth is pretty darn important,” he said a board should treat a CEO lying about a personal matter differently from lying about something that could endanger the company’s business. If he were running a comeback campaign, Ackman said he would “present the facts, and you call a special meeting.” Huang would have heft: Having co-founded the company, he still owns more than 3% of Nvidia. — J.D. events.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
events.summary: Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns. Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students. Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education. Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students. International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities. "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues." Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships. By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars. Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators. That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported. It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth. Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing. Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies. International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk. Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report . Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition. Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students. A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices. Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit. The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue. The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent. "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect." events.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth. California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards. The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet. list 1 of 3 Australia tightens AI oversight rules after OpenAI government breach list 2 of 3 US nonprofits sue tech giants to halt AI development list 3 of 3 Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company? It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face . In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors. “The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement. The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions. The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”. “The simple truth is that the attack was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s decision to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” the complaint reads. The Hugging Face incident became a catalyst for anxieties in the US about the explosive growth of the AI industry and the relatively light oversight it receives from the government. President Donald Trump’s administration has largely opposed blanket regulations on the AI industry, warning that such rules could stifle the industry’s growth. In December 2025, for instance, Trump issued an executive order attempting to limit the ability of individual states to pass laws that might govern AI development. “United States AI companies must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulation. But excessive State regulation thwarts this imperative,” the order reads. “My Administration must act with the Congress to ensure that there is a minimally burdensome national standard — not 50 discordant State ones.” Polls, however, show that a majority of Americans want to see greater oversight of AI development and are wary that the technology could fuel economic and social disruptions. The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, for instance, found in October that 64 percent of US adults believe AI is developing too rapidly. Roughly 81 percent said the technology should be kept under human control, rather than be left to operate independently. Several high-profile resignations in the AI sector — notably that of Jacob Coxon in September — have also spurred concerns about the lack of oversight. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon, formerly a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic, wrote in a social media post about his departure. “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.” In Monday’s lawsuit, California officials accuse companies like OpenAI of failing to “adequately secure and monitor” their AI tests. It also alleged that the company had obstructed state investigators when they attempted to look into incidents like the Hugging Face hacking. “OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI has responded to July’s incident by stating that it would reinforce its safety measures and acknowledging the need for greater transparency. In September, it also published a framework for “tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment” to better inform lawmakers and the public.

events.title: Top Chamber of Commerce official says the midterms weren’t just about prices: They were about 20 years of 2% growth
events.summary: Less than two weeks after voters handed Democrats both chambers of Congress in an election defined by frustration over the cost of living and perceived corruption , the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s top policy official warned a room of executives that Washington might already be misreading the message. Neil Bradley, the Chamber’s executive vice president, chief policy officer and head of strategic advocacy, said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit that the affordability anger is real. He also argued it sits on top of something voters have been signaling for two decades that “no one has been paying attention to”: 20 years of roughly 2% real GDP growth, after 60 years of more than 3%. That gap is the difference between a kid who grows up richer than their parents and one who doesn’t. Harvard economist Raj Chetty and his co-authors found in a 2017 paper that the share of Americans earning more than their parents fell from about 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s. “The concept of the American dream isn’t 3% growth, but it’s highly correlated to it,” Bradley said. The easy button Bradley’s real target was what Congress does next. “There’s a real temptation to hit the easy button,” he said, like capping credit card interest rates, price controls on pharmaceuticals, or limits on stock buybacks and dividends. These are “proposals that both ends of the political horseshoes are coming together on” and they might ease voters’ angst “for a brief period of time,” he said, “but they won’t solve our long-term challenges.” The horseshoe part is accurate. President Trump called for a one-year, 10% cap on credit card rates in January, and Sens. Bernie Sanders and Josh Hawley have a bill to do it. The Senate’s version of this year’s defense bill carries new restrictions on buybacks and dividends by defense contractors. The list also lines up with the Chamber’s membership. Card issuers, drugmakers and any public company with a buyback program would pay for each of those buttons. Bradley’s alternative is growth: expand supply, expand trade, and expand the labor force “through legal immigration reform.” The growth math holds up Bradley’s numbers check out against the government’s. Real GDP grew at a compound rate of about 3.5% a year from 1950 to 2005 and about 2% a year from 2005 to 2025, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data compiled by the St. Louis Fed . At 3%, an economy doubles in about 23 years, roughly the time from birth to a first job. At 2%, it takes about 35. His election count holds, too. In the 11 national elections since 2006, voters took control of the House, the Senate or the White House away from the party holding it every time except 2012. Chetty’s research complicates Bradley’s argument when it comes to the remedy. The paper found that “increasing GDP growth rates alone cannot restore absolute mobility” to the levels of the 1940s cohort. Shifting the distribution of growth back to the more equal pattern that cohort saw “would reverse more than 70% of the decline.” Bradley acknowledged this point, too: “Of course, a doubling in pie doesn’t guarantee that anyone’s individual slice will be bigger.” A record, with an asterisk Bradley’s case for optimism was what he called “a little-known record”: 5.68 million new business starts last year. “No one’s an entrepreneur if they’re pessimistic about the future,” he said. Census tracks those as business applications , meaning requests to the IRS for an employer ID number, not businesses that opened. Summed from the bureau’s monthly data, applications came to about 5.67 million in 2025 before seasonal adjustment, the most for any full year since the series began in 2004. The applications that Census flags as likely to become businesses with payroll tell a different story. Those totaled about 1.69 million in 2025 on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 1.86 million in 2023 and lower for a second straight year. More Americans are filing to start something, and fewer of the filings look like future employers. About nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, according to The AP Voter Poll . The new Congress is sworn in in January. The Congressional Budget Office’s January outlook has real GDP growing 1.8% a year in 2027 and 2028. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Sam Altman doesn’t 'know enough' to answer whether Jensen Huang should pull a Sam Altman
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Godofredo A. Vásquez/AFP via Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman isn't sure about calling for Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's return. Altman said at a Semafor event that he didn't know enough about Huang's situation to answer about such a scenario. The OpenAI leader called Huang one of his heroes while adding, "heroes have flaws." Don't put Sam Altman 's name on the list of tech luminaries calling for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return just yet. "I don't think I know enough to answer that question," Altman said Monday during an interview at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and several prominent Nvidia employees have called for Huang's reinstatement after the Nvidia board of directors announced last week that he had resigned following multiple reported affairs. On Monday, President Donald Trump said he too was supportive of the idea of Huang returning. Altman called Huang one of his heroes and said the Nvidia founder has had a major impact on the AI boom. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine," Altman said. "I am grateful for the company he has built." The OpenAI CEO also said he has "empathy" for Huang's situation, acknowledging how some have compared Huang's ouster to the brief period in 2023 when Altman was forced out of OpenAI. Altman was famously reinstated after a short number of days. "I do have, like, personal, strong empathy to a situation like this," Altman said. "I remember what it was like, although it feels like forever ago." Some on Wall Street and in tech have questioned what the AI boom will look like if Huang remains outside the company he led to become one of the industry's biggest champions. Altman said it is "hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen." At the same time, Altman expressed confidence that the industry will avoid any ripple effects from the Nvidia turmoil. "Look, at this point, I think there is so much demand, and it's so clear that AI is real and people want to use it," he said, "and revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine." events.title: JPMorgan works to fix ‘technical issue’ that triggers online banking delays for major US banks
events.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co said some transactions are taking longer to process due to a technical issue while ruling out a cybersecurity breach. JPMorgan Chase & Co said some transactions are taking longer to process than normal as the bank grapples with a “technical issue.” Customers still have access to their accounts and funds, the bank said in an emailed statement on Nov 16. The firm is working to resolve it as quickly as possible, according to the statement. The disruption isn’t tied to a cybersecurity issue, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified citing confidential details. Tech challenges have been plaguing US companies and entities in recent weeks. Microsoft faced one of its longest outages last week , with disruptions to Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence tool. US airlines were hit by one of the longest nationwide shutdowns in decades, with the Federal Aviation Administration saying the ground stop was tied to a router located near El Dorado, Arkansas. Downdetector had logged more than 3,000 reports of disruption on Nov 16 with JPMorgan. Other financial firms also saw a spike in reported disruptions including Bank of America and Wells Fargo & Co. Zelle, the payments system overseen by Early Warning Services and owned by banks, was also among the apps listed as customers flagged problems. A representative for Bank of America declined to comment, while a Wells Fargo spokesperson had no immediate comment. A Zelle spokesperson said its system isn’t down and is operating as it should. JPMorgan shares fell 2.6% to $337.26 at 2.45pm in New York, narrowing this year’s gain to 4.7%. Bank of America was down 2.4%, while Wells Fargo dropped 2.2%. Spokespeople for the Federal Reserve, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Only 49 songs have stayed at No. 1 on the chart for 10 weeks or more — here they all are
events.summary: Lil Nas X, Olivia Newton-John, Mariah Carey, and Shaboozey. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for The Recording Academy; Erik Hein/American Broadcasting Companies via Getty Images; Kevin Winter/Getty Images; Axelle Bauer Griffin/FilmMagic; Rebecca Zisser/BI A small fraction of all No. 1 hits have ruled the Billboard Hot 100 for 10 weeks or more. Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" is the latest song to reach the milestone. "Choosin' Texas" has surpassed "All I Want for Christmas Is You" for most weeks atop the chart. The Billboard Hot 100 is widely regarded as the definitive all-genre singles chart in the US. Since the chart launched in 1958, hundreds of songs have reached the coveted No. 1 spot. However, far fewer have remained there for double-digit weeks. Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" recently notched its 28th week at No. 1, setting a record for the most in history. Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" holds second place, while Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road" and Shaboozey's "A Bar Song (Tipsy)" are tied for third. Keep reading for a roundup of every song that has ruled the chart for at least 10 weeks, listed in the order they reached that milestone. Listen to the complete playlist on Business Insider's Spotify . 1. "You Light Up My Life" by Debby Boone Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images "You Light Up My Life" was the first song in history to chart at No. 1 for 10 weeks. 2. "Physical" by Olivia Newton-John Olivia Newton-John/YouTube "Physical" charted at No. 1 for 10 weeks. 3. "End of the Road" by Boyz II Men Boyz II Men/YouTube "End of the Road" charted at No. 1 for 13 weeks. 4. "I Will Always Love You" by Whitney Houston Whitney Houston/YouTube "I Will Always Love You" charted at No. 1 for 14 weeks. 5. "I Swear" by All-4-One All-4-One/YouTube "I Swear" charted at No. 1 for 11 weeks. 5. "I'll Make Love to You" by Boyz II Men Boyz II Men/YouTube "I'll Make Love to You" charted at No. 1 for 14 weeks. 7. "One Sweet Day" by Mariah Carey and Boyz II Men "One Sweet Day" was released on November 14, 1995. events.title: Kalshi plans to launch stock trading soon
events.summary: Kalshi will offer stock trading within the next few months, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The expansion comes as Kalshi faces growing legal challenges from states about its sports contracts. Leading prediction market platform Kalshi will offer stock trading within the next few months, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The platform's move to offer equity trading is the boldest so far in its ongoing push into traditional financial markets and comes amid an escalating fight by states and lawmakers against its sports trading business. Sports contracts continue to account for a large share of trading on the platform. In September, the platform introduced perpetual futures tied to precious metals such as gold and silver after it had originally filed in July to offer beyond prediction market event contracts with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal regulator overseeing derivatives contracts. Perpetual futures are futures-style contracts that have no expiration date. Kalshi also received approval to list perpetual futures tied to cryptocurrencies in late May. The prediction market's stock trading offering was enabled by its purchase of broker-dealer FB Securities in July, the source said. FB Securities was founded in Delaware in 2024 and became registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission in December 2025. The broker did not respond to a request for comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported that Kalshi plans to introduce stock trading. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: SNL's 'Sister' sketch captures the hidden burden of caring for aging parents
events.summary: Elder care often falls more on women than on men. NBC A new SNL sketch highlighted the gender gap in elder care. It focused on sisters taking on the care of aging parents. Women, in general, are more likely to do care work, whether paid or unpaid. A dark SNL sketch from this weekend about the gender gap in elder care struck a nerve — and there's a strong element of truth behind the joke. Comedian and host John Mulaney featured in the "Sister" segment, intended as a parody ad. The ad positions actor Jane Wickline as a "24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister." Other men in the ad talk about the perks of having their sister take on caring for aging parents . "My dad means the world to me. So when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible," Mulaney says in the ad. "I didn't want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn't know where to turn. That's when I heard about Sister." The parody ad resonated sharply with viewers, garnering over 2 million views on YouTube since airing. Comments overwhelmingly agreed that this arrangement was "too real," "so true," and "triggering." Business Insider has been covering the challenges facing long-term caregivers over the past year and how the burden of care often falls on women. Business Insider is looking for people to tell us about how much they've paid for caregiving. Fill out this survey if you're interested in sharing. The SNL skit taps into that trend. Waterlily, an AI-powered financial planning platform, found that "America's family care system runs on daughters ," based on its own data and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services data. They are about twice as likely to provide hands-on care, such as helping with dressing and bathing. Among those providing care, daughters typically spend more hours a week helping provide care than sons. In interviews, well over a dozen women caregivers have told Business Insider that they wish their siblings, often male, did more for their loved one's care. Many said that their parents had expected their daughters would care for them so their sons could focus more on their careers or families. It was on them to handle their loved ones' finances, take them to appointments, and, in some cases, quit their jobs to be a live-in caregiver. However, most refused to talk about their siblings on the record. They feared retaliation from their siblings and didn't want to make it seem as though caring for their loved ones was a burden, though they said so in private. The burden of elder care often falls on women Women accounted for 55% of the 38 million unpaid elder care providers in the US, based on 2023 and 2024 Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Unpaid caregivers tend to be older, with over 11 million women elder care providers being 55 and older. While the majority of providers are women, many men are primary caregivers to their aging parents. Dina Mabry's grandmother lived alone in her mobile home until she poured boiling water on herself, after which she moved into a skilled nursing facility. Mabry's mom became her primary caregiver, as her two brothers said they couldn't take her in or help pay for her care. It caused a rift between the siblings, which took years to heal. Mabry's parents had set aside thousands to retire and travel, but $6,000 to $8,000 each month of this went to her mom's six years in care facilities. It pushed back their retirement by years. Mabry, 58, works in long-term care and disability insurance and used this experience to inform her clients about the benefits of planning ahead. She advises her clients to discuss care preferences with loved ones years before a crisis, ensuring there is enough money to hire home care nurses or move into an assisted living facility. One of the worst-case scenarios, Mabry said, is a daughter suddenly being responsible for full-time care. Are you taking care of an elderly loved one? How much does that compare to your siblings? Reach out to these reporters to share at nsheidlower@businessinsider.com and mhoff@businessinsider.com . The prices of nursing homes and adult day services have risen faster than overall consumer prices since the '90s and can end up costing families six figures. AARP found caregivers spend over $11,000 on average a year out of pocket. A large share of that is due to household expenses like food and housing. Sana Sheraz is the youngest of five siblings, but caring for her aging parents mainly falls on her. She suspects it's because of her earnings and financial stability rather than having the free time to balance caring for her parents and her children. "When it comes to medical expenses or big decisions, the weight tends to shift toward me," Sheraz said. "Sometimes it's a direct request. Sometimes it's simply the expectation in the air, the pause after a cost is mentioned, the assumption that I'll handle it — because I can." Care can be like taking on a second job Angelina Grigoryeva, associate professor of sociology at the University of Toronto, has researched the division of labor among siblings caring for elderly parents . She said it comes at a cost — financially and emotionally, with women often having to adjust their relationship to the workforce. Grigoryeva said women provide more care and are also the ones receiving more care, likely because they might feel more comfortable getting dressed, bathing, or similar activities with the help of their daughter. "When working caregivers reduce their hours or need to quit their job entirely, they lose not only their current salary and benefits but also opportunities to save for retirement and build future Social Security benefits," Debra Whitman, executive vice president and chief public policy officer at AARP, said in a press release. Carla Romagnano, who is in her 60s, had her mom, who is in her 80s and has dementia, move in with her. Romagnano said caregiving is the hardest job she's ever had. "When I come home from work, I sit in the driveway to decompress and go into the house because my second job starts," Romagnano previously told Business Insider in an as-told-to essay. "I take care of the needs of my mom, whatever I need to do, take care of my two border collies, and then figure out what's going to go on for the rest of the day. It's two full-time jobs, and I would not wish this on anybody." Grigoryeva said that while caregiving duties can involve daily living activities, they can also involve organizing paid care, such as arranging for caregivers that their parents feel happy with and paying for it. That paid care also often falls on the shoulders of women; 86% of home health aides and 87% of nursing assistants in 2025 were women. events.title: US Fed’s Warsh says emerging technologies to have ‘significant impact,’ but there are risks
events.summary: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh the risks, including higher unemployment and the use of AI by “bad actors,” could be “highly disruptive and economically costly.” SAN FRANCISCO - Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said on Nov 16 that emerging technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing. Warsh refers to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence,” the language preferred by President Donald Trump, and said it could prove distinct from earlier technologies as a force to “supercharge idea generation.” In the best scenario, Warsh told a Fed conference on AI in San Francisco, the technology could lead “to an increase in productivity and economic gains that are shared broadly across labour and the owners of capital. “In that event, real GDP growth rises persistently above its long-run average, and the US stays close to full employment.” But Warsh said the risks, including higher unemployment and the use of AI by “bad actors,” could also be “highly disruptive and economically costly.” “Our job is to prepare for whatever comes next,” he said of the Fed’s convening of a group of AI experts to explore the implications of the technology for the economy and central banking. “Our role in all this is neither advocacy nor opposition. Our responsibility is to recognise that the widespread adoption of this technology will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road,” Warsh said. “The big questions are about magnitude, scope, and timing.” The discussion between Warsh and tech industry leaders and academics took place in a San Francisco Fed auditorium before a small invitation-only audience. Those in attendance included Fed Governor Lisa Cook, venture capitalists, money managers, philanthropists, CEOs of technology, healthcare, and other companies, as well as an assortment of economists from across the Fed system, private companies and universities. While Warsh said the current moment was a “paradigm shift,” much of the conversation remained speculative. Panelists discussed how AI might allow the US economy to outpace economies in the rest of the world because of the speed with which new technology and methods are being applied in the US, but also raised concerns that it could undermine learning among students as they become too dependent on the technology. events.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry
events.summary: Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africa’s biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy “openly racist” and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. “All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,” Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “You’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans. Ramaphosa also said Musk should be “loyal” to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years. An ‘ambush’ Musk has been a powerful figure in American politics as well business since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The Trump administration shuttered the US Agency for International Development, its main overseas aid agency, under Musk’s guidance as a government adviser. And his influence is widely seen to have played a role in Washington’s increasingly fractious relationship with Pretoria. South Africa has refused to meet US demands for reforms of BEE, and has previously provoked the Trump administration’s ire over Pretoria’s criticism of Israel. Ramaphosa said their highest-profile flashpoint since Trump took office — an Oval Office meeting in which the US president accused him of presiding over a white genocide — was an “ambush.” He said Trump was “seriously misinformed.” Ramaphosa said he and Trump had not spoken since that meeting, having previously held conversations. He added that it was a pity that the US president’s belief in a white genocide — a widely discredited allegation — underpinned Washington’s approach to South Africa. The South African president said he was in California this week for meetings with tech executives, and will hold talks with a number of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google. Asked about the opposition to the data center buildout in some parts of the world, he said South Africa welcomed them. — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: 'Heroes have flaws': Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. On public sentiment toward AI Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” On going public Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” On espionage OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” On memory and RAM Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. On the next generation of tech Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. On AI safety Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: North Korea outreach in the mix for Trump’s Asia swing
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia may include a sitdown with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Though Trump floated that possibility today, telling reporters that Kim “might come,” one senior US official said days ago that there are “no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.” The White House declined to comment further on the prospect, pointing to Trump’s earlier comments. While the president met with Kim during his first term, he has yet to organize a second-term meeting. Trump’s trip will culminate with an unprecedented trilateral meeting between the US, China, and Russia. Trump is not expected to discuss Ukraine at that sitdown, the senior US official said. Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin are instead expected to discuss “the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Sudanese army air attack kills 13 in western Sudan: Rights group
events.summary: ‘Preliminary monitoring’ shows women and children killed, homes destroyed, in West Kordofan, according to Emergency Lawyers. An air strike launched by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) has killed at least 13 civilians in the Abu Qalb area of West Kordofan state, according to the Emergency Lawyers rights group. Warplanes belonging to the military government carried out the attack on the Abu Zabad locality, with the victims including women and children, “according to preliminary monitoring” the legal collective said in a social media post on Monday. Al Jazeera was unable to immediately verify the report. list 1 of 3 Sudan teachers go on strike over meagre salaries and dilapidated schools list 2 of 3 Drone attacks on power stations plunge Sudan’s cities into darkness list 3 of 3 South Sudan postpones first-ever national elections until February Several homes were also destroyed in the strike, which took place the previous day, Emergency Lawyers said. The group, which documents human rights violations and crimes in the war between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), cited videos circulating of “horrific scenes” of destruction. “The continued use of indiscriminate airstrikes on residential areas poses a direct threat to civilian lives and constitutes a grave violation of the rules of international humanitarian law,” it said in its statement. Mohamed Didan, the official spokesperson for the Special Operations Forces that fight alongside the SAF, said on Facebook that his troops had moved through Abu Zabad and “eliminated” RSF positions in West Kordofan. The war between the army and the RSF, which began in April 2023, has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, according to several aid organisations. Reports say the war has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced about 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine. Much of the fighting is concentrated in Darfur and Kordofan, although it recently shifted towards the Blue Nile province. Drone warfare has also surged during the war, becoming the deadliest threat to civilians. Both sides are being supplied with drones by countries in the Middle East and beyond, experts have said. The SAF has gained control over several strategically important villages and localities in West Kordofan recently in a push into the western reaches of the country .

events.title: Advocates dub midterms the ‘care election’
events.summary: This month’s midterms were the “care election,” according to a sweeping new report by Care Can’t Wait Action that was shared first with Semafor . The coalition points to its role in boosting turnout — citing nearly 24 million impressions via events, media and other outreach — as well as exit polling that found voters want the next Congress to focus on issues like paid leave and child care. “There’s this undeniable sense of momentum,” leader Ai-jen Poo told Semafor, adding that she is “looking to Congress to pass a whole set of bills that will address the entire care agenda, because I think voters are ready.” Seven in 10 voters said it’s important for Congress to pass a paid family and medical leave bill in the next six months, according to included polling by Lake Research for MomsRising Together and Paid Leave for All Action. Eight in 10 voters who are mothers said it was important to their vote that the federal government “immediately works to lower the cost of raising a family,” including by tackling child care. Nearly 8 in 10 voters said presidential candidates should make paid leave a top priority, according to separate post-election polling by Change Research. That includes 95% of Democrats and 69% of men. “Democrats won on these issues, and now they need to take action within the first 100 days of this new Congress,” Sondra Goldschein, executive director of the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, told Semafor. She called for lawmakers to “put them on the president’s desk, and then force him to decide whether he wants to veto.” GOP cuts to Medicaid funding helped mobilize “many first-time care-worker activists,” SEIU Executive Vice President Leslie Frane said. Advocates are hopeful the Trump administration agrees to repeal some of those cuts — but they’re not holding their breath on other issues. “When the time comes to be smart about making choices and tradeoffs, we will. But I think we’re really far from that time,” Poo said. “So this is a moment where we have the momentum to do big things, and there’s no reason why we should not.” Democrats had tried to enact paid leave and universal pre-K amid the pandemic , but fell short given their narrow Senate majority. Advocates are now optimistic that the latest wave of policymakers will see more success. “We have a whole crop of new leaders coming in with a clear mandate on these policies — and that was intentional,” Poo said. “That was a big lesson from Build Back Better, is that we need a whole different level of consensus.”

events.title: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond
events.summary: Robert Pattinson will star in the 26th James Bond film, the first installment since Amazon MGM took control of the franchise. Denis Villeneuve will direct the film with producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman. Pattinson has been in major films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey," and will soon appear in "Dune: Part Three." Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise. Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement . "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team." Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime ," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic. The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin." In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios , which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion . Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

events.title: Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks
events.summary: As promised last month , Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.” “Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple warned in its blog post aimed at app developers. Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf. While the tools can be useful, Apple has grown concerned about the increased risks to users’ data and privacy that these AI agents introduce. At the same time, the company has been benefiting from sales of Mac minis and Mac Studio computers that AI early adopters have been purchasing specifically to run their local AI models. To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents. In one, a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app read their private messages without consent; a separate report from Wired cited a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app that could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. Now, Apple is sharing the changes it’s making. For starters, it’s splitting up Device Control and Data Access into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The changes are designed to help users better understand that selecting the first option means overriding built-in security protections. To streamline configurations, Apple says there will now also be a single method for granting permissions that involves selecting the requested app from a list. The company will also introduce new guidance encouraging users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it when they enable the System & App Protection Override setting. Similar guidance will appear when users enable Full Disk Access to allow an app to access their folders. The company will also provide users with “increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted,” the blog post notes. Another change will give users more granular control over when an AI agent or app can gain access by allowing users to configure their apps to ask for permission every time access is needed. While arguably tedious and a potential obstacle to true automation, the feature could allow users to experiment with local AI without giving the agent carte blanche. There will also be a new transparency indicator that appears when an app is controlling another app through the System & App Protection Override option. The changes, which are arriving with macOS 27.3, don’t appear to prevent Mac users from installing and running AI agents or other apps that ask for higher levels of access. Instead, they give users more nuanced options, control, and information about the choices they’re making. Apple advises app developers to adjust their onboarding processes to account for the new changes and suggests that their apps learn to “gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps.” Developers of apps that request Full Disk Access for disk backup or to provide assistive technologies can request exceptions to the new rules (which Apple calls “entitlements”) to preserve the same functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update. events.title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage
events.summary: Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week. The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections , and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said. The disruption began Thursday with US users reporting interrupted access to their Outlook email accounts. As it continued into the next day, millions of people worldwide said they could not access their email in any capacity as well as other Office 365 services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach. In a post on X on Monday, Charles Lamanna, the executive vice-president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said there was a latent bug or defect from July that caused Microsoft’s servers to “become overwhelmed and unresponsive”. Lamanna wrote that the company typically has two available networking gateways, or entry and exit points that connect separate systems and allow data to pass between them. However, one of them was not working for Microsoft Teams which overwhelmed the primary gateway. Subsequently, over 14% of the company’s server capacity was also not working due to an unrelated issue from the previous day. “Taken together, the increased load and the reduced server capacity, caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna wrote. “This caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding. This occurred during the peak window of traffic in the United States.” The company also had trouble mitigating the bug because it originated months before, Lamanna said, so it would not be easy as rolling back a recent change to undo the defect. “Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” he wrote. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state. Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.” The company plans to publish a final report which will include more information, he said. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Analysts say Microsoft’s global outage highlights the need for companies to examine how much they rely on a single operating system. “This is a prime example of the importance of not only cyber resilience, but business resilience,” said Matt Hull, vice-president of cyber intelligence and response at NCC Group . “Reports that hospitals, schools and other essential services are affected demonstrate the wide impact that a system outage can have, regardless of the cause.”

events.title: ‘We’re having to overcome brand America’: Kraft Heinz CEO says made-in-U.S.A. designation is more ‘complicated’ in appealing to Canadian customers
events.summary: As U.S.-Canadian relations go frosty, one American food brand is having to be more intentional about appealing to its northern neighbors. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane said the made-in-the-U.S.A. moniker doesn’t carry the same positive connotation as it did in decades past. As a result, he said, the Chicago- and Pittsburgh-based food giant—behind Jell-O, Lunchables, and Heinz ketchup—is having to tweak its messaging. “Brand America is not as strong as it once was, and that’s been the case for some time,” Cahillane told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “We’re having to overcome brand America. Whereas, in the ‘50s, ‘60s, ‘70s, into the ‘80s, brand America was a badge of honor, it’s a little bit more complicated today.”  Ongoing trade tensions, including a 50% tariff on $20 billion of Canadian goods , have chilled Canadian attitudes towards American productions, as have repeated threats from U.S. President Donald Trump about making Canada the “ 51st state ,” claiming it relies too heavily on the U.S. economically. While Canadians have continued to pour money into U.S. investments , many have also made a concerted effort to boycott American goods in favor of Canadian counterparts.  In some areas, these boycotts are taking a toll on the U.S. economy. A report from the Canadian government published last month found that despite Canadian visitations to the U.S. beginning to increase, visitations from Canadians are 29% lower as of September 2026 than they were two years ago. According to the U.S. Travel Association, those decreases in visits cost the U.S. economy $4.5 billion last year. Kraft Heinz has worked to adapt to Canadians’ changing attitudes toward American goods by giving its consumers reassurance their products are being made in the Great White North, according to Cahillane. In March, subsidiary Kraft Heinz Canada announced a $250 million investment to bolster operations at its Montreal production facility. “We had to remind the Canadian consumer that all of the Heinz ketchup that they’re consuming in Canada is made in Canada,” Cahillane said. “We have a couple of big plants up there, and so when we talk to people about the local nature of our products, it may be brand America, but it’s produced in your backyard by your friends and neighbors, grown locally,” he added.  As Kraft Heinz navigates a turnaround after a 10-year slump, the company is beginning to find more solid footing outside the U.S. Despite reporting falling revenue last quarter, it was particularly offset by growing sales in Canada. Its Kraft Mac & Cheese Cheesy Ramen debuted in Canada in July, and, according to Cahillane, it sold out three months of inventory in a week. Kraft Heinz is also finding ways to navigate tariffs after initially being hit hard by the implementation of the import taxes. The food giant reported in May 2025 it would need to shift suppliers and potentially reformulate products as a result of the levies. “We’re already local. We have to be hyperlocal,” Cahillane told Fortune . “We have to build in redundancy. We have to build in the ability to do things faster than we ever have before, and that becomes hyperlocal for us.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Photos: California residents gather to watch massive El Nino-fuelled waves
events.summary: The National Weather Service warns that waves of more than 10 metres (33 feet) high could impact some parts of the US’s California coast. Residents have flocked to the waterfront in coastal towns across California to watch giant waves brought on by a potentially historic El Nino climate pattern. For days, heavy surf has pounded the West Coast of the United States, slamming into piers and inundating coastal areas. The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Monday that a Pacific storm is expected to bring further rain and snowfall to the western US this week. A day earlier, the weather service issued a high surf advisory for all beaches along the Pacific Coast, forecasting waves to break as high as 10.7 metres, or 35 feet. “Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean,” the NWS added, citing the risk of “sneaker waves” — powerful surges of water that can reach higher than expected on a beach, only to pull back into the ocean with potentially deadly force. Despite the warnings, big-wave watchers gathered at famed lookout points like Mavericks Beach in northern California’s Half Moon Bay. Mavericks is considered one of the premier big-wave surfing spots in North America, with water cresting as high as a five-storey building. Surfers from across the world have descended on the beach in recent days to catch swells reaching approximately 18 metres, or 60 feet. Some of the offshore waves have been so strong that they were detected by the Berkeley Seismology Lab, which wrote about the phenomenon on its blog. “A few miles offshore, there are no beaches for the waves to hit, but their bottoms bang into the continental shelf, where the shallow coastal waters drop off sharply into deeper ocean regions,” the lab explained. “This impact is strong enough to make all of California shake. In fact, it makes the entire continent wiggle a little.” While it is typical for California to experience storms in November and December, this year’s heavy rainfall and powerful surf have been turbocharged by a climate phenomenon known as El Nino . The El Nino pattern occurs when the recurrent warming of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean releases heat into the atmosphere. Already, experts say ocean temperatures off of California are reaching record levels for this time of year, making the water feel warmer than normal. El Nino can also alter weather patterns around the world. Scientists and state officials expect an especially strong El Nino this year to result in heavy rain for California in the coming weeks. “The odds of an unusually wet, and perhaps exceptionally wet, second half of November continue to rise in California,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said in a social media post.

events.title: Online bookmaker targets netball club for inducements, signs up 18yos
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT Wagering Commission fines bookmaker $83k over Instagram inducements The scheme targeted a community football and netball club, with young women making up the majority of new sign-ups. ( AAP: Scott Barbour ) A bookmaker has been hit with a hefty fine over an inducement scheme targeting a community sporting club. The scheme saw about a dozen 18-year-olds sign up to bookmaker Amused Group's promotional offer. The NT-registered bookmaker has since collapsed into liquidation, owing an estimated $5 million to creditors. An Australian online bookmaker has been fined more than $83,000 after an inducement scheme targeting a community football and netball club drew in about a dozen 18-year-olds. It came after an official from the sports club uploaded an Instagram post announcing BetDeluxe as a new club sponsor offering a promotional deal to players who signed up with the company. The promotion, which promised new sign-ups access to $300 and other benefits, saw about 15 people create new accounts with BetDeluxe, an arm of Northern Territory-registered bookmaker Amused Group. More than 10 18-year-old women were among those found to have responded to the promotion. A sporting club official promoted the deal in a post on the club's Instagram page. ( Reuters: Thomas White ) In a decision last month by the online gambling regulator NT Wagering Commission, Amused Group was found to have been involved in "a sustained, employee-facilitated inducement scheme operating over several weeks" involving the club. A series of text messages between a senior Amused Group employee and the sporting club official who made the post were aired in the findings, although none of the people or the club were named. The texts showed that the gambling employee, cited as Mr R, "actively encouraged [the sporting club official] Mr K, to solicit further sign-ups from his personal network" over several weeks in 2025. "Can see a couple sign-ups so far, but not many have come through," read one text by Mr R. The NT Wagering Commission regulates online gambling in the NT, but is also Australia's de facto regulator for the sector. ( ABC News: Jasmine Hines ) The commission found the Instagram post uploaded by Mr K for the club was done without the knowledge of the gambling company, which then tried to get the post immediately removed once it became aware of it. "Under 1,000 views and we have avoided a major issue," Mr R told Mr K in a text. The post was also shared on Facebook groups and via private WhatsApp messages. The Facebook and Instagram posts were later deleted. New bill could restrict major gambling companies An independent politician is set to introduce a private member's bill to the NT parliament, which if passed would impose a string of new laws on some of Australia's largest online gambling companies. However, the commission rejected Amused Group's submission that the "conduct was not intentional" and ruled the post should have been detected by the company's "internal compliance controls". "[Amused Group's] persistence and the involvement of a senior employee place it materially above an administrative or technical failure," the decision read. The commission said the fact that between 10 and 15 "individuals at the lower end of the legal wagering age were among those that responded to the promotional arrangement" was a "matter of concern in context of the licensee's responsible gaming operations". The company was fined $83,250, which the commission said reflected the "serious and knowing character of the breach, the consumer harm that occurred, the aggravating and mitigating circumstance and the objectives of general and specific deterrence". The commission also found none of those who signed up "suffered any financial loss". Amused Group collapses, owing creditors millions Since the commission's decision was handed down, Amused Group has been placed under administration, with corporate documents showing the company owes millions to creditors. In a report released on November 13 by appointed administrator Costa Nicodemou, he said, "To date, I have identified 54 unsecured creditors with claims totalling $5 million". Mr Nicodemou's report said the unsecured creditors included "a number of racing bodies". Alastair Shields says Matchday is now operating Amused's former business and "has assumed responsibility for all client funds". ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) NT Wagering Commission chair Alastair Shields told the ABC that "the wagering business previously operated by Amused Australia Pty Ltd is now being operated by another company, Matchday Entertainment Pty Ltd (Matchday)".
