events.title: HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider
events.summary: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads. “Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial . “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.” The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard , the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself). A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects. The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids. Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it. While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well). The Web’s about to get lit Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas. Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example , the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls , can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js , or to create charts with D3.js . Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon. Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas , then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code. HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X . A trippy demo from html-in-canvas.dev shows a dragon slithering through the opening chapter of an online book, with the text smoothly reflowing in its wake. Try to shoo the beast off with your cursor and it will burn the virtual text with its fiery breath. The source code reveals that “Margin Dragon” was rendered in 881 lines of vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. Another demo on the sample site is a “mouse-driven elastic displacement effect,” in which a “radial bulge” and drop shadow follow the cursor across the canvas. Of course, such stylistic enchantments will not always be used for whimsy. Inevitably, unscrupulous marketers will discover powerful new ways to annoy us about all the virtues of late-stage capitalism. “The world is not ready for HTML-in-Canvas,” a punter wrote on X . Here be dragons As per norm, HTML-in-Canvas has plenty of bugs (and it hasn’t even gone cross-platform yet). In some cases, the CSS doesn’t get painted on where it should , and timing with the reactive frameworks could be better synchronized . And there is a lot for the lowly web maintainer to learn. The core developers resolved the issue of canvas copying sensitive cross-origin data where it oughtn’t (as per CORS ), but the API does not indicate when it declines to copy the data, leaving the community to file bug reports of what appear to be silent failures. Likewise, developers must learn to properly document on-screen bounding boxes to keep accessibility tools like screen readers and click targets operating properly in 3D environments. ®

events.title: Altimeter’s Gerstner says Nvidia’s board should keep door open to Huang’s return: ‘Get this right’
events.summary: Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged Nvidia’s board on Monday to reconsider Jensen Huang’s ouster, saying the board needs “to get this right.” Gerstner said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he wasn’t calling for Huang’s immediate reinstatement as Nvidia CEO but that “everyone is rushing to judgment…and I simply don’t know the facts.” Gerstner acknowledged that Huang “engaged in personal behavior that was pretty bad,” but that he’s messaged the former CEO to express his support. He told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith that Nvidia’s success is “too critical to the future security of our country” for the board to make a wrong decision. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Gerstner co-authored a letter with Atreides Management CEO Gavin Baker sent to the Nvidia board on Friday calling for “a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Gerstner said Monday people are misinterpreting his letter as a call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement, rather than a call for a thorough investigation. “We don’t want to take shortcuts,” Gerstner said. An August SEC filing showed that Nvidia is Altimeter Capital’s largest disclosed equity holding, worth almost $1.9 billion as of June, according to CNBC . On ‘Trump accounts’ Gerstner, who was one of the architects behind the Trump Accounts, founded Boston-based Altimeter Capital in 2008. He said he expects the accounts to survive future Democratic administrations, saying they are universally popular across ideologies. He said he expected Elon Musk to personally contribute to the accounts. “Elon’s always told me he wants to do something big here,” Gerstner said. — Ben Kesslen

events.title: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
events.summary: A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide. Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel. Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said , with thousands more delayed. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday. Read more below. What caused the nationwide groundstop? What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds." Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal . The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris , has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide. After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement. How did a router disrupt flights nationwide? How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft. The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft. A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications. The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds. The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights. What to know about radio frequency outages One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions. Some reports described this as a " rolling frequency outage ," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time. This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers. Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy. What happens to pilots during the outages? Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail. These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual . The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage. Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities. Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected. What does this mean for flights? Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions. Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports. Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft. What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris. The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.

events.title: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
events.summary: One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup. With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade. To be clear, this feature is not Face ID. Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay. The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is closed. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity. The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it. Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images. The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness. Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month . Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a web page, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify. Apple is also expanding access to Apple News puzzles for News+ subscribers in Australia, the U.K., and for French-Canadian users. Australian News+ subscribers will get access to a daily quick crossword, crossword mini, and Sudoku, as well as Apple’s original puzzles, Quartiles and Emoji Game . U.K. users will get the quick crossword, the crossword mini, and Sudoku, while French-Canadian subscribers will get access to Apple’s original puzzles. The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete. events.title: SCOTUS gives DEI a boost after national assault
events.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear three conservative appeals tied to battles over diversity, equity and inclusion , leaving lower-court rulings intact in disputes over federal research grants, medical training and transgender-related speech. The big picture: The denials mark a reprieve after years of backlash against DEI, though the justices stopped short of settling the underlying constitutional debates. One of those Monday decisions set back President Trump's administration push to cancel swaths of DEI-related research grants. Driving the news: The justices rejected President Trump's bid to revive cuts to federal research grants awarded to University of California researchers over their perceived DEI-related viewpoints. A U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel ruled in May that challengers were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim that their grants were terminated because of the "perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints." That decision partly upheld a preliminary injunction from U.S. District Judge Rita Lin reinstating grants terminated over perceived DEI-related viewpoint, while reversing relief for a separate group. What they're saying: Trump's DOJ argued to the high court that allowing the grants to continue would force taxpayers to fund ideologies "their public stewards reject." A DOJ spokesperson told Axios the department will continue fighting the preliminary injunction and "will continue to advocate for the Executive Branch's lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives." Catch up quick: The challenged funding represents just a slice of the DEI-related grants ensnared in the administration's terminations and ensuing litigation. Trump has led a top-down campaign to undermine federal and corporate DEI efforts, disputes over state policies have also crept onto the national stage. Case in point: The Supreme Court also declined to hear a challenge from the anti-trans Gays Against Groomers against Colorado lawmakers' restrictions on misgendering and deadnaming during legislative hearings. The Tenth Circuit had found lawmakers were shielded by legislative immunity. Meanwhile: The justices also declined to hear a challenge to required implicit bias training for California continuing medical education courses. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated he would've heard the appeal brought by an ophthalmologist and a conservative medical advocacy group. Justice Clarence Thomas penned a dissent, joined by Justice Samuel Alito. Thomas' argument indicates there may be an appetite for a similar question about government speech in the future: "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny," he wrote. What we're watching: Both in the courts and in the public arena , disputes over the federal administration and state leaders' handling of DEI initiatives are still playing out with many more sure to come. But on Monday, a high court that hasn't always sided with DEI initiatives declined to further some key debates — for now. Go deeper: Trump says he "ended DEI." Courts disagree

events.title: How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment
events.summary: Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”. The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions. Many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill. That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable. On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people. Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work. In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line. After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity. Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them. “Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.” He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard. Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip. Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead. Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market. Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment. His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”. The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term. The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have. His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs. So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people.

events.title: There's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costs. How it could impact your bill
events.summary: As Americans wrestle with inflation, there's a growing "property tax revolt" to reduce or limit property taxes amid rising home values. In 2020, the median sales price for U.S. single-family homes was about $300,000, compared with roughly $419,000 in 2025, according to the National Association of Realtors. During the midterm election, property taxes were on the ballot in several states, including Florida, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Property tax relief could impact local government services and infrastructure, experts say. Affordable housing was a key midterm election issue , and as Americans wrestle with rising home costs , there's a growing movement to reduce or limit property taxes. Amid soaring home values , some states want to cap how much local governments can collect from homeowners. Experts have described the trend as a " property tax revolt ." During the Nov. 3 midterm election, Florida voters approved Amendment 3 , which increases the portion of primary residences exempt from property tax for non-school levies and lowers the cap on yearly assessments for certain properties. North Carolina voters approved an amendment to require the state legislature to enact limits on property tax increases, while voters in Oklahoma and Wyoming rejected other property tax measures. Despite the "mixed bag" on midterm ballot initiative results, "I think we'll continue to see property tax reforms," said Matthew Chase, CEO of the National Association of Counties, or NACo, a nonprofit organization that represents county governments. Property taxes are levied as a percentage of a home's assessed value, based on its estimated market rate. Some municipalities use a millage rate — with one mill equaling $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable assessed value — to calculate property tax bills. That rate can adjust up or down based on changes in home values and the local government's budget needs. In some cases, property tax bills can be bigger due to higher assessments, even when local governments lower the millage rate, experts say. Property taxes vary widely throughout the U.S., with yearly bills ranging from less than $250 in some rural counties to more than $10,000 in areas near large cities, according to 2026 data from the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research organization. Affordability concerns prompt tax cuts Nationwide, the property tax cut movement has been "driven by affordability," according to NACo's Chase. As "home values have gone up, property taxes have gone up with it," he said. In 2020, the median sales price for U.S. single-family homes was about $300,000, compared with roughly $419,000 in 2025 , according to the National Association of Realtors. Last year, the median property tax bill for owner-occupied homes was around $3,300 , the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey reported. Higher property tax bills have been a burden, experts say, as homeowners have wrestled with rising costs for groceries, gasoline and other living expenses. That's sparked more demand for property tax relief. From January 2020 to June 2026, state lawmakers enacted at least 168 property tax measures — including exemptions, credits, refunds and more — across 40 states and the District of Columbia, according to an October report from NACo. Property tax cut proponents argue local governments should rein in spending . But other experts say the relief will cause revenue shortfalls that impact local schools, police and fire services, roads and other infrastructure. "There's no realistic way to replace property taxes in most states," said Jared Walczak, a senior fellow at the Tax Foundation. Typically, property taxes are a more stable revenue source compared to income or sales taxes, which can decline during an economic downturn as consumers earn and spend less, experts say. Reliance on the tax varies, but property taxes are the single largest local levy revenue source for most local governments, accounting for about 28% of local funding nationally in 2024, according to the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, an independent, nonpartisan foundation and think tank. "It's easy to savor property tax cuts in abstract," Walczak said. "It can often be much more challenging to define a replacement system that anyone actually likes.

events.title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
events.summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement. The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers. In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.” But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union. Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already. Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said. “We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post. UPS plane, Copa Airlines flight collide on taxiway at Miami International Airport Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal. Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely. Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration. “We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said. In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later. But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court. events.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy. “He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims. The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report. Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang. “A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. events.title: US won’t restrict foreign tech companies in allied countries, State Dept. official says
events.summary: The US government has “no plans” to target or “orchestrate the deep pruning” of technology companies headquartered in allied countries from American supply chains, Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg said Monday. Speaking alongside ASML’s President and CEO Christophe Fouquet at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Helberg rejected “top-down government-mandated plans that intentionally discriminate” against companies based on their country of origin in comments to Semafor’s Ashley Gold. He named ASML, Samsung, and SK Hynix as key partners to US firms in the technology supply chain. Discussing Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains, Helberg said that the Trump administration wants to ensure companies across allied economies benefit from a “level playing field.” He described the initiative as a “capability-centric coalition” that draws on the comparative strength of participating countries. Helberg also argued that Washington must balance technological leadership with global market share of AI-focused companies, warning that innovation alone will not secure America’s dominance in the fast-growing technology field. “We need both in order to win the AI race,” Helberg said. “We need to lead the world qualitatively and have the best innovation out there. But we also need market share, and those two things need to happen in conjunction.” Helberg also stopped short of endorsing three bipartisan bills that lawmakers are considering including in the year-end defense bill that would tighten AI chip export controls following the Nvidia controversy. Asked about the investigation involving Nvidia, Helberg described the company as critical to US technological leadership, saying “there is a really compelling argument for national security to have Nvidia continue to be a leading beacon of innovation.” He called for investigations to establish the facts quickly, adding, “Our hope is obviously to see serious work being done through the investigations to uncover the facts and get to the truth quickly in order to get to the right outcome.” Nvidia has attracted scrutiny from Congress as well as the administration amid revelations that now-former CEO Jensen Huang had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. — Lauren Morganbesser

Traders are preparing for this week's blockbuster Anthropic IPO in different ways, including buying options on one publicly-traded fund that invests in private assets. The Destiny Tech100 (DXYZ) is a publicly-traded, closed-end fund that invests in equity, equity-linked instruments, or shares of private funds and venture companies to gain exposure to private companies. Traders may want to be wary of how the fund traded around the SpaceX IPO: DXYZ surged almost 150% in May before unwinding all the gains in the weeks ahead of SpaceX's debut. events.title: I started a handbag company at 22 and grew it into a fashion sportswear brand with partners like MLB. Here's what I've learned.
events.summary: Zara Terez Tisch is the founder of Terez, a fashion sportswear company based in New York City. Natalie Keyssar for BI At 22, Zara Terez Tisch launched a handbag company called Terez from her parents' home. Terez evolved into a fashion and sportswear brand with MLB partnerships. Her advice is to build an excellent product with a distinct point of view — not just a story. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Zara Terez Tisch, the founder of Terez, a fashion sportswear company based in New York City. It has been edited for length and clarity. I started Terez as a handbag company, from my parents' home on Long Island when I was 22. After college, I was fortunate to live at home without paying rent, which allowed me to save money while my friends moved to Manhattan. I worked in marketing and branding and had always been a creative person, but I was going through a difficult period in my life. I had experienced a lot of loss and was trying to get on my feet. I knew I wanted to create something that made me feel good about myself, and Terez was born. The business has taken several turns over the years. After handbags, I moved into activewear and eventually found an opportunity to bring fashion to professional sports by partnering with major leagues. Today, Terez sits at the intersection of sports and fashion. Natalie Keyssar for BI The early days of building Terez In 2008, when I was still working in marketing, which I quit later that year, I was walking through the West Village in Manhattan on an errand. I came across a leather shop with a sign that said, "Customize your own leather handbags." I walked in and asked, "Do I just draw a handbag and you make it?" I also asked whether they could make 500 bags, or even 1,000. They thought I was crazy, but said they could do it. I decided to work with them to start a business. I started with handbags with fun interiors, including comic-book strips and disco sequins. I wanted to get the happiness inside me out again while representing New York City. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch I started gaining some traction I was doing it all myself, carrying samples with me. I didn't sell them on a website. Instead, I did trunk shows at people's homes. The first one was at my sister's friend's house on Long Island. Not long after I started, I asked my father to come back with me to meet the manufacturers. I thought it would help them take me more seriously. Zara's father, Richard Zimmerman, and sister, Darlene Barzilay, at his Budget Dress showroom during Darlene's 21st birthday celebration in 1986. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch My dad was a garment manufacturer — a 'garmento,' as people in the industry called it. He had worked in the industry in the 1970s, 1980s, and into the 1990s. As manufacturing moved to China and overseas, he had to close his company. I witnessed that, and bringing manufacturing back to New York became part of my story. In 2012, the business took another turn The linings I used in my handbags were made of spandex. I was wearing leggings all the time, so I started making them out of the same spandex at a factory in Queens. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch My parents had started a business manufacturing clothing for tweens. I brought the leggings to one of their children's trade shows to see if it would stick. A store called Lester's picked them up and put them in its store over Thanksgiving weekend. The buyer called me on Monday and said, "You really have something here." The leggings started taking off. We became a popular brand for tweens and teens We created prints and styles that made them feel confident in who they were. We started with galaxy leggings and star-themed designs, then added emojis to them. We would drop new designs every month. Natalie Keyssar for BI The next decade was a period of significant growth for Terez. As demand for activewear grew, department-store buyers began creating dedicated categories for it, and Terez became a key brand in that expansion. We partnered with SoulCycle on limited-edition drops and with Bloomingdale's. We opened our first store in 2022 In the fall of 2022, we opened our first physical store on the Upper East Side. It's the smallest part of the business in terms of revenue, but it's the heart and soul of the brand. Soon after the store opened, a woman came in, and I helped her shop. I showed her our whole collection and told her everything about the brand. When she was checking out, she asked, "Have you ever thought about working with Major League Baseball?" I hadn't. She pointed out that nobody was really focusing on women's clothing for the fans. The options were mostly bubblegum V-neck T-shirts with sequin script logos. Natalie Keyssar for BI The next day, I got a text from an exec at Major League Baseball. The woman who had come into the store was associated with the organization. He told me they wanted Terez to shape the look of the women's collection. I immediately called our head of design and said, " We have to stop everything that we're doing right now and focus on a women's collection for Major League Baseball." Working with professional sports opened up new ways to reach customers Today, we work with multiple professional sports teams and leagues. We sell through our own site, our Upper East Side store, licensed sports channels, and fashion retail partners like Revolve. Natalie Keyssar for BI Partnering with sports has opened up completely new channels for us. Since making our debut with Major League Baseball, our revenue has tripled. I've learned that hiring more people doesn't necessarily make a business more efficient When we were first doing activewear, we had a period of high growth, and the company grew to around 40-something people in 2018 and 2019. Up until that point, I hadn't felt confident enough in myself to run the business side and manage the company's numbers. I always thought I should surround myself with people who were smarter than me. What I realized was that people weren't always efficient in their roles, so we would hire more people to do the same job, sometimes two or three times. I called them Band-Aids. By the end of 2020, we narrowed down to a team of around 10 people. I picked up all the pieces after a rocky situation with one employee and told everyone, "We're either going to do this all together, and we're going to succeed together, or we're going to fail together." Natalie Keyssar for BI Since then, I haven't wanted to grow our team. The majority of the people on my team now were on my team 10 years ago. To have people on your team who care as much as you do is extremely rare. I want the business to reflect what we believe in When people ask me for advice about starting a business, I always come back to the product and deeply caring about your team. You can only tell a story for so long. You need to make sure your product is excellent, high-quality, and has a distinct point of view. What differentiat

events.title: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
events.summary: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind. The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan . But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs , each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz. The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer , built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking. Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger. ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs. Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64. As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale. In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with enough vector and matrix units to put more than a few modern GPUs to shame. With enough of them – by which we mean 22,680 dual-socket nodes – NSCS catapulted China to the top of the Top500 for the first time in nearly a decade. Not the benchmark it used to be The US has no shortage of systems capable of eclipsing El Capitan or even LineShine’s performance if someone were motivated enough to get HPL running on them. SpaceXAI’s 300 megawatt Colossus supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, boasts 200,000 Hopper GPUs each good for 34-67 (vector/matrix) teraFLOPS of FP64 grunt. Even assuming an abysmal 25% efficiency, the cluster should be more than capable of breaking three exaFLOPs in HPL. It might need 10x the power of El Capitan, but the thing is, beyond winning points with the White House — a ship that has almost certainly sailed for Elon Musk after the DOGE fiasco — renting out the cluster to Anthropic to train and run Claude is a far more lucrative endeavor. The same could be said of any number of AI clusters, from Meta’s Prometheus to OpenAI’s Starship. It used to be that the systems to summit the Top500 were among the largest computers humanity has ever built. But this hasn’t been true in some time. The US is starving for compute. HPL or even its sibling High-Performance Gradient Conjugate just aren’t the benchmarks to beat any longer. The new battleground isn’t nuclear proliferation; it’s one of AI models, agents, and the means to harness them. We’re not talking about tokens, LLMs, or chatbots, but the ability to harness these models to automate laboratories and formulate and test hypotheses long after the scientists they serve have gone home for dinner. It’s why the US’s Genesis mission puts such a strong emphasis on AI. AI-driven labs present an opportunity for researchers to iterate faster. Rather than running hundreds or thousands or simulations trying to find a needle in a haystack, a task for which a bigger iron is warranted, AI analysis and automation could focus that search. High-performance computing (HPC), and by extension the Top500, will remain relevant as long as more FLOPS means more simulations per unit of time. But these systems can only move as fast as the men and women who operate them. ®

events.title: Every actor who has played James Bond, ranked from worst to best
events.summary: Daniel Craig, Sean Connery and Pierce Brosnan as James Bond. MGM Robert Pattinson is the newest James Bond. Before he gets his license to kill, let's celebrate who came before him. Business Insider ranked all seven actors who have portrayed Bond in film. Over 60 years and 25 movies, seven actors have played the legendary spy James Bond on screen. Daniel Craig was the latest to take on the character created by novelist Ian Fleming, bringing a darker, grittier tone to the franchise. His run came to an end in 2021's " No Time To Die ," when his Bond, well, died. Now a new 007 has emerged. Robert Pattinson is officially the next James Bond . Before he debuts his version of Bond, here's where all the best Bonds rank. Zac Ntim, Eammon Jacobs, and Ayomikun Adekaiyero contributed to previous versions of this story. David Niven (1967-1967) David Niven as James Bond in 1967's "Casino Royale." Columbia Pictures While most audiences automatically think of Daniel Craig when thinking of " Casino Royale ," there was actually another version of the story that arrived on the big screen back in 1967. (Yes, in the same year as Sean Connery's "You Only Live Twice.") Columbia Pictures' "Casino Royale" starred David Niven as James Bond, and takes a more comedic approach to Ian Fleming's book of the same name. The parody movie isn't connected to any of the other films, nor was it made by Eon Productions and Albert Broccoli. It was only made because Fleming sold the singular rights to the book before it was published in 1953. Niven's Bond is a much older agent who's brought out of retirement to fight a nefarious organization called S.M.E.R.S.H. The Oscar-winning actor brings some charm to the role, but the absurd story — which ends with him going to heaven — ruins the character and sucks all the suave out of 007. George Lazenby (1969-1969) George Lansbury as James Bond. MGM Australian actor George Lazenby is on this list as another matter of courtesy. He was drafted by Eon Productions, the film's producers, to play Bond once in 1969's "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" after Sean Connery decided to step away. He was promptly replaced by Roger Moore when the series resumed in 1973 with "Live and Let Die."  Pierce Brosnan (1995-2002) Pierce Brosnan filming "007" in 1997. Markus Beck/picture alliance via Getty Images After 15 years of Daniel Craig — who is eulogized later in this list — it is easy to forget the damage Pierce Brosnan did to the James Bond franchise. But it's important to revisit our lowest moments so we can grow. So here, I humbly ask, do we remember the unfortunate orange spray tan Brosnan sported throughout his time as 007? Or the awkward hyperpop theme songs like Madonna's awful "Die Another Day"? It's important to note that Brosnan's first Bond film, "GoldenEye," was also the first film in the franchise not produced by Albert R. Broccoli: His daughter, Barbara Broccoli, and his stepson, Michael G. Wilson, took over. But it's been reported that Brosnan was favored by Albert Broccoli. Nonetheless, across his four-film run, Brosnan pushed Bond away from its steely, cool origins to something more Hollywood and less interesting.   Roger Moore (1973-1985) British actor Roger Moore, playing the title role of secret service agent 007, James Bond, is shown on location in England in 1972. AP Photo Roger Moore suited up as James Bond a record seven times. The bulk of his films were helmed by the British director John Glen, who had an unparalleled skill for capturing pure chaos on screen. And that is what Moore's Bond was best known for. In his seven-film run, Moore went to space, fought off a pack of crocodiles, and defused a nuclear bomb. While Moore's Bond was charismatic and entertaining, there was rarely any substance to what he said, and there was even less plot to hold together the big-budget stunts. For this reason, Moore's seven films don't make for great rewatching.  Timothy Dalton (1987-1989) Timothy Dalton as James Bond. MGM The sole reason Timothy Dalton is not at the top of this list is that he portrayed Bond only twice. This wasn't due to bad ratings or box-office numbers, however. His films, "The Living Daylights" (1987) and "Licence to Kill" (1989), are two of the most beloved Bond films, and Dalton's dark and often serious take on 007 is widely considered the most accurate interpretation of Fleming's books.  "I wanted to make him human," Dalton said of his interpretation of Bond during an interview in 2008 . "He's not a superman; you can't identify with a superman. You can identify with the James Bond of the books. He's a tarnished man, really. I wanted to capture that occasional sense of vulnerability and I wanted to capture the spirit of Ian Fleming." As many people have stated before, Dalton's grounding of Bond paved the way for the franchise's most profitable period of releases with Daniel Craig's 007. Dalton's tenure, however, was cut short due to complex legal wrangling between the film's producers MGM and Eon Productions, which halted production until 1994, when his contract expired.  Sean Connery (1962-1967) Sean Connery as the original movie James Bond. United Artists Sean Connery had a legendary acting career that spanned over 50 movies and included appearances in some of Hollywood's most iconic films like 1964's "Marnie," 1989's "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade," and 1987's "The Untouchables," for which he won an Oscar for best supporting actor. But when he died in 2020, he was best remembered as the first 007.  According to Connery, however, his interpretation of 007 managed to charm everyone but Fleming. "I never got introduced to Fleming until I was well into the movie, but I know he was not happy with me as the choice," Connery said on "The South Bank Show" in 2008. Despite Fleming's reservations, Connery played the secret agent in seven films from 1962 to 1983, and his version is remembered as not only the coolest in the franchise but one of the coolest characters in cinematic history.  Connery's powers as 007 came from his own charisma. As Barbara Walters described him in a 1987 interview, the Scotsman was someone who didn't try to be sexy; he simply oozed class. Connery can also claim to be the only Bond actor who actually managed to pull off the famous catchphrase, "Martini, shaken, not stirred" and make it sound cool. Best: Daniel Craig (2006-2021) Daniel Craig as James Bond in "No Time to Die" MGM Daniel Craig's Bond films are dark, physical, and entertaining. But it is Craig's commercial success that has landed him atop this list. The numbers simply don't lie: 2012's "Skyfall," Craig's third outing as Bond and first collaboration with the British director Sam Mendes ("American Beauty"), raked in $1.1 billion at the worldwide box office, making it the most commercially successful Bond film of all time.  Craig's portrait of the top-secret British spy helped to revive th

events.summary: Disney reports earnings Tuesday before the bell. The market is unable to divert its attention from anything not related to the ongoing saga that is Nvidia and its embattled former CEO Jensen Huang. It's understandable, given both the detail of the story and Nvidia impact on the market. It remains the tech story du jour, and it's getting plenty of ink. I think investors should remember there are other big names reporting this week outside of Nvidia that deserve time and attention. One such name is The Walt Disney Company (DIS) . After a prolonged period of strategic transitions, the company may finally be turning the corner. Driven by a renewed focus on the bottom line, management's cost discipline now supports a runway for double-digit earnings-per-share (EPS) gains through fiscal 2027, even as it continues to trade at about its 5-year average forward multiple of 14.3x, well below the broad market multiple of more than 18x. Trading back to a market multiple, justified if it establishes above-market EPS growth, suggests ~26% upside, which is also consistent with a sum-of-the-parts analysis that points to an intrinsic valuation of $140 to $160 per share versus the Friday, November 13th closing price of $118.97. Disney reports Tuesday before the bell. Despite broader macroeconomic anxieties, the theme park and cruise divisions are showing surprisingly resilient demand. Domestically, the metrics are highly encouraging: attendance is climbing, and more importantly, per-capita spending continues to rise. On the digital front, Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) Disney's streaming margins currently sit in the low teens, respectable given the segment's previous lack of profits. But the real upside scenario requires looking ahead: if Disney can scale these DTC margins to 20% or higher, the stock could at least trade at a multiple comparable to streaming king Netflix (which would imply a share price of ~ $139 or so. Part of the reason the studio segment remains a mixed bag is that, while there are periodic blockbuster bright spots, Disney's theatrical recovery remains uneven overall. Furthermore, legacy media continues its secular decline. The pay-TV industry has likely lost around 40 million subscribers—representing a staggering 40% erosion of the user base since 2015—and will likely lose more this year. However, the critical takeaway for investors is that the pace of cord-cutting is finally slowing down. With linear TV stabilizing, the parks firing on all cylinders, and streaming marching toward higher profitability, Disney offers a highly asymmetric risk-reward profile. The magic is returning to Disney's financials, and the current share price heavily discounts a business fundamentally engineered for double-digit growth. Right now, the options market is pricing a ~6% move by the end of the week (the company reports Tuesday, pre-open), which is below the 8 quarter median move of 7.4%. Anticipating a "vol crush" after earnings, I like selling December premium to help finance the purchase of a longer-dated call - a diagonal call/spread risk reversal. When selecting an option trade consider the key things that affect its value and how those things differ from simply buying (or selling) the underlying asset. For these option trades, let's consider three sensitivities (Greeks): Delta, the rate at which the option position changes in value for changes in the underlying price. Theta, or decay, which measures how much the value of an option declines as time passes, and Vega, the change in an option's price associated with changes in the implied volatility of an option. In the case of the diagonal risk reversal each of these factors plays into the structure to our benefit. The delta of the structure is less than 100, meaning that the p&l associated with moves up or down will be less for one spread than they would be for 100 shares of stock. We like this because the stock has already had a decent run recently, and the option structure will lose less than the stock will if it gives that back. Because nearer dated expiration decay more rapidly as a percentage of the options value than longer dated options do (and out of the money options also exhibit accelerated decay), the shorter dated December options we're selling should decay in value more quickly than the longer dated March options we are buying, even though the March option has a higher premium. Vega can work in our favor as well due to "vol crush". When option premiums are elevated due to a catalyst such as earnings we should expect that much of that premium will be sucked out or crushed once the event has passed.

events.title: Trump says he's OK with Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO, sees no national security risk
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he is open to Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia as CEO following his resignation last week under fire for an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said he had no plans to replace Howard Lutnick, despite criticism leveled at the commerce secretary over the Nvidia scandal and the sale of advanced AI chips to China. A spokesperson for House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast told CNBC "negotiations are still going" about Huang testifying before a trio of House committees. President Donald Trump said he would be open to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returning to the company he resigned from last week amid the fallout from an extramarital relationship he had with an alleged Chinese spy. "I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said of Huang when asked by reporters on Monday whether he wants to see the company co-founder reinstated as CEO. Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for a trip to Asia, downplayed national security concerns stemming from the affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company that U.S. officials suspect of having funneled Nvidia's advanced chips to China. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. Trump is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. How Trump traded Nvidia stock as he championed the chipmaker Trump says Nvidia scandal did not put U.S. national security 'at risk,' defends Lutnick Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on China workaround of restrictions Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe The president told reporters he is not planning to replace Howard Lutnick as commerce secretary after questions arose about the Cabinet member's handling of export controls involving Nvidia's advanced chips. Republican and Democratic members of Congress have raised concerns about the national security implications of the episode after it was revealed that Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in the 1990s, had an extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading global supplier of advanced artificial intelligence chips. Critics argue the affair could jeopardize the U.S.' global dominance in AI and that it raises questions about influence exerted by Nvidia's Huang on regulators and lawmakers as he opposed export controls that limited the sale of the company's chips to Chinese firms. The New York Times reported Tuesday that the U.S. believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that Secretary of State Marco Rubio alerted Trump to the situation aboard Air Force One in May before Jensen Huang joined the president on a flight to China. The Washington Post reported Friday that Rubio had issued a memo to Trump warning the president about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. But Trump on Monday said "I haven't heard that" when asked about Rubio's warning. "I don't know that she is a spy. Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said, of Alice Huang. "I don't know that she was a spy at all." Trump also attempted to defuse tension bubbling within his Cabinet between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Lutnick. Axios reported last week that Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, prompting a Situation Room confrontation between the men. Both are traveling with Trump on Monday to Asia, as is Rubio. And Bessent, in an appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday, seemed to express frustration at Lutnick for not putting Megaspeed, Alice Huang's former company, on a Commerce Department list of companies that pose national security concerns. The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the 'entity list' for months," Bessent said. Trump acknowledged on Monday that Lutnick might have delayed putting Megaspeed on the list but defended his rationale as essential for diplomacy. "He was doing that because you could have — if you didn't delay it, If you didn't do something — you could have a blow-up with China," Trump said. "We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides." Trump, who previously had said he did not plan to raise the Jensen Huang issue with Xi when they meet this week, said he may do so.

events.title: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
events.summary: A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content. This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft. Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit. Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying. “Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be. “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.” With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves. “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said. What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning. Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks. The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience , which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps. Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch , Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj. Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer. The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed. The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year. events.title: Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar said. A petition for Huang's return has circulated online, with signatures from people like Elon Musk. Huang resigned as CEO last week. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider. The confirmation comes as support mounts for Huang's return both inside and outside the company, including an online petition that has garnered more than 180,000 signatures from bold-faced names like Elon Musk and Garry Tan. CNBC first reported the board's position on Monday, adding that it remained focused on the ongoing investigation. Nvidia announced last Thursday that Huang had resigned from his role. It follows an extramarital affair scandal and a board investigation into concerns that he may have been the subject of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia's board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct that investigation, with former federal prosecutor Joon Kim leading it. The Financial Times reported over the weekend that Huang had discussed the possibility of returning to Nvidia, and that fellow Silicon Valley executives were supporting him, including trying to rally support from the White House. President Donald Trump said Monday that he "would not mind" seeing Huang back at the chip giant's helm. Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress became interim CEO on Thursday. The board's new chair, Harvey Jones, said that the company would seek a permanent succeessor, and that it was considering both internal and external candidates. Have a tip? events.title: The man with the golden touch: James Bond franchise is a money-spinner
events.summary: Big-screen debut of Ian Fleming’s creation in 1962, with Sean Connery as lead in Dr No, was start of marketing dream New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson Robert Pattinson’s journey to James Bond J ames Bond may be 73 years old but the superspy holds a licence to print money, at the centre of an evergreen multibillion-pound franchise spanning blockbuster films, merchandise, licensing deals and sponsorship. The announcement that the Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson is the next Bond comes seven years after Daniel Craig revealed that No Time To Die would be his last outing as 007. This means that by the time Pattinson makes his first appearance it will have been the longest gap in instalments in the 64-year history of the film franchise, an agonisingly long hiatus for the centrepiece of a sprawling commercial enterprise. While Ian Fleming initially struggled to get Hollywood interested in his debonair, womanising British novel creation, the big-screen debut of Sean Connery in 1962’s Dr No marked the start of a marketing dream. The 25 feature films to date – the world’s second longest-running film franchise after Godzilla – have taken almost $8bn (£6bn) at the global box office, making it the fifth most successful property in cinema history, behind only the sprawling Marvel Cinematic Universe, Star Wars, Harry Potter and Spider-Man. When Amazon acquired the famed Hollywood studio MGM – home to 4,000 film titles including the Rocky and Bond franchises, as well as 17,000 hours of TV programming – four years ago, some analysts estimated that the superspy could be worth half of the $8.5bn price tag of the whole library. The estimate of the on-screen value of Bond was underscored last year when Amazon paid more than $1bn to take full “creative control” of the franchise from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the longtime stewards of the films who had retained significant power, unlocking the potential to develop a Star Wars or Marvel-like “universe” of film and TV spin-offs. Plans for one potential spin-off in 2002 – a movie based on the character Jinx, played by Halle Berry in Die Another Day – were scrapped the following year, while the highly successful Young Bond series of books for young adults has never made it beyond print. Beyond the box office, the carefully cultivated prestige image of Bond has proven a brand association dream, a marketing juggernaut impervious even to Daniel Craig’s critical assessment a decade ago that the spy was a “lonely, sexist misogynist” . Charlotte Mair, the founder of The Fitting Room, a communications and culture agency, says: “Bond is a brand in its own right, with associations of sophistication, adventure, luxury and craftsmanship, timelessness and, of course, Britishness. “Bond is a standalone entertainment property, with its own identity, heritage, mythology and extraordinary brand equity. Its partners aren’t simply buying exposure around a film release. They are aligning themselves with a brand that has been building its own cultural currency and influence for more than 60 years.” The 141-year-old Turnbull & Asser, the personal shirtmaker to the king – who bestowed the company with his first royal warrant as the Prince of Wales in 1980 – has created shirts for Bond actors since Connery appeared in the first film. Lock & Co, the world’s oldest hatters, with roots dating to 1676, started its Bond relationship with one of its hats appearing in the now-famous opening credit gun barrel scene that debuted in Dr No. Aston Martin has long been considered Bond’s sports car of choice, debuting in 1964’s Goldfinger, and a bespoke DB10 was created for 2015’s Spectre to celebrate a 50-year partnership with the franchise, but deals remain on a film-by-film basis. The N.Peal cashmere turtleneck worn by Daniel Craig in the poster for Spectre sold out almost immediately. A grey, custom-made Tom Ford suit worn by the actor in Skyfall went to auction last month with hopes it would fetch as much as £40,000 . The “Bond effect” lures big sponsorship deals, reportedly worth anywhere from $45m, with deep-pocketed corporates. Heineken, which has partnered Bond films since 1997, has spent as much as $100m on sponsorship, product placement and global marketing supporting a single film – even if many fans were outraged to see 007’s “shaken not stirred” Martini staple replaced by a pint. Omega’s long-running sponsorship, dating back to 1995 when it replaced Rolex as Bond’s timepiece of choice, included being directly namechecked by the superspy in Casino Royale. Various guesstimates have been put on the value of sponsorships, from as much as $5bn over the lifetime of the franchise to date, to about $200m a film in the modern era. “If the Super Bowl is advertising’s biggest stage, James Bond is the ultimate brand partnership platform,” Mair says. “Some brands have become so intrinsically linked to the franchise that they are part of Bond’s DNA.
