events.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
events.summary: Salon owner: 'We have parents offering to pay their kids' wages' National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge. There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show. Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest. Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads". She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages. "I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said. Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters. "I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs." The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full. He has already unveiled some of his proposals including: Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits. Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000. This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100. Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase. Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank. Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money. But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing". Milburn told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers. "Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said. "The state has a responsibility to help them with that." On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit. People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales. McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029". events.title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
events.summary: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. events.title: Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed
events.summary: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon. During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators. NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size. Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation.” “It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained. Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained. In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems. A compute chameleon LANL is one of several labs tasked with ensuring that the US’ nuclear deterrent remains effective decades after underground testing was banned. The lab is also responsible for running simulations on energy sources like fuel candidates for future fusion reactors. Both of these workloads, Shipman tells us, fall into a category called multi-physics simulations. These workloads aren’t really one workload, but multiple simulations that can have wildly different compute requirements. A “good example is inertial confinement fusion. At the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, you're using lasers to implode a fuel capsule, and the goal is to generate more energy through yield than you do from depositing energy to the capsule,” Shipman explained. “That's inherently multiphysics.” There are simulations for the lasers, the hydrodynamics within the fuel capsule, and the chemistry and material interactions taking place during the fusion process. The problem, Shipman explains, is that a system that’s ideal for one of those simulations may not be well suited to others. “Identifying one specific platform that is optimal for that type of simulation is challenging.” CPUs, he says, are well suited to workloads with large serial sections, irregular access patterns, and jobs that benefit from deep cache hierarchies. Meanwhile, GPUs are fantastic for dense, matrix-multiplication heavy workloads. "Where NextSilicon fits in is being able to reconfigure to match the workload, on demand,” Shipman said. “The hope is that we won't have to make these rigid determinations upfront like, ‘we need this much CPU or we need this much GPU.’ We can use a much more adaptable, reconfigurable architecture to meet the workflow where it is at.” A closer look at Maverick 2 Despite some visual similarities to Nvidia’s current crop of GPUs, Maverick-2 is not a GPU. Instead it employs a dataflow architecture which overlaps communication and computation. Rather than waiting for load-store operations to shuffle data around as you would with a conventional CPU or GPU, the chips themselves comprise a grid of arithmetic logic units (ALUs) which are configured to perform an operation like addition or multiplication in the order that they’re needed. Data is computed as it moves from one ALU to the next, a bit like how a ball moves through a Rube Goldberg contraption. This can make dataflow architectures extremely efficient in bandwidth-bound scenarios, which has implications not only for HPC and scientific computing but also for AI. It’s why we’re seeing dataflow accelerators, like Nvidia’s Groq, Cerebras’ WSE-3, and SambaNova’s SN50, being deployed as decode accelerators in AI inference clusters. Where NextSilicon stands out is that its designs, so far, have been specifically tailored toward sparse double-precision FP64 workloads. Real FLOPS are rarely advertised Programming dataflow architectures, historically, has been a challenging endeavor. To overcome this, NextSilicon claims to have developed a compiler that can decompose any existing C, Python, Fortran, or CUDA codebases into a graph that can run directly on its chips. So far, NextSilicon has managed to validate its systems against the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the LAMMPS molecular dynamics test suite, and the Sparta Monte Carlo simulation suite. But as NextSilicon CEO Elad Raz notes, the roofline performance of Maverick-2 is different from one workload to another, and so the company has opted not to advertise peak theoretical performance the same way GPU vendors like Nvidia or AMD have traditionally done. That’s not to say NextSilicon is shy about Maverick’s performance characteristics. Rather than advertising peak performance that the chip may not be able to hit in the workloads its customers actually care most about, it published performance figures across a swath of HPC benchmarks. For example, in HPCG, one of the closest watched HPC benchmarks after High Performance Linpack (HPL), NextSilicon says a single Maverick achieves 600 gigaFLOPS of performance, which it says is on par with contemporary GPUs but at half the power. That’s just fine and dandy as far as Shipman is concerned. He tells us peak advertised performance is rarely a useful proxy for real-world performance. “The thing that my team spends the most time on is how do we generate representative proxies, representative kernels; how do we generate specifications that communicate our needs to the broader ecosystem so that vendors like NextSilicon can meet us and co-design with us.” ®

events.title: Who is Leo KoGuan, the Singapore-based billionaire backing Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Indonesia-born investor Leo KoGuan has also backed Elon Musk’s Tesla. Leo KoGuan, a Singapore-based billionaire, said he would not buy more Nvidia shares without Jensen Huang, whom he called “the supreme creator”. Huang’s exit after reported affairs and a 33-year run shook Nvidia, sent shares down 12.8%, and sparked calls from tech leaders for his return. KoGuan built his fortune through SHI International and Tesla, and has made major Singapore buys, including the Dysons’ Wallich Residence penthouse and 21 Carpenter hotel. SINGAPORE – Billionaire investor Leo KoGuan on Nov 13 said that he would not buy more Nvidia shares without co-founder Jensen Huang at the helm. This came a day after the US chipmaker announced Huang’s resignation. KoGuan, who called Huang “the supreme creator” in posts on X, argued that his achievements should count for more than his mistakes and said that he had invested about US$1.3 billion (S$1.7 billion) in Nvidia. The artificial intelligence and semicon heavyweight has a market capitalisation of about US$3.9 trillion as at Nov 16. KoGuan’s backing for Huang comes as prominent tech figures push for his return to Nvidia. Elon Musk, Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator president Garry Tan and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick were among the signatories of an open letter urging Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. More than 7,500 signatories reportedly identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia followed reports of three extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US authorities suspect of spying for China. His departure ended a 33-year run at the helm of Nvidia, the company he co-founded and whose chips now power much of the AI boom. The company named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive officer. Amid the turmoil, Nvidia shares fell 12.8% in the week to Nov 13, closing at US$162.85, even as chip stocks as a group rose about 8% the same week, noted Kenneth Goh, director of private wealth management at UOB Kay Hian. He added that the shares could remain under pressure until Nvidia’s board names a successor who has the confidence of key stakeholders. “KoGuan is saying out loud what a lot of investors feel. Many of them bought Nvidia because of Jensen Huang,” Goh said. “His own holding is small, well under 1% of the company. He has also only said he will stop adding. He has not said he is selling.” KoGuan first drew wider attention for his bet on Tesla. In Singapore, he made headlines for his high-profile property purchases, such as that of the Dysons’ Wallich Residence penthouse. KoGuan, 71, was born in Indonesia to Chinese parents. He moved to the US, where he earned a master’s degree in international affairs from Columbia University and a law degree from New York Law School. In 1989, he and his then wife, Thai Lee, paid less than US$1 million for a struggling New Jersey software reseller with five employees and about as many customers. The business became Software House International, now known as SHI International. SHI has since expanded beyond software reselling into hardware, cloud computing and cybersecurity services. It serves more than 17,000 customers, including Boeing, Johnson & Johnson and AT&T, and employs about 7,000 people worldwide. KoGuan told Bloomberg in 2021 that he had stepped back from day-to-day operations around the turn of the century. He remains chairman, while Lee is president and chief executive officer. In October 2025, SHI said it reached US$16 billion in gross sales over the preceding 12 months. It also announced an investment in AI engineering consultancy NStarX, giving clients of its New Jersey AI and cybersecurity lab access to NStarX’s data scientists. KoGuan began buying Tesla shares in 2019. He built a concentrated position through shares and options. Bank records showed that he held 6.3 million Tesla shares and 1.8 million options as at September 2021. The options gave him the right to buy Tesla shares at prices ranging from US$450 to US$550 apiece. He was one of the carmaker’s largest individual shareholders at the time. As the stock rallied, the value of his Tesla holdings climbed to more than US$7 billion by October 2021. In 2024, KoGuan said he was cutting his Tesla stake and buying three-month US Treasury bills. He said in a post on X that he still planned to hold Tesla for the long term but feared a stock market crash on the scale of 1929, which was the catalyst for the Great Depression. In March 2026, the 71-year-old said he was “still mostly in Tesla” and Treasury bills. He had grown more critical of Tesla and its CEO, Elon Musk, including over a pay package that could be worth up to US$1 trillion. He declined to say how much of his Tesla stake he had sold. On March 3, KoGuan said he bought one million Nvidia shares.

events.title: Ex-Barclays CEO Bob Diamond on investing in the Gulf and the irrelevancy of Bitcoin
events.summary: The News Speaking from the Bahrain capital Manama, which a few months earlier had been bombarded in Iranian attacks, Bob Diamond, chief executive of private equity firm Atlas Merchant Capital, says he’s still optimistic about the outlook for the Gulf’s future, the US economy, and the prospect to raise more capital to consolidate the banking industry around the world. Panmure Liberum, a UK investment bank he’s invested in, is expanding into the Gulf. Wall Street investors increasingly see the region as a place to invest, not just a place to raise money, and the war isn’t deterring that. “This is a really serious economy,” he said. Diamond has experience in the region spanning decades. His contacts in Abu Dhabi and Qatar helped secure a £11.8 billion bailout for Barclays during the Great Financial Crisis, enabling the bank to avoid a taxpayer-funded rescue. He left Barclays in 2012 in the wake of a scandal around its role in manipulating interbank rates, and has since reinvented himself as a private equity investor, backing bank consolidation deals and fintechs. He is also chairman of the advisory committee of the Export-Import Bank of the US and chairman of Abu Dhabi’s tokenization platform Finstreet. Diamond also said that Bitcoin, the most well-known and biggest digital asset by market capitalization, is “irrelevant” (though useful as a store of value untethered from governments) and that the future of finance is tokenization — an industry is being led by the US as well as the Middle East. Q&A Matthew Martin: You just announced Panmure Liberum, the UK investment bank you own, is expanding into the Gulf — how do you think about the opportunities in the Gulf now, particularly with the conflict that’s still going on? Bob Diamond: I don’t mean to be dismissive of the severity of the situation here for a second, with the invasion of Iran, but when you’re here, as you and I are today, it feels pretty normal. For people who have not spent time in this region, I don’t think there’s a recognition of how developed the economies are, how developed the leadership is. And then I’d say that since we started Atlas Merchant Capital just over 10 years ago, I’ve been as interested in investing Middle Eastern money in other parts of the world as I have been in how we can find ways to help develop business here on the ground. I think there’s just a tremendous opportunity in this region for an on-the-ground advisory and M&A business for middle-market and family-owned businesses, because, as we are seeing here, the entrepreneurial spirit is very, very strong in many of these countries. Financial services here is a great example of an industry where the vast majority of banks are ultimately state-controlled. As governments need to redirect capital to other things in the wake of the war, is there an opportunity for private equity investors to come in and play more of a role in the financial services industry in the Gulf? One hundred percent. But I think you hit on a key issue, which is that traditionally that state control made things more opaque, so you couldn’t get outside investment because it was opaque. And two, it was intrusive and more focused on subsidized business. And you can see why, right? Because as the Middle East was growing, much of the commercial real estate, for example, had to be “if we build it, they will come.” So some of the unbelievable commercial real estate, whether it’s in Abu Dhabi or Dubai or Qatar, or the financial services center that was built in Riyadh, was done really with strategic impetus, if you will, as opposed to pure commercial activity. And I think that’s changing, because a lot of those initial strategic investments have been done. I think it was the same in the early days of the development of Singapore. You could say the same thing, that it was strategic investing, but if you go to Singapore today, it’s a very commercial city. You don’t see commercial buildings being put up. What impact do you see the conflict in the region having on how Wall Street sees the Gulf? I think sometime around 2024, 2025, we hit an inflection point where the Middle East being seen purely as a source of funding for the Western world changed to “this is a really serious economy.” Going forward the Gulf will be focused much more on inward investment, as well as outward investment. I think it probably happened already with Saudi Arabia, and they’ve been a little bit ahead of it. But I think it’s really true across the region. But there are still significant pools of capital in this region — if you just look at the sovereign wealth funds, that’s the best example but not the only example — for investment in good ideas wherever they happen to be. Dubai and Abu Dhabi are both making this big play into fintech and tokenization. How much are you getting involved in that, and what do you see as the chances of centers in the region becoming hubs for this new asset class? I feel very strongly. Bitcoin’s irrelevant. It’s not that Bitcoin isn’t going to go up or down, and I’m not questioning whether Bitcoin’s going to have a significantly higher price or not. I’m personally not an investor, but I have a number of close associates who believe strongly. My point is different. In its best version, Bitcoin is a store of value away from a government, much as gold is. And if it doubles or triples or quadruples in value, it doesn’t have a single strategic implication for financial services. It’s just made somebody money, and it’s a good store of value. Compare and contrast that to stablecoins, basically making payments electronic institutionally for the major currencies around the world. Compare and contrast that to blockchain, which is 24/7, instantaneous settlement, a permanent record of every transaction that happens, everything at the speed of the internet and a fraction of the cost of conventional financial services. That’s the future. That’s the underpinning of financial services going forward: blockchain, and finally tokenization. In the last two to three years, the US has moved very, very aggressively forward in terms of recognizing Circle, USDC, stablecoins, payments. Under Gensler at the SEC, it was just ignored. Nothing was approved. Outside of the US, we’re not seeing the same kind of attitude in London or Europe, but we are seeing it in the Emirates and in the Middle East. Abu Dhabi’s only a few hours’ time difference from London and Europe, and I think it has a real chance to emerge as a more important financial center with the progress of tokenization and the advance of digital. What do you have planned for the future of your digital asset business Hyperliquid Strategies? I’m very, very positive on Hyperliquid. events.title: Africa’s power drive is short of developers, Gridworks CEO says
events.summary: The News Africa has plenty of investors ready to finance much-needed electricity projects, but too few developers with the expertise and early funding to get them off the ground, the head of a UK government-backed power developer told Semafor. More than 40% of sub-Saharan Africans lack electricity, with private investment central to a World Bank and African Development Bank push to connect 300 million across the whole continent by 2030. “People spend a lot of time talking about a lack of capital for infrastructure projects in Africa. There is not a lack of capital,” said Chris Flavin, chief executive of Gridworks, which develops and invests in electricity networks across Africa. The issue for him is that investors generally want to get involved once projects are ready for construction, leaving the four or five years of preparatory work harder to finance. Gridworks, which has electricity projects in countries including Uganda and Mozambique, is set to become the majority shareholder in a planned $300 million power line linking Zambia’s grid to DR Congo’s copper-mining region, under an agreement signed in October. Lenders have shown “very strong interest” in the line, Flavin said. When it develops its own projects, though, Gridworks faces the same hurdles as others despite its UK backing, he added, from permits and environmental approvals to years of planning “before you even get close to the financing.” In DR Congo, for example, commercial banks will not lend at that stage, said Archip Lobo, co-founder of Nuru, a solar mini-grid operator in the country’s east. “They will take the risk on something that exists,” he told Semafor. Instead, Lobo highlighted the existence of state support for early development costs and World Bank Group insurance against political risks. But the World Bank’s own evaluators are less sure capital is plentiful. They found in a recent review that private financing remained too limited to meet Africa’s electrification needs. The narrow pool of investors, such as development lenders’ private arms, government-sponsored funds, foundations, and impact funds “are unlikely to meet the scale of financing needed for electrification growth,” the group said. Industrial advantage Private power projects in Africa are easier to develop when they serve large industrial buyers, such as mines, rather than households and small businesses, Flavin said. A mine with a strong balance sheet and known electricity consumption gives developers a clear customer to design around. For projects aimed at individual customers “the challenge is one of guaranteed demand.” In southeastern DR Congo, CrossBoundary Energy, a Mauritius-based power producer, commissioned a 233-megawatt solar farm with battery storage in August to supply Kamoa-Kakula, a copper complex co-owned by Ivanhoe Mines. “Kamoa’s books are very good,” Auguy Bakome, a project manager at the mine, told Semafor in an earlier interview. He said its expected 40-year operating life and a 15-year contract to buy the electricity helped reassure lenders. Utilities must estimate consumption across tens of thousands of customers. Building networks to serve them is “at the much harder end of the spectrum, full stop,” Flavin said. Moyi Power, a Gridworks-backed utility planned for three cities in northern DR Congo, relies on donor grants for about a quarter of its $190 million first phase and is not expected to deliver electricity before 2029. Notable Africa’s shortage of reliable power is stalling its industrialization , Bloomberg reported, citing World Bank data that put manufacturing at 11% of sub-Saharan Africa’s GDP , half East Asia’s share.

The catch was a remarkable achievement: Starship returned to the same launch tower it had left almost a day earlier, settling into its giant mechanical arms. Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said. The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale. Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day. Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left. Many more development flights remain before SpaceX can deliver its promised fully reusable launch system. NASA's Space Shuttle came close, but the large external tank was expended with every launch, and the orbiters never matched the cadence SpaceX reckons it can achieve with Starship. SpaceX boss Elon Musk admitted that "many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)." Cadence will be key if Starship is going to meet NASA's needs for the Artemis missions. Somewhere between 6 and 22 launches (depending on who you ask) will be required for a lunar mission, and SpaceX has yet to demonstrate in-space propellant transfer between vehicles. Next year's Artemis III mission also calls for docking tests between NASA's Orion spacecraft and a test version of SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System (HLS) in low Earth orbit. The booster fumble shouldn't obscure what the engineering teams achieved. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Councils waving through majority of proposals as government turns on the AI-friendly planning taps US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China now Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric 10 hours ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 13 hours ago Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis 4 days ago US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity 5 days ago Datacenters made up nearly three times as large a share of UK planning applications in the year to September 2026 as they did three years earlier, with councils receiving 59 submissions. The figures come from planning data site Plota, whose Q3 2026 Planning Index draws on applications from every council across the UK. Plota has logged 416 datacenter applications since 2016, though these include extensions and alterations, not just new bit barns. Estimates put Britain's existing fleet at between 477 and 602 facilities. The peak for volume came in the 12 months to March 2021, when 63 campus applications were filed. However, overall planning applications were also higher then, so datacenters accounted for just 1.1 in every 10,000 filed. In the current period they equate to 1.4 in every 10,000. The figures show that applications for building new server halls are about as high as they have been over the past decade, and close to their recent peak as a share of all applications. Even so, the application numbers don't show the dramatic jump that the steady stream of bit barn announcements might suggest. Nor do they tell us how many facilities are actually being built. Applications did bounce around the middle of 2024, when the current government - and its fetish for all things AI - was elected. But it didn't publish the AI Opportunities Action Plan , which recommended "AI Growth Zones" with streamlined planning to speed up datacenter builds, until the start of 2025. Plota links the rise to datacenters being recognized as critical national infrastructure (CNI) in September 2024, and a December 2024 update to the planning framework that told councils to identify suitable sites for them. The facilities are getting larger. One site being built for Equinix near London's M25 motorway will feature three data halls with more than 250 MW capacity, while another planned for Havering in East London could go up to 600 MW. Both were billed as being among Europe's largest campuses. According to Plota, just 3.3 percent of datacenter applications decided between 2016 and 2024 were refused, against 11.3 percent across all applications. The government has also overturned some local council refusals, controversially, as at a site near Abbots Langley in Hertfordshire last year. Slough leads Plota's tally of applications since 2016 with 28, followed by Tower Hamlets in East London with 16, Leeds with 12, and West Northamptonshire with 11. Developers in England can also ask ministers to bring qualifying datacenter projects into the nationally significant infrastructure planning regime , shifting the consent decision from the council to central government. Projects taking that route fall outside Plota's council-based figures. events.title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year
events.summary: Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis. The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs. Renewable energy projects built between 2003 and 2014 are expected to claim £4.5bn in subsidies over the next financial year, on top of £4.2bn in wholesale market revenue. The analysis showed developers will receive almost 50% more than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent gas prices soaring in 2022. The analysis by the Energy Competitiveness Unit (ECU), a non-partisan research and policy project, said the legacy support scheme – which is paid via taxes and energy bills – must be reformed “if we are serious about getting costs of the electricity system down in the short and medium term”. Unlike newer renewable energy projects that earn fixed-price subsidies for their generation, older projects access support via the renewables obligation (RO) scheme, which provides payments on top of what developers earn via the wholesale market, meaning that higher gas market prices lead to higher subsidy costs for renewables. The scheme was credited with kickstarting the UK’s renewable energy industry when it was put in place almost 25 years ago, but the ECU said it “has been allowed to persist unsustainably”. Andrew O’Brien, the ECU director, told the Guardian that the rise in wholesale prices over recent years has meant that many renewable energy developers are earning “well above what they could reasonably have expected” when first taking the decision to invest in the projects. The government announced last year that it would remove three-quarters of the RO scheme’s costs from home energy bills, and move these levies into general taxation from April 2026 to help temper the steep rise in energy bills. The government later warned that legacy generators could face higher windfall taxes unless they give up the existing RO scheme in favour of a new partially fixed subsidy contract as part of its plans to protect bill payers. The ECU believes that the government’s consultation on plans to fix the generators’ wholesale revenues to help to weaken the link between volatile global gas markets and the UK’s electricity costs “falls short”. It argues ministers should go further to fix their subsidy payments and create a new scheme. Since 2013, renewable energy developers have been required to compete in an auction to secure a contract for a fixed price for each megawatt-hour of electricity generated, known as a contract for difference (CfD), which means costs remain fixed regardless of global markets. Under an alternative proposal set out in the ECU’s research, the government could cut electricity costs by £3.8bn next year, and £9.2bn over 10 years, if all generators moved on to an entirely fixed-price contract, which it calls a fair value CfD. The new private law contracts could also offer a degree of legal protection against the political risk that any potential future net zero sceptic government could dismantle renewable energy support through the government’s RO scheme, a threat signalled by the rightwing populist Reform UK party . Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “It is in the interests of everyone – investors, generators, businesses, households and government – to get a credible long-term plan in place that can withstand shocks in this increasingly uncertain world,” the ECU said. In his budget speech last month, the chancellor, John Healey, said : “We will further break the grip of international gas prices on our bills by moving more of our old renewables on to fixed-price contracts.” Tara Singh, the chief executive of RenewableUK, said the renewable energy projects were still helping to keep a lid on bills by “pushing expensive gas off the system”. Singh said: “UCL found wind has saved consumers £100bn since 2010 even allowing for support schemes like the RO by reducing the need for expensive imports.” She added that the government’s windfall tax, which took effect from July, has meant that renewable energy projects using the RO scheme pay the Treasury up to 80p of every additional pound it earns from market prices above £82.61 per megawatt hour. “To put this into context, the average wholesale price of electricity over the last 12 months is over £100 per megawatt hour, and frequently higher than that,” she said. “The fastest way to protect consumers from future price shocks is to build more cheap, homegrown renewable power.”

events.title: Zambia's mining investor seeks to borrow $700M
events.summary: The News Zambia’s majority state-owned mining and energy investor plans to borrow about $700 million by 2028 to expand its business, its CEO told Semafor, as Africa’s second-largest copper producer seeks a bigger share of the wealth from its minerals. The money, which ZCCM Investments Holdings has yet to secure, will help fund a $2.7 billion investment proposal it unveiled on Monday. Over the next decade, the company looks to back new infrastructure including a coal-fired power plant in southern Zambia and to raise its stakes in copper mines , among them a project led by Bill Gates-backed Kobold Metals. “We don’t want to be a quiet minority shareholder,” CEO Kakenenwa Muyangwa said. He added that any changes would be negotiated on commercial terms, and that “investors who share the ambition will find us a committed long-term partner.” ZCCM-IH holds stakes in mines run by other companies and earns much of its income from their dividends, which depend on what is left after the mines pay their costs and debts. “For a country that owns a share of its mines, that is not good enough,” Muyangwa said. The company now aims to earn more from royalties, a share of a mine’s sales that is paid regardless of profit. Its only such arrangement, with Canadian miner First Quantum’s Kansanshi mine, will bring in more than $990 million over the next decade, the company forecasts. ZCCM-IH aims to add at least one more later this decade. The investment company said it now owes $5 for every $100 of its own capital, down from about $66 in 2021. Muyangwa said a cleaner balance sheet had put ZCCM-IH in a strong position to fund its expansion. Trading ambitions ZCCM-IH also plans to negotiate with its mining partners to get a share of the copper produced at each mine, which it would then sell directly. That would give the company “a trading income on top of its investment income” and build “the skills to market Zambian metal from Zambia,” Muyangwa said. The plan comes as state-backed companies across Africa’s copper belt seek a more influential role over the trade of the metal. In neighboring DR Congo, state miner Gécamines sells copper through a venture with Swiss trader Mercuria. Zambia’s state-owned Industrial Development Corporation also has a trading venture with Mercuria, which last month named ZCCM-IH as a regional partner. The goal is greater control over the money countries earn from their minerals, Ekpen Omonbude, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, told Semafor. As demand for critical minerals grows, governments are looking to take a more active role in their sale, an approach he said is more common in oil and gas than in mining. Notable Zambia’s copper output rose just 1.5% in the first nine months of the year , far short of what it needs to meet its goal of 3 million tons a year by 2031.

events.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. “We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.” Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.” “If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.” The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada. Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs. The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market. Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant. Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained. events.title: Dar Global launches $267m project in Jeddah amid Saudi expansion push
events.summary: London-listed real estate developer Dar Global is launching a new mixed-use development in Jeddah , with an estimated value of about 1 billion Saudi riyals ($267 million) as part of its expansion plans in the kingdom. The project will be developed on a plot of land acquired for $56 million and forms part of Dar Global's programme to expand its Saudi Arabia portfolio by up to 4 billion riyals, the company said on Monday. On completion of the programme, the company's worldwide development pipeline is expected to reach about $24 billion, it added. A new international luxury brand will be introduced to Jeddah as part of the development, as the company plans to announce more land acquisitions in the kingdom. Dar Global has partnerships with more than 10 brands, including the Trump Organisation, Aston Martin, Automobili Lamborghini, Missoni, Pagani Automobili and W Hotels, among others at its developments. “With buyers from 61 nationalities already investing in our Saudi portfolio, we are witnessing accelerating international confidence in the country's real estate sector,” said Ziad El Chaar, chief executive of Dar Global. “This new development marks another significant milestone in our global expansion strategy.” The Arab world’s largest economy is looking to boost home ownership for Saudi citizens as part of its Vision 2030 programme. It has also opened up the property sector to foreign ownership, a move expected to attract increased demand. However, buyers remained “selective” in the kingdom during the third quarter amid regional uncertainty triggered by Iran war, a recent report by JLL said. In the July to September period, sale transaction volumes in Riyadh fell by about 30 per cent year-on-year to 9,100, while values decreased 51.8 per cent to 8.5 billion riyals. Residential transaction volumes in Jeddah fell by 25.8 per cent on an annual basis to 3,100. Transaction values fell by 5.8 per cent to 3.9 billion riyals, JLL said. With a presence in 14 international cities across nine countries, Dar Global’s portfolio of 4,200 units completed or under construction, spans the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, the UK, Spain and Greece. It is building three residential projects in Saudi Arabia in partnership with the Trump Organisation, including a $1 billion Trump Tower in Jeddah and a Trump-branded ​luxury project in Wadi Safar in the capital. Dar Global and the US President are also in partnership for the development of a $1 billion Trump Tower on Dubai 's Sheikh Zayed Road. Other international developers, including UAE-based Arada, are also expanding to Saudi Arabia. Last month, Arada unveiled a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh, with plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years. Up to 3,500 villas and townhouses will be built in Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a 2.5 million-square-metre plot.

events.title: Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia
events.summary: Elon Musk and a bunch of Silicon Valley heavyweights want Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, and they've decided an online petition is the way to make it happen. An open letter addressed to Nvidia's board had attracted more than 173,000 signatures at the time of writing, just four days after Huang's departure following revelations about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The campaign, launched under the banner "Stand with Jensen," calls on Nvidia to reinstate its co-founder and former CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, give him a chance to respond to the allegations, and publicly explain why he was forced out. "For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," the letter reads. "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes. "Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took. This company is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now." Among the supporters are Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator boss Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. More than 8,000 signatories also identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to roughly a fifth of its workforce. However, how many of those signatures are genuine is anyone's guess. The site doesn't verify names or employers, so there's nothing stopping someone from signing as Musk, Huang, or Nvidia's entire board if they fancy it. The campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12 , ending his 33-year reign at the GPU giant he co-founded in 1993. His departure came after reports of an affair with Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, and a separate alleged relationship with an Nvidia employee. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been handed the unenviable job of running the company while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Huang's departure has left the chipmaker facing something of an identity crisis , with rivals undoubtedly watching the chaos with interest. Huang himself may not be ready to hang up his leather jacket. According to the Financial Times , the former CEO has discussed a possible comeback with associates, while an ally is reportedly assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. The effort could even involve seeking support from the White House, although Washington appears rather less enthusiastic about the prospect. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shake-up" and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also wants answers about whether Nvidia knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach China in breach of US export restrictions. None of that seems to have put off Huang's supporters. "He has erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company," Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick said. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, giving investors their first major opportunity to grill management about the leadership crisis. Whether the board will be swayed by a petition full of unverified names is another matter. Running one of the world's most valuable companies is, after all, not supposed to be a popularity contest. ®

events.title: SIA logs 3.5% rise in October passenger traffic; sees ‘healthy’ demand for semiconductor shipments
events.summary: SIA and its budget arm Scoot carried 3.7 million passengers during the month, up 4.5% from a year ago, the group said in a bourse filing. SIA reported a 3.5% rise in October passenger traffic, with 3.7 million travellers and an 87.8% passenger load factor, showing resilient demand for air travel. Scoot kept strong momentum, with a 91.6% load factor for its fourth straight month above 90%, while both airlines added new services to Madrid and Guiyang. Cargo traffic rose 10.1% as demand stayed healthy, especially for semiconductor and cloud-computing shipments, lifting cargo load factor to 59.1% despite slightly lower capacity. SINGAPORE – Singapore Airlines on Nov 16 reported a 3.5% rise in passenger traffic in October from the year-ago period amid “resilient” demand for air travel. The group’s October passenger capacity concurrently rose 2.9%, while the passenger load factor (PLF) – the percentage of available seating capacity occupied by passengers – was up 0.5 percentage point at 87.8%. SIA recorded a monthly PLF of 86.8%, thanks to “robust growth” across all regions, including East Asia, Europe and the South-west Pacific, where “traffic marginally trailed capacity increase”. Scoot’s PLF stood at 91.6%, making October its fourth consecutive month with a PLF exceeding 90%. Both airlines had launched new services during the month: SIA to Madrid in Spain, and Scoot to Guiyang in mainland China. Cargo loads rose 10.1% in October amid “healthy, broad-based demand across all verticals, particularly for semiconductor and cloud-computing shipments across the Pacific”, SIA said. Cargo capacity for the month was lower by 0.4%, translating to a rise in cargo load factor of 5.6 percentage points to 59.1%. The group’s passenger network as at end-October covers 138 destinations in 35 countries and territories; SIA serves 79 destinations, while Scoot serves 85 destinations. The cargo network comprises 141 destinations in 36 countries and territories.

events.title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix
events.summary: Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email. According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued. It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored. The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues. At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in. It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over. "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons." Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action. By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled. However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation – an update that reverted the defective change." At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update. A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control? The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®

events.title: Americans relying on heating oil brace for harsh winter: ‘We’re often cold in our own home’
events.summary: Surge in prices is forcing many to cut back on spending, with a projected 21% increase in costs of those households Millions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil. The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases. About 3% of US households rely on heating oil as their primary heat source. In the winter of 2023-2024, 4.79m US households used heating oil as their primary heat source, 82% of which were households in the north-east. A recent report from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association found that overall, heating costs are expected to climb over 7% nationwide, with average heating bills rising 16.9% in the north-east. Residents in Maine , where the temperatures can reach below 0F in many parts of the state, said they are bracing themselves for a pricey winter. “My home heating oil costs have doubled this year,” said Heidi Unruh, 61, of Kittery, Maine, where the winter chill comes in December and lasts through the end of March. “They were already impossibly high in Maine before Trump took office, and I will feel serious pain as the Maine weather dives to it’s typical winter chill” It costs more than $1,500 to fill her 250-gallon tank at home, which has to be refilled every 47 days when the temperatures are low. The increase in costs has forced her to try to cut back on other expenses. “Between oil prices, tariffs, and rising food and energy prices, it will be an especially difficult winter,” Unruh said. “Mainers everywhere will struggle along with me. To compensate, I grew a lot of my own food this year. I have cut back on unnecessary expenses, and am trying overall to need less.” Nikki Papadopoulos, who lives in Piscataquis, a county in the central part of the state, said that her family has started to use a wood stove because the cost of propane has also been high. They have also cut back on hot water, trying to use cold water to wash dishes, as the water heater also uses oil. “We keep our thermostat turned down to the absolute lowest setting available, and honestly, we’re often cold in our own home. We’re wearing layers, sweaters and jackets indoors just to stay warm,” Papadopoulos said. “We’ve cut out pretty much all unnecessary spending. We’re down to the bare essentials.” Though her husband recently received a pay increase, it’s been nearly eaten up by the higher cost of heating. “We’re essentially making compromises in our everyday routines just to stretch what’s in the tank,” she added. “We’re taking the hit from every direction.” Around 50% of households in Maine relied on heating oil in 2024, a reliance that has declined in recent years, though Maine still has the highest proportion of homes using heating oil in the US. “It’s a necessity. For people in colder regions of America, they need it, it’s what they keep themselves warm with,” said Justin Barnes, a fuel delivery driver in the Bangor, Maine region, who has had to give residents bills that have been much higher compared with recent years. “It seems like these politicians ain’t doing a lick to lower the prices or make our lives easier, which is their responsibility.” Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger and former state senator, won his election against longtime Republican senator Susan Collins in the recent midterm elections, where Republicans across the country lost their races in what was largely seen as a repudiation against the rising cost of living. Much of it has been driven by the war in Iran, where the closure of a key oil trading route has led to a prolonged spike in energy prices. Gas prices at the pump have risen over 30% compared with last year. Other oil products, such as diesel and heating oil, have gone up even higher. Recent data showed that heating oil saw a 74.2% increase from September 2025 to September 2026, costing over $6 a gallon on average. Russia’s export ban on diesel, which is similar to heating oil, amid the country’s war with Ukraine has also affected energy prices, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. In 2025, Russia exported 10% of internationally traded diesel. The Trump administration has attempted to strike a deal with Russia to export some diesel to the US, but the effort has failed so far. Bob Carpenter, an electrician in Greenville, Rhode Island, relies on heating oil to heat his home and has had to save up, bracing for the price hikes to refill his home’s oil tank. When his heating oil was delivered last month, it was $1,425 for roughly 240 gallons – about $600 more than he paid in previous years. The higher cost of heating oil comes atop other bills that have gotten more expensive, including electricity bills. “Two years ago, I thought $250 was expensive.

events.title: Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement
events.summary: In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis. In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work. In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling. What You Will Learn: How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects Register now for this free webinar!

events.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
events.summary: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success.

events.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
events.summary: President Donald Trump announces tariffs at the White House in April 2025. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.  Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:  Its own leaders.  The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies. Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies. Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.   “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.” The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.  Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries. “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.” Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.  That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.  The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year. The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president , asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”  Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event. Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.  “The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference . “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.” “I got a feeling the American people won’t see” the refund money. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs. Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx , have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products.
