events.title: ASEAN to remain supply chain priority for US firms even as Trump’s tariffs face pushback
events.summary: US goods imports from ASEAN increased from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion (S$583.8 billion) in 2025. US firms are keeping ASEAN, especially Singapore, as a key supply chain base. They are diversifying away from China to reduce tariff, geopolitical and disruption risks. US imports from ASEAN rose from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion in 2025, up about 144%, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. Experts say tariff fights may continue, but companies are still strengthening traceability, audits and origin records. Smaller firms may return to China if South-east Asia loses its tariff advantage. SINGAPORE – The fate of US President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs may remain in limb o for the next two years after his party lost the majority in both houses of Congress, but American manufacturers reliant on Asian imports are not waiting for a resolution. Instead, they are busy bolstering supply chains painstakingly built over recent years to avoid getting blindsided by disruptions from protectionist measures or geopolitical tensions. And as US manufacturers seek to move sourcing of industrial components and supplies to more reliable, trustworthy and quality-conscious exporters, they are increasingly ending up in South-east Asia, including Singapore. US goods imports from ASEAN increased from US$185.8 billion in 2018 to US$453.6 billion (S$583.8 billion) in 2025, representing an increase of about 144%, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. When the US-China trade war started in earnest around 2018, large corporations and multinational companies pivoted from a just-in-time strategy to supply-chain resilience. A couple of years later, Covid-19 pandemic disruptions intensified the trend. In more recent years, however, smaller and mid-sized US manufacturers have turned to the just-in-case strategy, as trade disruptions turned into chaos amid Trump’s new and harsher tariffs, geopolitical conflicts and unending uncertainty over costs and pricing power. “Our clients aren’t unwinding diversification,” said Joseph Jurken, founder and managing director of US supply chain management firm The ABC Group. “They’re making it origin-defensible” to withstand US Customs scrutiny on tariff avoidance. US consultant Baker McKenzie believes the Democratic Party will use its congressional majority to try to undo certain tariffs. However, enacting legislation impervious to a presidential veto will require Republican support. While congressional committees may hold oversight hearings on how tariffs drive up consumer prices, trade enforcement and tariffs targeting unfair trade and China will continue to enjoy bipartisan support, it noted. “A Democratic-led Congress will likely push for tighter technology export restrictions, particularly regarding advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence, alongside broader limits on US investment in China,” Baker McKenzie said in a post-midterm commentary. In an interview with The Straits Times, Jurken said his firm is gradually adding to its offering qualified suppliers across South-east Asia, including Singapore, for clients looking to diversify outside of China. He added that India is becoming an increasingly important ex-China market. The ABC Group is a Milwaukee-based supply chain management firm that runs sourcing, quality control and supplier management in Asia for mid-market US manufacturers. It manages more than US$350 million in supply chain spend across six Asian markets. In the past few years in Singapore alone, ABC has helped insulate the supply chains of several clients from China-specific risks and disruptions in areas such as precision watch movements, complex injection mouldings, food and beverage processing, and high-end LED lighting. Jurken said: “With competition between the US and China intensifying around AI and robotics , markets like Singapore provide advanced manufacturing capabilities along with a way to reduce exposure to geopolitical risk in a single country.” However, for more price-conscious clients looking for low-end manufacturing products, Vietnam, Thailand and India remain in focus, he added. In Malaysia, factories in Johor with links to Singapore are also getting a lot of attention. While Jurken launched ABC only in 2021, he has been in the business of helping American companies navigate Asia for more than three decades. He said that cracks in the decades-old sourcing and supply management models had always been there. Tariffs and other trade distortions from 2018 onwards made them impossible to ignore. “The tariffs helped us broaden our market reach. It was the impetus for American firms to listen to why they should have a China-plus-one initiative,” he added. In fact, even before the US-China trade war began, ABC had started looking for alternative suppliers across South-east Asia.

events.title: Indonesian rupiah falls to record low as Fed bets boost dollar
events.summary: The rupiah dropped as much as 0.4% to 18,271 per US dollar on Nov 16. The Indonesian rupiah hit a record low of 18,271 per US dollar as a stronger dollar and higher Fed rate bets hit the currency. Investor worries grew over President Prabowo Subianto’s policy uncertainty, key policymaker exits, and MSCI’s warning of a possible market downgrade. Bank Indonesia said it will stay in markets to support stability, and it is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged on Nov 18. The Indonesian rupiah fell to a fresh record low, pressured by a stronger dollar amid hawkish US Federal Reserve expectations, lingering worries over domestic political stability and a potential market downgrade. The rupiah dropped as much as 0.4% to 18,271 per US dollar on Nov 16 . The currency has weakened about 9% in 2026 to underperform regional peers. Investors have soured on the nation’s assets in 2026 due to concerns over President Prabowo Subianto’s policy uncertainty, the exits of several key policymakers and MSCI’s warning that it could downgrade Indonesia’s equity market to standalone status. Most recently, the resignation of Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka compounded those worries, while growing bets on Fed interest rate hikes boosted the dollar and further pressured the rupiah. Bank Indonesia (BI) has said that it will remain present in the markets to maintain the rupiah stability. It regularly intervened in the currency’s spot market as well as offshore and onshore non-deliverable forwards. events.title: Qantas strands Christmas Island students on mainland after cancellations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qantas cancellations leave remote island residents stranded on mainland Qantas operates the only air services between Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and the Australian mainland. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) An ongoing series of Qantas cancellations have left residents on Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands outraged. Twenty-five students from Christmas Island are among those stranded by the cancellations. Qantas says delays have been unavoidable for safety reasons. A group of school students are among residents left stranded on the Australian mainland after several weeks of Qantas flight cancellations to the country's most remote inhabited territories. Residents of Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands are reliant on the national carrier for their sole freight and transport link with Western Australia. But the delays have outraged residents of both islands, with some accusing Qantas of neglecting the critical route. A group of 25 Christmas Island students were part of those affected by the most recent disruptions, and have been stranded in Perth for two days. They were participating in a school camp on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, but found themselves diverted 2,700 kilometres away to Perth during the return journey. "Our kids weren't packed to go to the mainland," Christmas Islander Avin McKnight said. His son, Callum, is now staying with a relative. "They had no phones because part of school camp regulations was they weren't able to take their phones," Mr McKnight said. A spokesperson from the Department of Education said Qantas was providing accommodation for students and accompanying staff, while some had opted to stay with family. The students are expected to board a recovery flight home tomorrow. Avin McKnight's son Callum (right) has been stuck in Perth. ( Supplied: Avin McKnight ) Two days of flights to and from Perth were grounded last week due to forecast low-lying cloud, Qantas said. Another landed in Cocos only, skipping its layover in Christmas Island to return to the mainland. In the month prior, about half of flights were delayed or rescheduled for various reasons. A Qantas spokesperson said recent weather had proven a challenge. "The monsoon season is the most challenging time for flying from the mainland to the Indian Ocean Territories," the spokesperson said. "We thank customers for their patience; however, we will always prioritise safety over schedule." It adds to existing tensions between islanders and Qantas, which slashed baggage allowances and increased prices earlier this year. Mr McKnight, a Christmas Island resident of 30 years, said the problem had grown worse since Qantas took over the flights contract from Virgin Australia last year. "Everyone's just really had a real kick in the guts this weekend and it's just not good enough for that airline," he said. Hundreds of islanders gathered on both islands to protest about luggage cuts and price increases in September. ( Supplied: Khaliesha Amin ) Other residents took to social media to voice complaints over lost bookings, accommodation and hire cars. Christmas islander Mark Stein said three consecutive cancellations had forced him to push a specialist medical appointment. "[Qantas] should really remove the spirit of Australia from the side of the plane, because the Australian spirit is to try and give something a crack." Christmas Island relies on twice weekly flights for access to the mainland. ( Supplied: Chris Bray Photography ) Last week, a Productivity Commission interim report counted Christmas and Cocos (Keeling) Islands as two communities most impacted by skyrocketing regional airfares . Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients. It urged the federal government to reform subsidy arrangements like those in place on the Indian Ocean Territories to ensure they provide better value for money. Indian Ocean Territories administrator Farzian Zainal said she was urgently seeking a meeting with Qantas. "Reliable air services are essential for our community and I understand the consequences extend well beyond travel inconvenience," she said. "It is important that the community has confidence in the air services it relies on, and that these concerns are heard and appropriately addressed.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts SA transport executives questioned over T2D alleged bikie link warning SA's Torrens to Darlington road project is currently at the centre of political controversy. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Transport Department officials have defended their probe into a Torrens to Darlington contractor that has since been terminated over a civil court case alleging bikie involvement. The officials say they did not receive information about a car wash firebombing that had earlier been raised with the Transport Minister's office. The opposition has accused the minister's office of not passing on "critical information" to the department, but the government says the allegations put to them were "very broad and non-specific". The public servants leading the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project have defended the checks they conducted on a project contractor that was, five weeks later, suspended due to a court case alleging bikie involvement. The Department for Infrastructure and Transport's checks were prompted by a call from the Transport Minister's chief of staff on September 11 shortly after he met with the lawyer preparing the court claim. The opposition has used a parliamentary committee to question whether "critical information" was left out in that call between the minister's office and the department. But the government says the issues raised by the lawyer were "very broad and non-specific" with "no documents provided", and since then "more has come out" to prompt the government to kick the company off the project. The company, Career Boss Australia, had its contract to supply workers on the South Road upgrade suspended on October 18, after it was revealed in the media to be the subject of a civil claim alleging bikie Jamie Brown and another man had attempted to coerce the transfer of company shares. No criminal charges have been laid in relation to the case, and Brown has told the ABC he "denies ever threatening any shareholders". The Supreme Court claim was lodged on October 12 by businessman Robert Cammarano, who is claiming full ownership of Career Boss Australia. Robert Cammarano outside an Adelaide court. ( ABC News ) Five weeks before the court case was publicised, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, met with Transport Minister Joe Szakacs's chief of staff Daniel Wills and Child Protection Minister Alice Rolls. At the September 11 meeting, according to accounts from both Mr Jelbert and the government, Mr Jelbert raised matters regarding the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project, the Career Boss contract, Jamie Brown, the impending court action and a car wash in Malvern. The car wash, which Mr Cammarano claims to part-own, was destroyed in March after three firebombings. The ABC is not suggesting the destruction of the car wash is linked to any of the parties listed in the civil case, only that it was raised by Mr Jelbert at the September 11 meeting. Straight after the meeting, Mr Wills called Transport Department executive Paula Norman. Ms Norman said Mr Wills asked her to check with the private sector consortium leading the project, the T2D Alliance, whether "Jamie Brown had been a shareholder and whether Career Boss had raised any contractual issues with the T2D Alliance". Paula Norman appeared before a parliamentary committee. ( ABC News ) Ms Norman said Mr Wills did not pass on any mention of firebombings. "The advice that I got was to check for a shareholding related to Jamie Brown who was a bikie … and had any of these allegations or contractual issues been raised directly to the Alliance," she told parliament's budget and finance committee on Monday. Ms Norman said she phoned the general manager of the T2D Alliance, Stephen Shaddock, to investigate these two things and heard back on September 14. "He advised me that Jamie Brown was not a shareholder and, more importantly, that there were no contractual issues raised by Career Boss directly with the Alliance," Ms Norman said. Opposition questions information chain During the hearing, Liberal Party MLC Heidi Girolamo suggested to Ms Norman that Mr Wills and Ms Rolls did not pass on "pretty critical information" about firebombings that "may have changed the way you approached things going forward". Ms Norman replied that she was responsible for checking whether contractual issues with Career Boss Australia had been raised with the Alliance. "Career Boss Australia, if they had those allegations or any issues relating to the contract, should have raised it directly with the Alliance," she said.

events.title: What Is Acoustic Micro Imaging? A Quick Guide To This Inspection Process
events.summary: We all know how important inspection is for advanced packaging. Not only are these processes critical for ensuring higher yield, but they’re also integral for maintaining device reliability. As the industry pushes for smaller features and tighter spacing, even the smallest defects can pose major challenges. For instance, delaminations and air gaps can be detrimental in a market that demands increasingly complex devices. Such defects will lead to electrical or mechanical failures down the road. One technology that’s mitigating these issues is acoustic micro imaging (AMI). AMI is a high-frequency ultrasound technology, and it’s being used by the industry as an inspection method. How AMI works At the core of AMI technology is a transducer, or a device that turns energy from one form to another. It starts with a pulse of electrical energy, then converts it to mechanical energy, or a high-frequency ultrasound wave. Because ultrasound doesn’t travel through air, this allows inspectors to obtain clear images of gaps and delaminations in the device that could otherwise be difficult to see. However, the transducers used for AMI are not all the same. Each transducer handles a specific frequency, and they’re chosen based on the sample that needs to be inspected. By moving the transducer across the sample, the inspector can generate multiple images that can then be analyzed by the AMI software. Through this analysis, the inspector can choose to accept or reject parts based on the number of defects the package is found to have. So, how do these defects typically present themselves? The biggest difference between ideal and defective samples is that some defective samples will have very clear air gaps. However, another common defect is thinning of the attach material on solder pads. When this material is too thin, any stress that would be put on the device could lead to delamination. An uneven solder or thermal interface material (TIM) layer may also indicate a larger problem with the build process. When to use AMI – inspection, destructive testing, and X-rays With the ability to gather so much information without damaging the device, why would anyone choose to perform a destructive test to identify a defect, rather than simply use AMI inspection to check for them? One reason is for R&D purposes. Oftentimes, companies want to ensure that a process is fully developed before integrating it into their production cycle, and a destructive test can confirm proof of concept for AMI. An example of this in action is a standard capacitor inspection. New capacitor companies will often require a destructive test to confirm the presence of voids or delaminations found by the AMI software. Once the destructive proof of concept has been completed, the company can then integrate the software into their inspection process. There are some key differences between AMI and its transmission technology counterpart, which is more comparable to X-ray. Whereas AMI is an ultrasound technology, transmission scanning uses both a sending and receiving transducer positioned above and below the sample. Both transmission technology and X-ray create composite images, unlike AMI, which inspects layer-by-layer. Ultrasound and X-ray are complementary technologies. There are some things AMI can do that X-ray can’t, and vice versa. For certain applications, both technologies may be recommended. For example, composite images are preferable for inspecting spherical objects like ball grid arrays. The challenges and future of AMI Although AMI technology has tangible benefits, keeping up with the industry’s rapid pace is a hurdle that AMI must continually overcome. As applications become more complex, AMI software needs to quickly adapt to changing components. For instance, instead of scanning a single flip chip, AMI software could now be required to inspect multi-die stacks. One way this mounting complexity is being addressed is through machine learning algorithms. For example, some wafers have via patterns that look similar or identical to delamination, and humans have typically been responsible for distinguishing them. However, through advancements in machine learning, AMI software can now identify via patterns and exclude those from the defect count. As machine learning becomes more robust, it will open new doors for inspecting increasingly complicated devices. In addition, customer requirements for higher resolution and better throughput are also driving new developments for AMI software. To meet these rising demands, Nordson Test & Inspection developed its automated SpinSAM tool that can inspect four 300mm wafers at a time. Traditionally, acoustic microscopy systems move the transducer in a raster pattern, which is a small grid made up of individual pixels. This approach allows inspectors to collect data at every XY point, but it also requires decelerating to turn the transducer at the end of each line, thereby reducing throughput. Some acoustic microscopes address the need for better throughput by skipping lines and interpolating data points, or by using multiple transducers and stitching images together – both of which have their own drawbacks. In contrast, SpinSAM spins the wafer to move the transducer and the wafer continuously, allowing inspectors to scan each pixel faster, allowing for better throughput without image stitching distortion. events.title: Are AI Agents The New Semiconductor IP?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI agents could make customized design workflows faster and less expensive to develop. Multi-agent systems introduce new challenges for orchestration, verification, and tool integration. Consumption-based pricing could reshape EDA business models, but trust and proprietary data remain obstacles. AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs. At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge. Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. And they can do all of this much faster than a human, even though an experienced engineering team is needed to verify those results and recommendations. “We have in-house specialized AI agents to do different things, to do spec analysis, RTL generation for design, for formal and functional verification, and then CDC linking, and place-and-route,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents . “We provide our optimized agents to a customer, and sometimes a customer builds their own AI agent. But there are some similarities with the IP business. Sometimes we’re specifically building an agent for one customer for a particular flow, which is similar to what happens in the IP business. What’s different is that we can do it in a very short amount of time. With IP, you need 10 months. Our cycle is much shorter because AI agents are very easy to customize. In some cases we can give solutions to the customer the same day.” Those solutions still need to be verified and debugged. But the ability to sort through many different options quickly is an attractive formula, especially with rapid evolution of AI. “I draw parallels to the early 2000s gigahertz wars, where all of a sudden everything was multicore,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus . “Now we’ve gone from,’ Everything is going to be a GPU,’ to ‘Oh, no, it’s CPUs and GPUs, and this is a one-to-one ratio.’ So effectively we’re going through the same architectural churn that we go through every 10 to 15 years.” The business of agents Business models still need to solidify around agents. but they also need to be flexible enough to evolve at the same pace as the technology. “If you look at how the EDA industry has evolved, we’re not selling perpetual licenses anymore,” said Rob Knoth, senior group director of Strategy & New Ventures at Cadence . “We moved to time-based licenses many years ago. Now we see similar things as agents roll around. They’re hitting up the tool usage even more because they want to find answers quickly, and they’re trying lots of experiments. So putting together more of a consumption-based model is really good because customers know how to use that.” This isn’t a simple transition, though. While the promise of agents is significant, their adoption in chip design will take time. In addition, security and permissions aren’t always well-defined. “There are some things where you’d really rather sell an agent than sell the software,” said Wally Rhines, CEO of Silvaco . “People are trying to figure out if anybody in EDA is actually pricing based upon tokens rather than traditional pricing models. It doesn’t seem like anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it. I’m very much open to selling an agent that will automate [manufacturing equipment] calibration, then jump back to my store of synthetic simulated data against the physical data. We don’t get to see the physical data, but we do know how many tokens our agents consumed. It’s a way that EDA can sell a product, get the benefit, and no one ever sees the underlying data that companies want to keep proprietary.” Divide and conquer, but with caveats One of the big changes with the shift from generative AI to agentic AI is the need for orchestration, and this has broad business implications. Orchestration is basically a blueprint that defines how tasks are assigned, how agents access tools and data, and how that work is coordinated. But it’s especially challenging if multiple agents execute at the same time and their actions overlap. “What’s different about traditional AI and agentic AI is the coordination of multiple agents that are working in parallel, but doing different types of work,” said Robbie Williamson, vice president of customer engineering for cloud AI at Arm . “It’s not like there’s a unique workload that we haven’t seen before. It’s more about how do you coordinate all of these at the CPU level, and have enough bandwidth, memory, etc., to do all of this at scale. Instead of an individual making a request and driving AI, we have computers that can do it much faster. The transition that we see when we talk to hyperscalers is now about what they need from the CPU. With training, that wasn’t as important because you’re just batching the job and waiting for it to come back.” That creates a new hierarchy in the design flow. “What has happened with this multi-agent workflow is that, in an organization, you’re trying to design a chip,” said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at Synopsys . “When they’re having a problem with the PPA, some engineers say they know exactly what changes to make to lower the power. They’ll do clock gating. But when you clock gate power, then it changes something else. It increases the area. So some area will come in — and this is exactly what happens in the real world with coordination when multiple people come together to design a system. The human manager is coordinating the activities of the human agents in the world of a multi-agent framework. We have agents for EDA tools and agents for the CAE (computer-aided engineering) tools. We have simulation with three core solvers — CFD (computational fluid dynamics), HFSS (high-frequency structure simulation) for the electromagnetics, and mechanical for the structural part. In the EDA world, we have things for the implementation, and things for sign-off. Each of these tools has sub-areas, and we have agents to do these things. events.title: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management and Emaar team up for Dh8 billion projects
events.summary: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management is teaming up with Emaar Hospitality to launch five property projects worth Dh8 billion ($2.17 billion) in Abu Dhabi amid continued demand for property in the emirate. The first project, consisting of 452 apartment units and some penthouses, will be built on Al Maryah Island , according to its group chief executive. Timelines and locations of other projects were not disclosed. The five projects will be built in an area spanning 4.7 million square feet, with Al Maryah Island project to be built in one million square feet. The starting price for a one-bedroom home will be Dh3.7 million and “sales will begin very soon,” Rabih Karam told The National. “It’s a standalone project in one of the most strategic areas of Al Maryah Island, directly connected to the mall, ADGM and Cleveland Clinic,” he said. The launch of the new projects comes as demand for property remains strong in the emirate, despite Iran-war-driven uncertainty. A total of 38,483 property transactions worth Dh171.26 billion were registered in Abu Dhabi in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 76.1 per cent increase in value and a 32.8 per cent rise in volume on an annual basis, according to data from the Abu Dhabi Real Estate Centre. A growing number of companies are setting up their base at the ADGM, boosting demand for property in and around the international financial centre, including Reem Island. Reem Island recorded the highest transaction value at Dh29.86 billion during the period, followed by Al Hudayriyat Island (Dh28.62 billion), Al Saadiyat Island (Dh18.69 billion), Yas Island (Dh13.4 billion) and Zayed City (Dh5.36 billion), ADREC data shows. Assets under management at ADGM grew 54 per cent annually in the first six months of 2026, with 49,027 professionals now based at Al Maryah Island and Reem Island, an increase of 34 per cent on the same period last year. “Demand has been amazing in Abu Dhabi. We are witnessing it in our other projects that we are selling currently," Mr Karam said. The company sold two mansions for Dh350 million each in one of its developments on Saadiyat Island this summer, he added. He, however, did not say who bought these villas, but he said, “these are profile of people that they can choose to be any place in the world, and they are choosing to be in UAE and in Abu Dhabi”. The privately owned company is chaired by Sheikh Hamdan bin Zayed. The latest partnership with Emaar follows the launch of Address Beach Resort and Residences in Dubai in JBR by the two companies in 2016, Mr Karam said. The collaboration has since expanded with the launch of Vida Residences Saadiyat Island, which introduced the Vida brand to Abu Dhabi for the first time. The company did not disclose how it planned to fund the new developments. Emaar is looking forward to introducing more of its hospitality brands to Abu Dhabi, Mohamed Alabbar, founder and managing director of Emaar, said in a statement on Monday.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Small regional Victorian town fights back against proposed AI data centre Dozens of people travelled from the Ballarat region to protest the proposal of a data centre in Miners Rest. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Thousands of Victorians protested against data centres on Saturday including dozens from the small town of Miners Rest. Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people and is the proposed location for a data centre to be constructed by Resi Ventures. Protesters are calling for a statewide moratorium on the construction of AI data centres. The small regional town of Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people. Locals say their quiet country life might be about to change after developer Resi Ventures announced to the Australian Stock Exchange in June its intention to build an AI data centre at the town's old quarry. Volunteer firefighter and First Nations man Jedd Willis said the proposal on a 67 hectare plot of land in his town had been overwhelming. "There been a complete lack of care for country which disturbs me as a First Nations person," Mr Willis said. "[The site] has a very valuable resource for water and for firefighting." Jedd Willis (left) says he often uses water from the proposed site to fill firefighting tankers. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Mr Willis, who is a CFA volunteer, said firefighters would often use the water at the proposed site for fighting bushfires. "Along that, the concerns around the lack of water availability across the state as a whole, let alone just this region and with the upcoming fire season being forecasted to be quite treacherous is concerning." On Saturday, dozens of Miners Rest locals joined thousands from across the state at the steps of the state library in Melbourne to protest against the rise of AI data centres in Victoria. As of September this year, there were 50 data centres operating across Victoria with another 18 in the pipeline. Protesters called for a statewide moratorium on their construction. Chris Phillips says the data centre proposed for Miners Rest could be up to 350 metres long. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Secretary for the No Data Centre Miners Rest group, Chris Phillips said the developer had not been open about its plans. He said locals learned about this proposal through the media, rather than consultation with the community. "The benefit to the community would be very little." Mr Phillips said one of his concerns was whether the company would be making use of an aquifer at the site. "There's an aquifer [at the site] that goes many hundreds of kilometres underground and people draw water out of that to grow food like, potato farmers," he said. 'Nervously watching' upcoming election Miners Rest locals say they are concerned about the light and noise pollution the proposed data centre may emit. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) Mr Phillips said locals were also concerned about the noise pollution that could come from the centre. "It's going to have a noise transmission of 63 to 65 decibels, which will be heard up to 1 kilometre away, over a constant 24 hours," he said. He said he would be anxiously watching the upcoming election and hoped politicians were listening to the local community. "I think if [politicians] don't listen to people they're going to get a very, very rude shock come this election," he said. "We are very nervously watching and we've had commitments from various political parties but we are also very nervous as to what could happen once the party is elected we could be steam rolled." Locals say there has been no consultation from the developer regarding the proposed data centre. ( Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram ) In a statement Ripon MP, Martha Haylett said Miners Rest families deserved to be consulted before decisions were made that could fundamentally change their local area. "There has been no planning approval, no permits issued, and no meaningful consultation with the community," Ms Haylett said. "A project of this scale and significance cannot be imposed on a community without proper scrutiny, transparency, and engagement." The City of Ballarat said in a statement it had not received any planning applications for the proposal. "While Council officers have had early conversations with the developer, no formal applications have been lodged," it said. "All planning applications are subject to a thorough assessment process." The ABC has contacted Resi Ventures for comment.

events.title: AIX investors urged to register claims before creditors' meeting in December
events.summary: Investors in AIX Investment Group's liquidated unit have been urged to register their claims by December 4, as its liquidators plan to hold the first creditors' meeting four days later. AIX Secure SPV, the Cayman-registered issuer of fixed-income notes linked to Dubai-based AIX Investment Group, was placed into liquidation on October 30 by the Grand Court of the Cayman Islands. The court appointed Angela Barkhouse of Kroll (Cayman) and Michael Byrne of Kroll Middle East Consultancy in the Dubai International Financial Centre as joint official liquidators. Claims must be filed online through the liquidation website, said law firm ALBM Excello Law, whose clients were among the creditors who supported the winding-up petition, in a statement on Monday. The firm is helping AIX investors file claims, appoint proxies and put forward members for the liquidation committee. “Many AIX investors are based in the UAE, and the liquidators have been authorised by the Cayman Islands Court to pursue proceedings before the DIFC Courts and the Dubai courts,” said Sujith Mathew, partner at ALBM Excello Law. “We will continue to monitor developments and keep investors informed as the liquidation progresses.” What went wrong AIX Secure SPV, which was registered in the Cayman Islands on December 9, 2022, was established to issue debt notes to raise funds for investment activities, either directly or through affiliated entities. However, investors alleged that AIX Secure SPV failed to make interest payments when due and filed claims against them. According to the Financial Times , investors have filed claims seeking to recover about $10 million, including two individual claims for almost $2 million and $8 million. The company reportedly suspended payments to thousands of investors after promising annual returns of up to 30 per cent. AIX on its website said that “a period of exceptional geopolitical uncertainty and significant volatility across global financial markets has affected valuations and investment realisation cycles within a limited part of AIX’s product offering”. Last month, the UAE's Capital Market Authority said it was reviewing AIX Financial Consultations' activities after receiving information that the company had delayed or even missed payouts. Without disclosing the details of the information it received or the nature of the review, the CMA said it would keep the matter confidential to ensure a thorough, fair and impartial assessment. Following the Cayman Islands ruling, AIX said it had written to its investors directly, explaining why it was proposing a restructuring rather than a forced sale of assets in the current market conditions. “AIX intends to apply to the court for a stay of the order within the period permitted, and will ask the court to consider in full the alternative to liquidation presented to investors in October,” it said on November 4. Steps for investors The liquidators have “determined that AIX Secure SPV should be treated as insolvent, so the liquidation committee must have between three and five creditors”, the latest statement said. While late claims will still be accepted, those creditors may be shut out of the meeting. “A claim admitted for voting is not yet admitted for payment; the liquidators will assess claims for distribution later,” it added. The liquidators have also asked investors not to visit their offices. According to the letter to creditors, nominations for the liquidation committee close on November 26. Submission of claim information for voting, notice of attendance and proxy forms are due by December 4. The creditors’ meeting will be held virtually on December 8. The committee will advise the liquidators on strategy and approve the basis of their fees.

events.title: Techie rigged off-spec fan near flammable liquid and an exposed motherboard, then left it to run for days
events.summary: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®

events.title: Labour hire syndicates have 'little fear of consequence', watchdog says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NSW anti-slavery commissioner criticises policing of labour hire syndicates exploiting migrants Topic: Business and Industry Regulation The Coffs Coast in NSW is Australia's largest blueberry-growing region. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor ) The NSW anti-slavery commissioner has released a report into labour hire firms, alleging a slew of illegal practices including extortion, blackmail and more. The report comes only a week after the government responded to 31 recommendations made by the Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery, which recommended urgent reform to the industry. James Cockayne has referred multiple allegations to NSW Police and the AFP. The New South Wales anti-slavery commissioner says he has seen no sign of proactive, intelligence-led policing of labour hire syndicates accused of exploiting migrant workers in regional NSW. James Cockayne made the comments in his formal response to a parliamentary inquiry into the modern slavery risks faced by temporary migrant workers, which handed down its final report in August. His response, tabled in parliament today, includes allegations that labour hire syndicates in the Riverina and on the Mid North Coast have underpaid workers and been involved in identity theft, money laundering and tax fraud. These cases have been referred to state and federal police. In a statement, NSW Police directed the ABC to the Australian Federal Police, which has also been contacted for comment. Dr Cockayne said the state government was not doing enough to combat issues in the labour hire industry, which supplied migrant workers to farms across the state. "For years, we pretended not to see the elephant in the room. The Committee changed that. Now the task is to move that elephant out of our homes and communities, and out of our supply -chains," Dr Cockayne said in a statement. James Cockayne has released a report on modern slavery. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) Dr Cockayne said multiple sources told him workers were moved off farms just before surprise inspections. He also reported unverified allegations that some had been moved out of the region involuntarily, for weeks or longer. The report said policing remained reactive, with fewer than 10 per cent of trafficking and modern slavery reports to the AFP reaching prosecution, according to Australian Institute of Criminology figures cited in the report. Only about 1 to 4 per cent end in a trial, guilty plea or conviction. The labour hire industry has been under intense scrutiny from advocates and government agencies for many months. In August, a Four Corners investigation highlighted how migrant workers had been exploited by labour hire firms , with some fruit pickers saying they were treated like "animals". During the same week, the NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery released its final report , detailing "harrowing stories of mistreatment" faced by workers and making 31 recommendations to the government. The report highlighted exploitation in the Coffs Harbour and Nambucca Valley regions on the Mid North Coast, asking for an investigation into allegations of systemic labour exploitation. In its response on November 9, the state government said it was working with state and federal agencies on a range of measures and had improved information sharing. Meanwhile, agencies have worked together to carry out surprise inspections on farms, while unions and migrant support groups ramped up their presence in affected regions. Migrant workers have seen increased assistance and resources from support organisations in recent months. ( ABC News: Lucy Cooper ) Dr Cockayne recommended police step up proactive investigations into labour hire syndicates and publish their national protocol for combating human trafficking and slavery. He also called for a plan to move high-risk industries away from exploitative labour hire, including support for worker-run cooperatives. He said major buyers need to do due diligence on supply chains to ensure they were not contributing to modern slavery. "Until licensing is in place, responsibility falls squarely on business," Dr Cockayne said. "The biggest players in these supply chains have the most weight with which to leverage the system. "They can afford to use it — and probably should, given big business may soon face criminal penalties for failure to prevent modern slavery in its supply chain. "This is not only about doing the right thing. Responsible businesses are being undercut by operators who cheat workers and dodge tax. Acting now protects workers, and fair competition too.

events.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
events.summary: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter. Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case. It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura. The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact. Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field Published 10 hours ago Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 21 October Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers. "It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security. "It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear." Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain". She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. "Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities." Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea". She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades". Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial? Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand. The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy. The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field. Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners. This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw. He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade". A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made. Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism". He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now." Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify". The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

events.title: India feels less threatened by AI than the US, official says
events.summary: Indians see AI as less of a threat than people in the US because fewer workers hold the “cognitive and office-oriented jobs” that the technology could replace, one of the country’s top tech officials said. Young Indians are drawn to technology and see AI as a way to raise productivity, reduce poverty, and help India become a developed country within two decades, S Krishnan, secretary of India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The gains, he predicts, could touch sectors such as agriculture, education, healthcare, and government. Krishnan told Semafor Deputy Editor-in-Chief Shelly Banjo that AI tools could help advise farmers with the expertise that’s only available to the largest companies, or screen chest X-rays for tuberculosis to enhance the productivity of the stressed healthcare sector. With around 6 million people in IT and related services, Krishnan said India has the workforce that can diffuse the technology throughout the economy. But the constraint, shared in many countries, is that “AI compute is still in short supply and expensive.” Krishnan said India and the US were “pretty close” to a trade deal, with one or two issues left to resolve. “We’d prefer to have it by yesterday, but, yes, as quickly as we can,” he said. Asked about a potential bilateral visit between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump, which hasn’t happened in Trump’s second term, he said: “Well, I think they still share a very good relationship.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads
events.summary: Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads. Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud. Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for. In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service. In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux. Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads. Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here . Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

events.title: Thrift shop asks shoppers to nominate a charity
events.summary: Julie Rindam (front) and Jeanette Worthington (back) plan to be transparent with donors by having a book in the shop which will evidence where money is going. Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises. Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month. Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years. "The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on." Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes. "All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said. "We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting." Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month. "Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said. The owner hopes that the store will also be a centre for the community. Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed. As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available. Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities. "People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said. "We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time." Janet Smart had been a regular donater to the shop before it was taken over by the new team. Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community. "When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said. "You meet such nice people in here as well." She added that the social side of the shop was equally important. "I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them." Jack Spencer is managing to find clothes and items that he wouldn't be able to find in more mainstream stores. Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items. "It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said. "You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it." For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit. events.title: CNMC Goldmine shares plunge as gold falls below US$4,000
events.summary: SINGAPORE – Shares of CNMC Goldmine Holdings plunged on Nov 16, extending recent losses as gold prices dipped below US$4,000 an ounce following a sell-off in the precious metal. The mainboard-listed mining stock sank nearly 11% to 85 cents at the midday trading break on Nov 16, bringing its losses to about 20.56% over the past five trading sessions and almost 30% over the past month. About 5.5 million shares changed hands during the morning trading session on Nov 16. Spot gold, meanwhile, fell 0.24% to US$3,872 an ounce, as signs that the US Federal Reserve could raise rates weighed on sentiment. This came ahead of remarks by Fed chair Kevin Warsh at a Nov 16 US conference that could offer further clues on the direction of interest rates. Gold has fallen nearly 6% since the start of the year, as elevated US Treasury yields and a stronger greenback dampened demand for the precious metal. Hashim Osman, a research analyst at Phillip Securities Research, attributed CNMC’s share price decline to growing expectations of further US interest rate hikes. This follows stronger-than-expected inflation data last week and consensus among Fed officials that inflation remains too high. “In this environment, the key differentiator among miners is their ability to limit margin erosion as gold prices ease,” he said. Elevated fuel costs remain a concern for investors, particularly for miners investing in exploration and development, he added. CNMC’s net profit rose 17.8% to US$18.6 million (S$23.9 million) for the six months ended June 30, 2026, from US$15.8 million a year earlier. The Singapore-headquartered gold and base metals producer, which operates in Kelantan, Malaysia, generated US$65.2 million in revenue for the first half of 2026, up 23.4% from a year earlier, driven by higher gold, silver and zinc prices. Revenue from gold produced at its flagship Sokor mine’s carbon-in-leach plant rose 32% to US$49.8 million, even as production fell 6% to 11,105 ounces. Including gold produced from lead concentrate at its flotation plant, which is used primarily to recover base metals, the company generated total revenue of US$56.7 million from gold in the first half of 2026, a 27.4% increase from a year earlier. Still, CNMC’s all-in production cost is about US$2,000 per ounce, so margins would still be intact even if gold retreats further.

events.title: 'Break-in and rising costs could kill my business'
events.summary: Gordon Kidd says he is struggling with business-related costs and a recent break-in has not helped The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs. Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about £20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop. Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue. A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates. West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing. "They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation. "That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop." He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business. "I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it." Burglars stole three cycles and a frame and damaged the shop in the raid Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses. "I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said. "We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough." He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever". "A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said. Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded. He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy". "Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general." A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people. "We are also making the business environment work better through our £4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments. events.title: Taiwan deputy minister on Jensen Huang scandal: ‘We feel sad’
events.summary: The scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has sparked a wave of sadness in his native Taiwan, the island’s deputy digital minister said Sunday. Huang had a close relationship with Taiwanese tech companies, meeting with them every year, Isabel Hou said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World. “The relationship is very personal,” she told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. “The supply chain leaders, I think, were concerned about how this kind of trust can be replaced. It will be tough.” Those ties went beyond business: Hou referenced a New York Times article in which Huang’s longtime hairstylist admitted he was too upset to sleep , drank a bottle of red wine, and prayed for the former chip CEO after his resignation. “We feel sad,” she added. The Nvidia ordeal has fueled calls in Washington for tighter chip export controls, given Huang’s years of lobbying to sell chips to China, and the revelation that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials suspect spying for Beijing. US authorities are probing whether Megaspeed, the company the woman formerly led, smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Singapore-based Megaspeed has denied the allegations. US lawmakers from both parties have pushed for tougher export restrictions, and Democrats have opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Taipei has been aligning its export control policy with the US. Hou said Taiwanese don’t want frontier chips going to China, where they could end up in military equipment aimed at the island. Reading a line prepared by her staff, she called for a policy that’s “precise, predictable, and coordinated with partners.” China, once the destination for the vast majority of Taiwan’s outbound investment, now draws less than 1%, Hou said, as companies expand elsewhere, many in the US. In AI especially, Taiwan needs “trusted partners.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: US official says government needs to make a better case for AI
events.summary: The US government has a responsibility to explain AI’s benefits to the public after the midterm elections showed widespread antagonism to the technology, a top State Department official said Sunday. Jacob Helberg, the undersecretary for economic affairs, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World that the election, in which many voters were opposed to AI and data centers, should be seen as an “opportunity.” “The onus really is on everyone serving in government at all levels, local, state, and federal, to do a better job of communicating to the public the opportunity and the upside of this great technology,” Helberg told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. Helberg pointed to data showing that AI has helped prop up the US economy through investment and productivity gains. He said AI hasn’t caused mass job losses, and “we haven’t seen any evidence at all that super intelligence has had an inflationary effect,” using the Trump administration’s preferred alternative term for AI. Competitor obsession Helberg, who has spearheaded the Pax Silica effort with US allies to secure global supply chains for critical industries, also said US global tech policy shouldn’t “obsess” over China. “Great companies don’t try to succeed by obsessing over their competitors,” he said. “One of the temptations in policy roles is you spend so much time studying what competitors do that it almost becomes easy to over-obsess on them.” While Pax Silica is building a bloc of US-allied nations to reduce their dependence on China, Helberg said the effort is intended to be “an America-centric initiative, not a China-centric initiative.” — J.D. events.title: Goldman Sachs predicts ‘sizeable surplus’ for oil market in 2027
events.summary: The Paris-based International Energy Agency said last week the global oil market is set swing to a surplus for the first time since the US-Iran war began. Goldman Sachs says the oil market will face a “sizeable surplus” in 2027, with crude supply minus demand at 2 million barrels a day. It expects Brent to average US$88 a barrel in 2027, then fall to US$78 by year-end as the “risk premium” fades. China’s weak fuel demand may limit prices, and Goldman says its total oil demand likely peaked in 2025. SINGAPORE – The oil market faces a “sizeable surplus” in 2027 that will drag prices lower even as supply risks remain, Goldman Sachs Group said. Crude production minus so-called end-use demand will reach two million barrels a day in 2027, despite accounting for supply disruptions half that size, analysts including Daan Struyven said in a Nov 15 note outlining their base case. Brent futures are expected to average US$88 a barrel in 2027 , easing to US$78 by the year-end “as the risk premium gradually normalises”, they said. The worldwide crude market has been rocked in 2026 by the US-Iran war, which initially choked off regional production before suppliers tapped alternative export routes and restored flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The Paris-based International Energy Agency said last week the global oil market is set to swing to a surplus for the first time since the conflict began. “For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and increasing market adaptation,” they said. “Under our base case, Middle East supply rises above its 2025 average on ongoing adaptation through ship-to-ship transfers and pipeline additions, while supply growth elsewhere stalls.” China – typically the world’s largest crude importer – is unlikely to prop up prices, with “persistent weakness” in road-fuel usage to scar demand by 400,000 barrels a day, according to the Goldman analysts. All in, “we estimate that China’s total oil demand peaked in 2025”, they added. Brent traded below US$95 a barrel on Nov 16 after dropping more than 1%. The benchmark peaked in 2026 above US$126 a barrel in April, hitting the highest intra-day price since 2022. Year to date, it has averaged about US$91. BLOOMBERG

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supermarket group Coles investigates cybersecurity incident but provides little detail Coles advised customers to remain vigilant after disclosing a cybersecurity incident. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) Coles says it is investigating a cybersecurity incident but provided little further detail to customers or investors. The supermarket group is looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect. Coles says it will provide updates on the investigation "as appropriate". Supermarket group Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, but has provided little detail on what occurred. Coles disclosed the cyber attack in a statement to the stock exchange on Monday morning, saying it is currently not aware of any data being accessed or stolen as a result of the incident. "Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," the statement read. On its website, Coles Group listed gift cards as working as normal, "no indication" of an impact on Flybuys accounts and no issues identified with Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery or QuiteLike subscriptions. However, the retailer said it was looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect, which it was investigating. It said it was working with global cybersecurity experts to "contain and secure the Coles IT environment". Coles says no action needed by customers Coles told investors and customers on Monday morning that it was business as usual for its operations. "Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online," the company website said. The supermarket group said customers do not need to take any action at this time but advised caution. Woolworths probes reports of drained digital gift cards Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers. "We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information from you — including by email, phone, text, or post — and potential scam activity," Coles said. "We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reusing the same password across multiple services." It urged similar caution from suppliers. "We apologise for any concern this may cause our customers and key stakeholders at a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world," the company said. In recent weeks, European supermarkets have been hit by IT incidents affecting fridge and freezer temperatures , which were believed to be cyber attacks. Over the weekend, customers of Coles' major rival Woolworths reported digital gift cards being drained by unauthorised transactions . Woolworths told ABC News it was investigating. A number of major Australian corporations have been rocked by cyber attacks and data breaches this year, including Origin Energy . The hacking incident in July left about 900,000 current and former Origin customers' data exposed. Coles said further updates would be provided "as appropriate".

events.title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
events.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy. The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country. The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.” Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations. Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April. “We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another. One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.” The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings. Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others. “We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.” Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom. He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves. Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion . His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry. "While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said.
